The burghers called her the Queen, or goddess, of the strong-thieves, and spoke of her as the heart and soul of their wickedness; they threatened her with an evil day if they could lay hands on her. Roger said she might be foul or very fair, young or old, cruel or kind; and that when she was kindest, her carles were cruellest. The old woman in the Little Plain praised her beauty, but spoke of the power she had over men and of the way other men had loved her. The priest, however, told me that she was a right holy woman: as fair as Venus, yet as chaste as Agnes, as wise as Katherine, and as humble and meek as Dorothy; that she bestowed her goods plentifully to the church, was merciful to poor men, and went barefoot by night to the chapel of St. Anthony. He wept because men and women mis-said her so sorely. I could not know the truth of all these tales; my own heart was troubled by the different things I heard, and I thought that when I saw her I could judge between the good and the evil.
2c25d906dfe34a93.txt.reason: The answer usefully attributes the conflicting accounts to their sources and captures Ralph's uncertainty. However, the supplied excerpt does not include the burghers' description of her as the heart and soul of their wickedness or threat to her, nor does it support the final claim that Ralph thought he could judge the truth when he saw her.

2d05f826105fce2b.txt.question: Why are you a Communist?
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.answer: I am a Communist because I know that the change which I hope for cannot be brought about as long as private property exists. The time may come when the social conscience will be so highly developed that coercion will be impossible, even on the part of the community; but then the community will be composed of men who so thoroughly realize Communism that there will be no chance of any of them attacking his neighbour in any way. All reasonable men, whatever they may call themselves, would rejoice at such a change. I do not consider myself a pessimist because I am driven to admit that such a condition of things is a long way ahead. In the meantime, as long as the individual acts unsocially, he has no right against the society which he himself has cast off.
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.reason: The answer combines Morris’s statements about private property and Communism with his separate description of a future social conscience. The latter is compatible with the excerpt but is not present in this source passage, and the omission of the Dr Wolff anecdote leaves out the original transition to Morris’s interim argument.

2d05f826105fce2b.txt.question: What do you mean by Communism?
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.answer: I use Communist as a more accurate term for Socialism, as implying equality of condition and consequently abolition of private property. In this sense, of course, you could not live Communistically until the present society of capitalism or contract is at an end. Living in small communities is not in theory essential to this great change, though I have little doubt that it would bring about such a way of living and abolish big cities, which I think much to be desired.
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.reason: It directly defines Morris’s use of Communist and preserves the excerpt’s account of equality, private property, capitalism, small communities, and cities in his original language.

2d05f826105fce2b.txt.question: Do you think society can do without coercion?
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.answer: The time may come, and I hope it will, when the social conscience will be so highly developed that coercion will be impossible, even on the part of the community. But then the community will be composed of men who so thoroughly realize Communism that there will be no chance of any of them attacking his neighbour in any way. Until then, the social conscience, which being social is common to every man, will forbid individual interference, and use coercion if other means fail; without that there can be no society. Man without society is not only impossible, but inconceivable.
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.reason: The answer accurately joins both positions in the excerpt: coercion may become unnecessary in a fully Communist society, while the social conscience uses it when other means fail. Its wording remains very close to Morris’s.

2d05f826105fce2b.txt.question: How should a community handle people who interfere with their neighbours?
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.answer: The social conscience, which being social is common to every man, will forbid individual interference, and use coercion if other means fail. Without that there can be no society; and man without society is not only impossible, but inconceivable. As long as the individual acts unsocially, he has no right against the society, which he himself has cast off. I think we should consider it pedantic to allow one man to beat two of us; if an individual acts unsocially, society will put a stop to it.
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.reason: The answer is largely grounded in the excerpt, but its final clause, “society will put a stop to it,” is an added formulation rather than Morris’s wording. It also repeats the conclusion about unsocial conduct after already stating it.

2d05f826105fce2b.txt.question: Do you believe decisions should be made by majority rule?
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.answer: All rule must be majority rule—that is, of the effective majority. If at any time the minority rules, it is because they are better organized, better armed, less stupid, more energetic than the mere nose-counted majority: this effective majority therefore coerces the minority; and as long as it can coerce it, it will. In a community, where differences of opinion remain after all possible arguments have been exhausted, the few would have to give way to the many, I should hope without any rancour. I do not see any divine right in a minority.
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.reason: It answers the question directly, faithfully combines Morris’s discussion of effective majority rule with his bridge-decision conclusion, and retains his distinctive phrasing and qualifications.

2d05f826105fce2b.txt.question: Why do you think some form of collective decision-making is necessary?
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.answer: However much the unit of association may be divided, people will have to associate in administration, and sometimes there will be differences of opinion as to what should be done. A community may discuss the building of a bridge; some say Ay and some No, and persist in that opinion after all possible arguments have been exhausted: what is to be done, and which party is to give way? If a decision must not be carried by a majority, then it must be carried by a minority. I fail to see any divine right in a minority. And if one obstructive could always prevent any business being done, that would establish the most complete minority rule conceivable; perpetual compromise would hinder all reasonable work or progress.
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.reason: Morris’s argument that association requires administration and a way to resolve disagreement is clearly presented, with the bridge example and objections to minority obstruction and perpetual compromise substantially preserved from the excerpt.

2d05f826105fce2b.txt.question: Could people freely associate under the society you live in now?
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.answer: The possibility of free association as things now are is a quite illusory hope, since those of us who are unprivileged are at the beck and call of the privileged. Where all men are equal, I believe ‘the give and take’ would have such influence over men’s minds that the authority of compulsory representative institutions, or whatever took their place, would be so completely at one with the Social Conscience that there would be no dispute about it as to principle. In detail, the few would have to give way to the many, I should hope without any rancour.
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.reason: It directly answers the question about present-day free association and contrasts it with Morris’s view of an equal society. The reordered excerpts remain coherent and closely preserve his wording.

2d05f826105fce2b.txt.question: What would a Communist society mean for cities and the way people live?
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.answer: Living in small communities is not in theory an essential of this great change, though I have little doubt that it would bring about such a way of living and abolish big cities, which I think much to be desired. Communism means equality of condition and consequently abolition of private property; you could not live Communistically until the present society of capitalism or contract is at an end.
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.reason: The response addresses both cities and the conditions for Communism. Its claims and distinctive wording are supported by the excerpt, with only a harmless rearrangement.

2d05f826105fce2b.txt.question: Why do you want fewer political labels and party distinctions?
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.answer: Whatever will give us equality, with whatever drawbacks, will content me, and I find that at bottom this is the ideal of all Socialists. So I think the fewer party-names and distinctions we can have the better, leaving plenty of scope for the inevitable differences between persons of different temperaments, so that various opinions may not make serious quarrels.
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.reason: The answer preserves Morris’s original wording and explains his preference for fewer party distinctions while allowing differences of temperament and opinion. It is concise and relevant.

2d05f826105fce2b.txt.question: What do you think is mistaken about some people’s opposition to Communism?
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.answer: I find that at bottom the ideal of all Socialists is equality, and many who call themselves Communist-Anarchists cannot differentiate themselves from the Communists. Their Anarchism consists in a somewhat exaggerated fear of a possible re-growth of some of the tyrannical methods of the destroyed Society, and a consequent distrust of the new Society, which they have no definite form for. On the other hand, I have met with Anarchists who were not at all vague, and who definitely opposed Communism. They wished to abolish organized monopoly, but supported unorganized monopoly, or the rule of the strongest individual, taking for their motto ‘To each one according to his deeds’. That means the upholding of private property with no association to uphold it, a position impossible and inconceivable.
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.reason: Most of the answer closely follows Morris, but the sentence about the “ideal of all Socialists” is appended from another passage. The phrase “which they have no definite form for” also relies on a correction to an apparent textual error, making it less suitable as unqualified historical wording.

2d05f826105fce2b.txt.question: Do you think majority rule guarantees that the majority is right?
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.answer: The majority is no more likely to be right than the minority, which I admit. But all rule must be majority rule—that is, of the effective majority. If at any time the minority rules, it is because they are better organized, better armed, less stupid, more energetic than the mere nose-counted majority. A toss of a copper would not settle the matter, for there might be a difference of opinion on that method also; and if one obstructive could always prevent any business being done, that would establish the most complete minority rule conceivable.
2d05f826105fce2b.txt.reason: It directly answers that majority rule does not guarantee correctness, then presents Morris’s argument for effective majority rule and against obstruction. The wording closely follows the excerpt.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: What do you mean when you say people should be equal?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: Whatever inequality I admit among people, I claim this equality: that everybody should have full enough food, clothes, and housing, and full enough leisure, pleasure, and education; and that everybody should have a certainty of these necessaries. In this case we should be equal as Socialists use the word. Socialists no more than other people believe that persons are naturally equal: there are amongst men all varieties of disposition, and desires, and degrees of capacity. Nevertheless, these differences and inequalities are very much increased by the circumstances amongst which a man lives and by those that surrounded the lives of his parents; and these circumstances are more or less under the control of society. If we are careful to be prudent and wise for ourselves and just towards other people, those inequalities which are natural can be used for making life pleasanter and more varied; but if we act stupidly and unjustly they become a source of misery to many, and of degradation to all.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The answer closely preserves Morris’s claims and wording from the excerpt, including his distinction between natural differences and the equality Socialists seek. Its combined passages directly address the question.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: What do you consider necessary for everyone to live a fully human life?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: We all need food, clothes, and shelter, and clearly, if we need these things, we need them in sufficiency, and of good quality, or else we have not really got them. But these are our needs as animals only; as men and women we have other needs: however much we may vary, we all of us need leisure and amusement and education of some sort or other, for all men have the power of thinking, and that power may be repressed and may be developed, just as a plant may be starved or made fruitful by the quality of the soil it is planted in and cultivation it has. If a person has not leisure, pleasure, and education, they fall short of human necessaries and there is something wrong somewhere. Everybody should have full enough food, clothes, and housing, and full enough leisure, pleasure, and education; and everybody should have a certainty of these necessaries.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The answer combines Morris’s statements about bodily and human necessities with largely original wording and his plant analogy. The selected material clearly answers what everyone needs.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: Why do you say poverty is not simply a natural condition?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: The very fact that there are rich and poor in the same community proves that the existence of the poor is not caused by natural laws but by artificial arrangements. The poor do certainly labour, and by their labour produce the things on which men live and the luxuries which they enjoy, whereas the rich either do not work at all, or, if they do work, do not produce wealth by their work: therefore the poor by their labour keep the rich: rich men are pensioners of poor ones. Nature bids us to work in order to live, and refuses to yield her treasure to anyone who does not work; it ought to follow that those who work most should have the most, and those who do not work at all should get nothing. Whereas under our present system exactly the contrary is the case: the great landowner, the rich shareholder, men who do not even pretend to do anything, are at the one end of the scale and are most wealthy; the unskilled workman, the field labourer working day-in day-out their lives long, and ending with the workhouse are at the other end of it.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The answer draws directly on Morris’s argument that rich and poor coexist because of artificial arrangements, then contrasts the labourers’ work with the wealth of owners. The excerpt supports its claims and distinctive phrasing.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: How do you explain the way factory owners profit from workers?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: A factory owner employs men in order that he may get a certain advantage from them. A fair bargain would be to let them have what they have produced by means of his factory after a fair deduction for the wear and tear of machinery, the expenses of bringing the goods to market, the risks incidental to manufacture and trade, and due payment for his superintendence, supposing him to be capable of superintendence. That would be a fair bargain, the details of which could be easily arranged among honest and reasonable men, and which would gradually tend to the perfecting of fairness between the associated workers. As a matter of fact, the advantage he proposes to gain is very different: what he does is to pay wages to his men, that is to give them as little as they will take without revolting or striking, and to keep for himself, and make the most of, all that they produce over and above those wages. The law gives him the power to force them to pay him for leave to work if by any means not illegal he has managed to acquire more wealth than he needs for his own use.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The answer preserves Morris’s account of both a fair bargain and the actual wage arrangement, and explains the legal power behind the owner’s profit. Reordering and omission of an aside do not distort the argument.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: What do you mean when you call the rich pensioners of the workers?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: The rich either do not work at all, or, if they do work, do not produce wealth by their work: therefore the poor by their labour keep the rich: rich men are pensioners of poor ones. The landlord or factory-owner lives on a pension, rent, or profit which is not paid voluntarily or consciously by the workers: they are compelled to pay it, and so cunningly that they do not understand the compulsion, though they feel it, and in an unconscious manner struggle against it. The owners of the raw material and instruments of labour have a privilege to compel people to pay for the use of these things, a privilege which is supported by the whole power of the law. Money can buy immunity from labour, but this means nothing more nor less than that the owner of it can force other people to work for him gratis after they have fed, clothed, and housed themselves poorly. Unless a man is well enough off to have at his command land, at least, if not machinery and capital, he cannot work wholly for himself; some part of his time at least he must pay as a poll-tax for leave to work, that is for leave to live.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The core explanation is supported and retains Morris’s language, but the sentence beginning “Money can buy immunity from labour” and the claim that workers work for owners gratis after poorly feeding, clothing, and housing themselves are not present in the supplied excerpt. Remove or verify this material before training.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: Do you think working people are poor because they are lazy?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: That is preposterous nonsense. The greater part of the workers are poor; but is it possible that it can be their faults? Its being their faults would mean that they do not work, that they are idle; but they do all the work that is done at any rate, and they do so much of it that they are not only enabled to live to work but they also have the honour—I won't call it a pleasure—of keeping those who do not work. It is absurd to put down the inequalities of modern Society to the nature or necessity of the case, or to say that the poor themselves are poor through their idleness. We must, I feel sure, come to the conclusion that it is the system under which we live that brings about those terrible inequalities which most thoughtful men lament.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The answer directly adapts Morris’s rebuttal and preserves his wording, reasoning, and conclusion that the social system produces inequality. The question is natural and the response is coherent.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: Why do you believe society's inequalities can be changed?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: Since it is the fault of a system, which has grown up to what it is by the carelessness and thoughtlessness of men, it both can be altered, and it will be, since it is of the very nature of all human systems to change into something else and to change in the direction of men's desires: and men's desires do now, and have for a long time tended towards equality, towards the extinction of classes, in a word towards the general happiness of the whole population. With a little courage, a little forethought, a little wisdom we could make such a different world of it, that we could make all the poor rich, or wealthy rather, without really injuring the rich one iota. That is what Socialists want to do. It can be done, and will be done; but if people delay too long trying to do it, the natural break-up of the system will bring about much misery and probably war and violence before the times get better, which we might avoid by being wise in time and trying ourselves to make the change from the bad old system to the better new come about with the consent of all thoughtful and well-wishing people.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The answer retains the excerpt’s explanation that human-made systems can be altered and its account of the direction Morris believed change should take. The omitted rhetorical material does not impair the response.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: What do you want Socialism to achieve?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: We Socialists want to alter the fact that some men, wishing to live without working, have managed to get into their hands those things which are necessary to the workmen to work with, and thus can compel them to keep them in idleness. We say, with St. Paul, that no one who can work has a right to live unless he works; and we also say that since every ordinary healthy and capable man can produce more than he needs to keep himself, every man who does a fair share of work ought to have a good livelihood. We want all persons to enjoy what they have fairly earned by their labour and what they can fairly use. We fully admit the right of people to use property, we deny their right to abuse it; and we would take from people that part of their property which they cannot use and which they now abuse by wronging other people by means of it. We would use it, and by using it would benefit the very people from whom we had taken it as well as other people. Labour will be free: no man will have to find a master before he sets to work to produce wealth; every man will be able to keep himself by his labour, and the combination of all these workers will supply those things which can only be used by the public.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: This combines several clearly stated Socialist aims in the excerpt: ending property-based compulsion, securing a good livelihood for fair work, limiting property abuse, and freeing labour. Its wording and argument remain strongly Morrisian.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: How would you change who owns factories, land, and other productive resources?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: The factories must cease to be owned by private persons and be owned by the people in general in some way or other. The people would allow the workmen who could use them for producing goods to use them on condition that they paid to the whole people for the wear and tear of their property, that they paid what was necessary to keep it a going concern, and that they dealt fairly in dividing amongst themselves what they earned by their work. This is what is called the Nationalization of the means of production. The land should be owned by no private person but by the people at large, to be used by those who can use it. They would indeed have to pay rent to the people, because if they did not, the man who got hold of a piece of extra-productive land would have an unfair advantage over his neighbour; but this rent would be so apportioned that it would not begin till the cultivator had made a fair living out of the soil. The capital of the country, the stored-up wealth to be used for further production, would also be owned by the people; no one would be allowed to take interest on money in order to live idly without labour. The railways and other means of transit, like all machinery, would be owned by the people to be used by everybody according to his convenience.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The answer faithfully summarizes Morris’s proposals for collective ownership and use of factories, land, capital, and transport. It omits some supporting detail but directly and clearly answers the question.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: Would your idea of Socialism mean simply dividing all wealth equally?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: The Socialists do not want to share up all wealth: they want all persons to enjoy what they have fairly earned by their labour and what they can fairly use. What a man has and can use is his own; but what sense is there in his calling a thing his own which he cannot use? You do not injure a man by taking away from him what he cannot use. If he abuses this property of his, which he cannot use, for doing a wrong to someone else, are you injuring him by taking it away from him then? If you see a man levelling a gun at another man, are you injuring him by taking the gun away from him? Certainly not; you are preventing him from committing a crime. We would take from people that part of their property which they cannot use and which they now abuse by wronging other people by means of it; but we would use it, and by using it would benefit the very people from whom we had taken it as well as other people. We fully admit the right of people to use property, we deny their right to abuse it.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The response directly rejects equal division of all wealth and explains Morris’s distinction between property use and abuse. It preserves the original reasoning and gun illustration; omitting the sugar-plum example is harmless.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: What would work and everyday life be like in the society you want?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: Labour will be free: no man will have to find a master before he sets to work to produce wealth; every man will be able to keep himself by his labour, and the results of their labour will be all their own. Everyone would have to work and everyone would be able to work according to his capacity: there would be no need for overwork, since everyone was working. Workmen would not need to beg to be employed by a master, because they would be able to employ themselves. The people would see that education was the same for everyone according to their capacity, and that the old, the infirm, and all who for natural reasons could not work should be properly taken care of. The people also would undertake great works for public utility and pleasure as they might well do in a country where no labour was wasted. Life and labour would be organized in the least wasteful manner, and the ordinary citizen would learn to understand at least some part of this organization.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The response covers Morris’s vision of free labour, work according to capacity, care, education, public works, and social organization. The slight shifts between “will” and “would” and the pronoun change in “the results of their labour” are minor editorial issues.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: Would your proposed society be run by a powerful central government?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: In my opinion there would be far less centralization than there is at present. A board of officials, a parliament, or any such-like body should not attempt to administer the affairs of people living a long way off, whose conditions and surroundings they cannot thoroughly understand: surely it is always and everywhere good that people should do their own business, and in order that they may do it well, every citizen should have some share of it, and take on his own shoulders some part of the responsibility. In the new Society, we should form bodies like municipalities, county-boards and parishes, and almost all practical public work would be done by these bodies, the members of whom would be working at and living by their ordinary work, and everybody who had any capacity for such work would have to do his share of it. These bodies would have to federate for national or international purposes: but no set of delegates would venture to consider itself the master of the public, it would be its servant rather.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The answer directly addresses centralization and accurately preserves Morris’s preference for local responsibility and federated bodies whose delegates serve the public. The omitted qualifications do not undermine the answer.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: Why do you think people would eventually share more freely in a Socialist society?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: My own belief is that when we are once bound together by ties of honesty and mutual self-respect all this will tend to get simpler and simpler, until our business becomes very easy to transact. We should find that when we ceased to fight with each other for livelihood and to rob each other, all ordinary necessaries and comforts would be so abundant and so cheap that they would be free for everybody to take as he needed. Of course we should pay for them, but in the lump. When a family that is comfortably-off sit down to a leg of mutton, how do they act? Do they bring in a pair of scales and weigh out to each one his share of the victuals? No, that is done in a prison, but not in a family: in a family everybody has what he needs and no one grudges it: Mary has one slice, Jack has two, and Bill has four; but Mary and Jack don't feel wronged, since they have had as much as they wanted. The reason for this is that enough has been provided, and that the members of the family trust one another.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The answer preserves Morris’s stated belief that honesty, mutual respect, abundance, and trust would make sharing straightforward, and retains his family illustration. The response is coherent and relevant to the question.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: What worries you might happen if people delay changing the present system?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: If people delay too long trying to make the change, the natural break-up of the system will bring about much misery and probably war and violence before the times get better: which we might avoid by being wise in time. The old system is tumbling to pieces, and the workers must now come forward and show the way to the new, by claiming to be allowed to work for themselves, and thus form a Society where all will be workers. If they do not do this, consciously and speedily too, there will be a terrible state of things before the new system is born: we now living may yet see people dying by the dozen of starvation in our streets before full shops and crowded warehouses; or people in their agony of necessity breaking through all restraints and sacking such shops and warehouses and destroying everything right and left in mad and ignorant riot. This lesson is what we have to teach them: it is not the day's stock of bread and beef or the year's stock of cloth that they need, but the raw material and instruments for making the bread, beef, and cloth, and the organization for employing these matters.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: The warnings of misery, possible war, starvation, and riot, as well as the call to teach workers about productive resources, are supported by the excerpt and retain Morris’s language. The final lesson is relevant, though it extends beyond the question’s focus on what he fears may happen.

2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.question: What do you think workers need to do to bring about change?
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.answer: The workers must come forward and show the way to the new, by claiming to be allowed to work for themselves, and thus form a Society where all will be workers. They must understand and make others understand that the world can only be happy if it is honest, and it can only be honest by not allowing persons to live by making other men poor. They must combine; the question is, will they combine? I answer they must combine or starve. But in order to combine in the best manner and to bring about the freedom of labour with least possible violence and misery, after they have learned what their position is and what it should be, they must cast aside all jealousy of one another, must understand thoroughly that they are not enemies to one another but all soldiers in one great army. They must be forbearing and slow to quarrel; and when they really feel this it will give them a courage which people can never have when they are acting in a selfish way each one for his own interests. Then they will be irresistible: they will attract to them all that there is of intelligence in the working-classes, and they will convince all those of the wealthy classes who are worthy and well-meaning.
2d60120ee8fa03e6.txt.reason: Most of the answer closely follows the excerpt’s calls for workers to claim the means of labour, combine, and overcome jealousy. However, the claims that workers “must understand and make others understand that the world can only be happy if it is honest” and that honesty requires “not allowing persons to live by making other men poor” are not in the supplied excerpt, so this should be verified before training.

2de57f7d53093eee.txt.question: Why do you think Ireland needs Home Rule?
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.answer: It is necessary for Ireland to take her own affairs into her own hands, whatever the immediate results may be. It is becoming impossible to impose the rule of the English bureaucracy in its worst form on Ireland. Those who, if they could, would coerce Ireland by any and every means perceive that the thing is impossible in the face of the gathering instinct of the English people against their forcible benevolence in favour of the landlords. As Socialists, therefore, we are bound to wish the utmost success to those who can at least see that it is necessary for Ireland to take her own affairs into her own hands.
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.reason: The answer closely reproduces the excerpt’s argument and wording, including the need for Ireland to manage its own affairs and Morris’s Socialist support for Home Rule.

2de57f7d53093eee.txt.question: What makes you distrust a compromise on Home Rule?
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.answer: The real danger to the success of Irish independence lies in those who come into the Gladstonian camp again while merely pretending to support Home Rule. A majority of such men, joined to the usual amount of waverers, might so dally with the question as practically to draw us back again into the trouble from which we have seemed to be emerging. Mr Gladstone’s declaration of the death of the Bill may mean compromise, or it may mean nothing more than electioneering vagueness, trying to make the sweep of the net as wide and inclusive as possible. If the Chamberlainites accept it as a body, the whole Liberal-Radical party will be pledged to shaving down the measure for the new Parliament to something less than the defunct Bill. A firm and strong minority would educate people somewhat: a sloppy majority would wear them out and make them languid as to the whole subject.
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.reason: The answer preserves Morris’s qualified concern about compromise and the consequences of a nominal Home Rule majority. It is assembled from the supplied passage with wording and style substantially intact.

2de57f7d53093eee.txt.question: Do you think Ireland could still be coerced by England?
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.answer: It is becoming impossible to impose the rule of the English bureaucracy in its worst form on Ireland. Even those who, if they could, would coerce Ireland by any and every means perceive that the thing is impossible in the face of the gathering instinct of the English people against their forcible benevolence in favour of the landlords. The Tories are beginning to see the impossibility of dragooning Ireland in the future, and are loudly disclaiming coercion. Yet a measure intended for the complete shelving of the question would have to be enforced by the usual method by which English gifts are presented to Ireland — coercion, to wit.
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.reason: The response reflects Morris’s distinction between the perceived impossibility of coercing Ireland and coercion as the likely means of imposing a measure shelving the question. Its language closely follows the excerpt.

2de57f7d53093eee.txt.question: Why do you call the issue “Home Rule or Humbug”?
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.answer: The broad question before the country is Home Rule or Humbug. It was necessary to put it so in order to break through the network of evasions, intrigue, and compromise that the end of last Session had woven round the question. The reactionists apparently seek to involve the whole question in a hopeless, lawyer-like muddle, so as to sicken people of it, and to get up the old cry of the impossibility of dealing with the Irish. Mr Gladstone’s answer to this must be considered an effective one, and none the less so because of its simplicity. If the elections go against Home Rule, this simplifying of the present issue will give force and distinctness to the powerful opposition which is the alternative to a success at the polling booths.
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.reason: The substance and most wording are supported, but the answer changes who puts the phrase before the country: Morris says Gladstone “puts the broad question,” not that it is simply the broad question. This is a correctable attribution/phrasing issue.

2de57f7d53093eee.txt.question: What do you think a failed Home Rule vote would mean?
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.answer: If the elections go against Home Rule, the simplifying of the present issue will give force and distinctness to the powerful opposition which is the alternative to a success at the polling booths. Mr Gladstone will at least have at his back a minority strong enough in opposition to prevent the passing of a measure intended for the complete shelving of the question. A firm and strong minority would educate people somewhat; a sloppy majority would wear them out and make them languid as to the whole subject.
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.reason: The answer largely uses Morris’s language, but its juxtaposition makes the “firm and strong minority” seem to be the minority resulting from a failed Home Rule vote. The excerpt does not explicitly establish that connection; the minority passage concerns preventing a shelving measure, while the election passage separately discusses the force of opposition.

2de57f7d53093eee.txt.question: How do you distinguish between different kinds of Radicals?
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.answer: Looking at them from the Socialist point of view, the Radicals may be divided into two sections. The first are the pedantic Radicals with certain party shibboleths on their tongues, and in their hearts bitter hostility to everything which seems to interfere even temporarily with the party game which they are playing. Between them and us there is and must be mere war; they will not even listen to us. They look upon us with more hatred than they do upon the Tories, for without the latter they could not carry on their game. But besides these pedantic Radicals, there is another Radical section who are on the look out for progressive ideas, and are the representatives of advancing Democracy. These may, and often do, oppose us as inconvenient impracticable persons, who interfere with what they have learned to consider progress, but they are not really unfriendly and are willing to hear us; when they have done so, many of them will find that they are Socialists after all.
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.reason: The answer accurately presents Morris’s two-part distinction from the Socialist point of view and retains his characteristic language and reasoning.

2de57f7d53093eee.txt.question: Which Radicals do you regard as allies?
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.answer: The Radical section who are on the look out for progressive ideas, and are the representatives of advancing Democracy, are not really unfriendly and are willing to hear us. They may, and often do, oppose us as inconvenient impracticable persons, who interfere with what they have learned to consider progress; but when they have heard us, many of them will find that they are Socialists after all. The Chamberlainite Unionist Radicals, many of whom are quite fanatical in their opposition to Home Rule, represent to us the hostile pedantic Radicals, while those who are championing Home Rule represent our Radical friends. As Socialists, therefore, we are bound to wish the utmost success to those who can at least see that it is necessary for Ireland to take her own affairs into her own hands, whatever the immediate results may be.
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.reason: The answer combines Morris’s description of progressive Radicals with his explicit identification of Home Rule champions as Radical friends, preserving the relevant qualifications and source wording.

2de57f7d53093eee.txt.question: What is your view of the Chamberlainite Radicals?
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.answer: The Chamberlainite Unionist Radicals, many of whom are quite fanatical in their opposition to Home Rule, represent to us the hostile pedantic Radicals. The pedantic Radicals have certain party shibboleths on their tongues, and in their hearts bitter hostility to everything which seems to interfere even temporarily with the party game which they are playing. Between them and us there is and must be mere war; they will not even listen to us. They look upon us with more hatred than they do upon the Tories, for without the latter they could not carry on their game. As things are going, they are getting themselves deeper into the mire at every step.
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.reason: Morris explicitly identifies the Chamberlainite Unionist Radicals with the hostile pedantic Radicals and describes both their stance and his view of their political position. The answer is relevant and retains his language.

2de57f7d53093eee.txt.question: Why do you support the Radicals who champion Home Rule?
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.answer: Those who are championing Home Rule represent our Radical friends, who are waiting to be told what Socialism really is, or at any rate waiting to find out what it is, and who when they have found out will become Socialists. They can at least see that it is necessary for Ireland to take her own affairs into her own hands, whatever the immediate results may be. As Socialists, therefore, we are bound to wish them the utmost success.
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.reason: The answer directly conveys Morris’s stated reasons for supporting Home Rule champions and closely preserves the excerpt’s wording.

2de57f7d53093eee.txt.question: Do you believe the people who oppose Home Rule are simply against Irish independence?
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.answer: Not all opposition is of the same kind: the Chamberlainite Unionist Radicals, many of whom are quite fanatical in their opposition to Home Rule, represent the hostile pedantic Radicals. But some Radical opponents are on the look out for progressive ideas and are the representatives of advancing Democracy. They may oppose us as inconvenient impracticable persons, who interfere with what they have learned to consider progress, but they are not really unfriendly and are willing to hear us. As for those opposed to a real Home Rule, unless the Chamberlainites are dead against any real Home-Rule, they may give up their present opposition to Mr Gladstone; and the danger is that men merely pretending to support Home Rule may dally with the question.
2de57f7d53093eee.txt.reason: The answer merges separate arguments in a way that blurs their subjects: the progressive Radicals may oppose Socialists, while the conditional prediction about Chamberlainites concerns whether they oppose real Home Rule. It does not clearly answer the question about whether opponents are simply against Irish independence.

2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.question: Why do you think kings are still a danger, even if the old kingship is dead?
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.answer: Though the old kingship may be dead, at least in England, we may perhaps have in these latter days fashioned a new kingship, not the less dangerous because it is not so obvious and brutal as the old one. Under class domination, modern democracy may tend to personal government. We Socialists may well take note of three kings who have ruled the sheepish multitude within the last thirty years of more or less reformed parliamentary government, and bear in mind how futile its boasts of reasonable freedom have been within our own immediate knowledge. When one failed, another must be chosen; we could not do without a king. The danger lies in the stupefying influence of his kingship, which stops people's qualms of conscience, relieves them of their sense of responsibility, and gives them just one duty to fulfill—shouting out for their leader.
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.reason: The excerpt supports the discussion of a new kingship and its effects, and the answer preserves Morris's wording. However, “Under class domination, modern democracy may tend to personal government” is not in the supplied excerpt, while the answer presents it as part of the source.

2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.question: What bothers you about people's devotion to Gladstone?
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.answer: The stupefying influence of Mr. Gladstone's kingship is obstructive: it stops people's qualms of conscience, relieves them of their sense of responsibility, and gives them just one duty to fulfill—shouting out for their leader; a leader too who for many years past has been careful of one thing at least—not to lead. This clinging to the personality of a mere politician, a man by his very profession bound to humbug at least his followers, and often, as in Mr. Gladstone's case, himself also, is a refinement of flunkeyism which makes one almost despair of getting anyone who bears any party name to look at realities, and try to deal with them himself.
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.reason: The answer accurately combines Morris's account of Gladstone's “stupefying influence” with his condemnation of clinging to a politician's personality. Its wording remains closely grounded in the excerpt and directly answers the question.

2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.question: What would you urge Radicals to do instead of relying on political leaders?
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.answer: I beg Radicals to lay aside this worship of names; to accept themselves a little responsibility for themselves, for the dreary wretched lives which they and their brethren lead; to ask themselves if they have all they want except the franchise, all that a man ought to want, and how they are going to get it. Let them ask themselves if they really think that a reformed House of Lords, whatever that may mean, or an Elected Second Chamber, with the First Chamber to help them, would or could give them anything of what they want. I entreat them to ask themselves why they are dirty, ignorant, ill-fed, ill-clad, ill-housed, and, when they have found out—or rather when they have gained an inkling of it, or even before—let them ask Mr. Gladstone why they are all this, why they are slaves; and if he can't tell them, let them try to do without him, and go elsewhere for leading. Only I warn them: let them have plenty of leaders, all knowing the way, all with one tale in their mouths, and let them take care that these said leaders lead. I think they will then take the road towards Social Revolution.
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.reason: This directly answers the question with Morris's own appeal to lay aside “worship of names,” accept responsibility, and seek effective leaders. The minor punctuation and clause adjustments do not materially change his meaning or style.

2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.question: Why do you think working people remain poor and oppressed, and what should they do about it?
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.answer: I entreat Radicals to ask themselves why they are dirty, ignorant, ill-fed, ill-clad, ill-housed, and why they are slaves. They should ask themselves if they have all they want except the franchise, all that a man ought to want, and how they are going to get it; and whether a reformed House of Lords, or an Elected Second Chamber, with the First Chamber to help them, would or could give them anything of what they want. When they have found out—or rather when they have gained an inkling of it, or even before—let them ask Mr. Gladstone why they are all this; and if he can't tell them, let them try to do without him, and go elsewhere for leading. They must have plenty of leaders, all knowing the way, all with one tale in their mouths, and take care that these said leaders lead. I think they will then take the road towards Social Revolution.
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.reason: The proposed action is grounded in Morris's appeal, but the answer does not actually explain why working people remain poor and oppressed; it mainly repeats his call for Radicals to investigate their condition. “They must have” also turns Morris's exhortation “let them have” into a stronger assertion.

2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.question: Do you think political reform alone can give people what they need?
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.answer: I beg Radicals to ask themselves if they have all they want except the franchise; all that a man ought to want, and how they are going to get it. Let them ask themselves if they really think that a reformed House of Lords, whatever that may mean, or an Elected Second Chamber, with the First Chamber to help them, would or could give them anything of what they want. The dreary wretched lives which they and their brethren lead, and their being dirty, ignorant, ill-fed, ill-clad, ill-housed, and slaves, are realities that they must look at and try to deal with themselves; and if Mr. Gladstone can't tell them why they are all this, let them try to do without him, and go elsewhere for leading. I think they will then take the road towards Social Revolution.
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.reason: Morris questions whether parliamentary changes would give people what they want, but the answer adds the connective claim that their conditions “are realities that they must look at and try to deal with themselves,” which is not stated in the excerpt. This addition gives the response a newly formulated answer rather than preserving Morris's wording.

2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.question: What do you mean when you say Gladstone is obstructive?
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.answer: Mr. Gladstone represents a certain amount of obstruction, not so much because of his genuine Conservative instincts, which lead him to make for ever just such concessions as may seem to serve to bolster up our present system of slavery; the course of events will inevitably reject such concessions and force on the real demand for revolution. Rather, he is obstructive because of the stupefying influence of his kingship, which stops people's qualms of conscience, relieves them of their sense of responsibility, and gives them just one duty to fulfill—shouting out for their leader; a leader too who for many years past has been careful of one thing at least—not to lead.
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.reason: The response preserves Morris's contrast between Gladstone's concessions and the more significant obstruction of his “kingship,” using his distinctive phrasing throughout. The restructuring is a harmless clarification of the original long sentence.

2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.question: Why are you so critical of people worshipping political names?
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.answer: This clinging to the personality of a mere politician—a man by his very profession bound to humbug at least his followers, and often, as in Mr. Gladstone's case, himself also—is a refinement of flunkeyism which makes one almost despair of getting anyone who bears any party name to look at realities, and try to deal with them himself. I beg Radicals to lay aside this worship of names; to accept themselves a little responsibility for themselves, for the dreary wretched lives which they and their brethren lead, and to ask themselves what they want and how they are going to get it.
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.reason: The critique of political devotion and the appeal to Radicals are authentic, but the ending replaces Morris's specific question about what people have “except the franchise” and what a person ought to want with the unsupportedly broad formulation “what they want.”

2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.question: What is your view of Gladstone's political concessions?
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.answer: Mr. Gladstone's genuine Conservative instincts lead him to make for ever just such concessions as may seem to serve to bolster up our present system of slavery; but the course of events will inevitably reject such concessions and force on the real demand for revolution. He represents a certain amount of obstruction, rather because of the stupefying influence of his kingship, which stops people's qualms of conscience and relieves them of their sense of responsibility, than because of those concessions.
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.reason: The first sentence faithfully states Morris's view of the concessions. The final comparison is a substantial reworking of his “not so much ... rather” construction and omits that the kingship gives people “just one duty ... shouting out for their leader,” an important part of his explanation.

2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.question: What do you think people should look at instead of trusting a party leader?
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.answer: They should look at realities, and try to deal with them themselves. I beg Radicals to accept themselves a little responsibility for themselves, for the dreary wretched lives which they and their brethren lead; to ask themselves if they have all they want except the franchise, all that a man ought to want, and how they are going to get it. They should ask why they are dirty, ignorant, ill-fed, ill-clad, ill-housed, and why they are slaves; and if Mr. Gladstone can't tell them, let them try to do without him, and go elsewhere for leading. Let them have plenty of leaders, all knowing the way, all with one tale in their mouths, and take care that these said leaders lead.
2e18a2f43f41ea2b.txt.reason: The opening directly answers the question with Morris's phrase about looking at realities, and the rest supplies his relevant appeal for responsibility and effective leadership. The modest shift to “They should” retains the substance and remains useful conversationally.

2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.question: Why do you think the Winchester election mattered to Radicals?
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.answer: To the Radicals one may preach a little from even such a contemptible text as the Winchester election, and ask them once more whether they are going to be dragged about through the mud by their Liberal allies, or are going to give free play to their aspirations towards the popular cause. The election itself, an affair of ‘ins and outs’, would be a matter of complete indifference if it were not that there is still a Radical tail hanging on to the official Liberal party. The Radicals have been making towards Socialism, under the educational influence of the Irish rebellion and the general force of circumstances which is driving them out of their barren negative position, and forcing them to consider whether there is any forward road for them except Socialism. The Liberals made this most trumpery faction-fight a kind of test-case; since it went against them so completely, they were bound to admit that the tide had turned again, and the Tory ship had weathered the dangerous headland for the present. The question for Radicals is whether they will assert themselves as men sincerely trying to learn what is to be done to carry the country out of this shabby period of the rule of the dregs of the bourgeoisie.
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.reason: The answer closely preserves Morris's wording and connects the election's test-case significance to his appeal for Radicals to pursue the popular cause and consider Socialism. The omissions are relevant cuts rather than distortions.

2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.question: Why do you think the Tory reaction happened?
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.answer: The upshot is the ‘Tory Reaction’, as real a reaction as any political reaction ever is. The Government is always a genuine Government of the middle-classes; whatever is done is done for them, even though it may sometimes take the guise of helping the working-classes. The events of the last five or six years, the change that has been coming over the commercial outlook, and the Irish question—founded as it is on the further question ‘How are the Irish peasants to live?’—sorely shook the middle-class, though at first it was looked upon as a mere political matter on which there might be difference of opinion between ‘respectable’ persons. As the English, Scotch, and Welsh working-men became educated into friendliness and sympathy with the Irish peasant, so the middle-class became educated into hatred of him. He is now to them a working-man asking for some of the property of the proprietary classes and not too nice as to the means by which to establish his claim. The clearer-sighted once-Liberals took the opportunity of Gladstone’s new departure to rat formally, leaving behind a group of Gladstonites whom habit and a vague, shadowy habitual idea of principle keep in the ranks. Meanwhile, the great body of middle-class non-politicals, fully equipped with votes, went solid for the Tory reaction. They have a blind and instinctive, but quite genuine hatred of the ‘other public’, the ‘lower classes’, whose misery it has made and lives upon. The Tories, it seems, had estimated the relative voting power of the working-class and this criminal class better than we had, and knew that they were safe; they started fair on their new career of Resolute Government, which gained them the enthusiastic support of the whole nonpolitical middle-classes.
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.reason: Most of the response closely reproduces the excerpt, but it changes Morris's “this criminal class” (the non-political public) to “the working-class and this criminal class,” making the working class appear to be part of the criminal class. That consequential wording error should be corrected before training.

2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.question: How do you see the middle classes and the working classes relating to one another?
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.answer: Most middle class men, ‘thoughtful’ or unthoughtful, never realize the fact that there is a working-class; the artisans or labourers that they may come across are to them but aspirants towards the middle-class, or failures from it, mere accidents of society in short. Whatever is done by the Government is done for the middle-classes, even though it may sometimes take the guise of helping the working-classes; and that only means helping such and such groups to manage the human machinery necessary to their welfare. The middle-class is blankly ignorant of the composition of modern society until events disturb that mood. The Irish question helped to do so: as the English, Scotch, and Welsh working-men became educated into friendliness and sympathy with the Irish peasant, so the middle-class became educated into hatred of him. To them he is a working-man asking for some of the property of the proprietary classes and not too nice as to the means by which to establish his claim. The ‘public’ has a blind and instinctive, but quite genuine hatred of the ‘other public’, the ‘lower classes’, whose misery it has made and lives upon; and, as the claims of the workers rise and are more distinctly formulated, this public will make civil war inevitable.
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.reason: The answer retains Morris's distinctive formulations and directly addresses class relations. Its concluding prediction is supported by the excerpt's statement that the public will make civil war inevitable as workers' claims rise; the abridgment does not substantially distort the passage.

2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.question: What would you urge Radicals to do now?
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.answer: Let all true Radicals take advantage of that effacement by educating themselves yet further; let them set to work seriously to learn what those popular claims are which the Liberal leaders steadily refuse to consider, but which form the only politics worth attending to. It is true that if they do this they will soon find themselves Socialists and outcasts; but they will be recompensed for that when the time comes, as it soon will, when all distinctions of party will merge into the two camps, of the people and their haters. They will then know clearly why they are on the right side, as they will have joined it consciously and not by mere compulsion. I believe that many Radicals are now taking this course, and I would encourage them to think that all these apparent Tory victories are only so many signs of the enlightenment of the workers of their own interests, and the consequent development of the middle-class hatred against them.
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.reason: The answer is an almost verbatim, coherent response to the question and preserves Morris's explicit advice to Radicals, including the original explanation of their future political alignment.

2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.question: Why do you think Radicals should move toward Socialism?
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.answer: The Radicals have been making towards Socialism under the educational influence of the Irish rebellion, and the general force of circumstances which is driving them out of their barren negative position, and forcing them to consider whether there is any forward road for them except Socialism. They should set to work seriously to learn what those popular claims are which the Liberal leaders steadily refuse to consider, but which form the only politics worth attending to. If they do this they will soon find themselves Socialists and outcasts; but they will be recompensed when all distinctions of party merge into the two camps, of the people and their haters. They will then know clearly why they are on the right side, having joined it consciously and not by mere compulsion.
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.reason: The response combines closely matching source passages to answer why Radicals are moving toward Socialism and what they should learn. The wording and reasoning remain substantially Morris's, with no significant distortion.

2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.question: Do you think the Liberals will stand by their Radical allies?
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.answer: The Liberals are not showing any signs of solicitude for their Radical allies, but are quite prepared to shake them off if need be. The Radical party is effaced from the Parliamentary record, because its education towards progress had been advancing. The Liberal leaders steadily refuse to consider those popular claims which form the only politics worth attending to. The party opposing the Tories is pledged, it is true, to grant Home Rule in Ireland—a pledge which may be as easily evaded as other pledges have been—but is so far from being pledged to help the whole people out of their misery that, when events press hardly on them, they also will have to take obvious measures to keep the people down, and avail themselves of the support of that party of blind wrong-doing.
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.reason: The answer directly reflects Morris's warning that Liberals may shake off Radicals and that the party opposing the Tories will not necessarily help the people. The phrase “the party opposing the Tories” is a clear, faithful clarification of the source's referent.

2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.question: What do you mean when you say the people will eventually divide into two camps?
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.answer: All distinctions of party will merge into the two camps, of the people and their haters. The popular claims are those which the Liberal leaders steadily refuse to consider, but which form the only politics worth attending to. As the claims of the workers rise and are more distinctly formulated, the ‘public’—the great body of middle-class non-politicals, fully equipped with votes—will act to keep the lower classes down. This public has a blind and instinctive, but quite genuine hatred of the ‘other public’, the ‘lower classes’, whose misery it has made and lives upon. It is the real danger to what of genuine society yet exists amongst us; the mass of blind wrong-doing led by ‘superior persons’ who know what is right and hate it, who have made wrong their right. Radicals who have learned the popular claims will know clearly why they are on the right side, having joined it consciously and not by mere compulsion.
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.reason: The answer is largely assembled from authentic passages, but “the public ... will act to keep the lower classes down” upgrades Morris's qualification that it “usually only acts as a dead weight to keep them down” into a categorical future action. The excerpt's separate claim about civil war should not be recast this way.

2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.question: How do you interpret the apparent Tory victories?
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.answer: All these apparent Tory victories are only so many signs of the enlightenment of the workers of their own interests, and the consequent development of the middle-class hatred against them. The Radical party is effaced from the Parliamentary record because its education towards progress had been advancing. The Tory reaction, meanwhile, has gained the enthusiastic support of the whole nonpolitical middle-classes, and this support will keep the Tories in power for many a day. But the apparent victories also show that the workers' claims are rising and being more distinctly formulated; the Radical should take advantage of the effacement of the party by educating himself yet further and learning what those popular claims are.
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.reason: The source supports the victories as signs of workers' enlightenment and middle-class hostility, and separately says that civil war will become inevitable as workers' claims rise. But the answer's “also show that the workers' claims are rising” wrongly presents that separate condition as something the victories themselves demonstrate. “The Radical should ... himself” also shifts Morris's collective address into an invented singular form.

2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.question: Why did the Irish question change the political mood?
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.answer: The Irish question, founded as it is on the further question ‘How are the Irish peasants to live?’, sorely shook the middle-class, though at first it was looked upon as a mere political matter on which there might be difference of opinion between ‘respectable’ persons. As the English, Scotch, and Welsh working-men became educated into friendliness and sympathy with the Irish peasant, so the middle-class became educated into hatred of him. To them he is a working-man asking for some of the property of the proprietary classes and not too nice as to the means by which to establish his claim. The putting forward of the Irish question by Mr Gladstone gave the middle-classes an opportunity for backing out with that ease and dignity which the British hypocrite manages to impart to the action of sneaking out through a back door. The result was a breaking up of the Liberal party and a Tory reaction, supported by the great body of middle-class non-politicals.
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.reason: The answer closely follows Morris's account of the Irish question's effects on working-class sympathy, middle-class hostility, and party politics. “The result was a breaking up” is a concise synthesis supported by the excerpt's statements about the Liberal split and Tory reaction.

2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.question: What is your view of the so-called non-political public?
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.answer: The great body of middle-class non-politicals, who include a great many ‘superior persons’, are an enormously powerful body; they form, in fact, what the newspapers mean when they speak of ‘the public’. This ‘public’, fully equipped with votes, goes solid for the Tory reaction, and is the central and really noteworthy part of it. It has a blind and instinctive, but quite genuine hatred of the ‘other public’, the ‘lower classes’, whose misery it has made and lives upon. It usually only acts as a dead weight to keep them down, but from time to time takes vigorous action enough. It is the public which applauded Napoleon the Little and the Butchers of the Commune, smiled safe approval on the slaying of the Chicago martyrs, egged on the evictions of Irish tenants, shut up Trafalgar Square, and beat helpless prisoners in their cells. It is the real danger to what of genuine society yet exists amongst us: the mass of blind wrong-doing led by ‘superior persons’ who know what is right and hate it, who have made wrong their right.
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.reason: The answer preserves Morris's distinctive characterization and examples, with only relevant omissions from the longer catalogue. It directly answers the question and retains the source's forceful concluding judgment.

2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.question: Do you think political parties can really help the whole people out of their misery?
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.answer: The party opposing the Tories is so far from being pledged to help the whole people out of their misery that it also, when events press hardly on it, will have to take obvious measures to keep the people down, and avail itself of the support of that party of blind wrong-doing. It is pledged, it is true, to grant Home Rule in Ireland, but that pledge may be as easily evaded as other pledges have been. The popular claims which the Liberal leaders steadily refuse to consider form the only politics worth attending to. The Government, in this country, is always a genuine Government of the middle-classes; whatever is done is done for them, even though it may sometimes take the guise of helping the working-classes.
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.reason: The answer faithfully combines Morris's caution about the party opposing the Tories with his critique of middle-class government and the Liberal leaders' refusal to consider popular claims. The selections are relevant and coherent.

2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.question: Why do you call the Radical position a barren negative one?
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.answer: The Radicals have been making towards Socialism under the educational influence of the Irish rebellion, and the general force of circumstances is driving them out of their barren negative position, forcing them to consider whether there is any forward road for them except Socialism. They should give free play to their aspirations towards the popular cause, and assert themselves as men sincerely trying to learn what is to be done to carry the country out of this shabby period of the rule of the dregs of the bourgeoisie. They should learn what those popular claims are which the Liberal leaders steadily refuse to consider, but which form the only politics worth attending to.
2e3a3a561e89b7b1.txt.reason: The answer preserves Morris's wording, but does not really explain why the Radical position is “barren” and shifts his description and appeal into prescriptive “They should” statements. It would need a more direct explanation of the negative position and the circumstances pushing Radicals toward Socialism.

3154893ef5c27b41.txt.question: Why do you think saving old buildings is so urgent?
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.answer: There is no time to spare in the preservation of ancient buildings. Every year in which the complete conversion of the public to the Society's views is still unfulfilled is replete with the greatest dangers to our ancient buildings. Every year which leaves their guardians ignorant or careless of their duties adds to the list of irreparable losses to art and history, which cultivated people are beginning to perceive and deplore, but are too often powerless to prevent. Though much has been destroyed or falsified, many genuine works of ancient architecture remain, and not one is safe until the Society's principles are generally acknowledged and acted upon, even in remote country places in England.
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.reason: Directly answers the urgency question with the excerpt's warning, reasoning, and distinctive phrases, while retaining the Society's institutional perspective.

3154893ef5c27b41.txt.question: What do you mean by preserving a building rather than restoring it?
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.answer: The Society's object is rational repair, rather than so-called restoration. The old work should be saved, not cleared away and replaced by an imaginary or modern copy. Even a decayed roof may be preserved by supporting the old timber with bolts, straps, and other ironwork, applied in an honest, straightforward manner, without any attempt at concealment. Many years of carelessness and neglect to keep the wet out may reduce roofs to a state in which modern architects say that complete renewal is necessary; then a large sum is collected under the pretence of saving an old building, the grand old roof is cleared away, and an expensive and worthless modern copy put in its place. A fraction of the sum wasted on the new roof would have kept the priceless old wood-work safe and strong for many generations.
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.reason: Explains the preservation principle with wording and examples closely grounded in the report. The initial generalization is a fair synthesis of the Society's stated object and its roof case.

3154893ef5c27b41.txt.question: Why are you against replacing old architectural features with copies?
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.answer: The old work is priceless, and an expensive modern copy is worthless in its place. At Tewkesbury, the west window contains a whole epitome of architectural history: though the tracery was rebuilt and partly renewed in the seventeenth century, in the main it follows the grand old lines of the Perpendicular work. To remove all the tracery and substitute an imaginary reproduction of a Decorated window would have been a wanton piece of destruction. At Deopham, a fraction of the sum wasted on a new roof would have kept the priceless old wood-work safe and strong for many generations. The Society therefore protested against the removal of the old work and urged that it be saved by honest repair.
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.reason: The cases and much of the language are supported, but the closing sentence blends the separate Deopham roof argument with the Tewkesbury intervention and claims the Society urged honest repair of the old work in this combined context. That specific conflation should be corrected before training.

3154893ef5c27b41.txt.question: How do you feel about the destruction of old buildings in Oxford?
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.answer: Among the Society's disappointments, none, perhaps, are more grievous than the hopelessness of attempting to prevent constant acts of stupid barbarism from being perpetrated by the University of Oxford. In spite of appeals both to the Town and the University, a memorial signed by a numerous and influential body of men, and the most energetic efforts of every kind, Magdalen Bridge is being pulled down and rebuilt in a way that will utterly ruin the beauty of its proportions, and create a blot in what was once one of the loveliest street-views in the world—the entrance to the High Street of Oxford. The authorities of Brasenose College have lately sold for old metal the group of sculpture that was one of the most characteristic features of their front quadrangle. Beam Hall, a fine specimen of sixteenth-century domestic architecture, is threatened; and, if things go on in this way, a few years will see the last of the picturesque old houses that for so long made the streets of Oxford a picture of unsurpassed charm and quiet beauty.
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.reason: The answer closely preserves the excerpt's strong judgment and specific Oxford examples, and adapts them naturally to the question without changing their meaning.

3154893ef5c27b41.txt.question: Have your efforts to protect old buildings ever succeeded?
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.answer: Yes. The proposed destruction of the Water-Gate at Norwich was stopped, and the gate is to remain untouched. The Society protested against the railway extension scheme, co-operated with the Dean and Chapter of Norwich and the Society of Antiquaries, and asked its Members in the House of Commons to oppose the clause in the Bill. At Wimborne, the Society's recommendations for preventing further failure in the piers of the great central tower were accepted and carried out; up to the present time there has been no sign of further damage. At Audley House, the building was saved from destruction and is being repaired by a local architect who promised to carry out the Society's views on the necessary repairs. The proposed removal of the tracery at Tewkesbury was also abandoned.
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.reason: Gives a direct, informative answer with several documented successes, preserving the source's institutional account and phrasing. The examples are relevant and coherent.

3154893ef5c27b41.txt.question: What makes you worry about the future of old buildings?
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.answer: Every year which leaves the guardians of these buildings ignorant or careless of their duties adds to the list of irreparable losses to art and history. The Committee has had to protest against several schemes for the mere unnecessary or wanton destruction of ancient buildings; but this does not show backsliding in public opinion, for there are hopeful signs of the impression the Society has made. Still, many genuine works of ancient architecture are not safe until the Society's principles are generally acknowledged and acted upon. The Oxford cases show the danger: Magdalen Bridge is being pulled down and rebuilt in a way that will ruin the beauty of its proportions; Beam Hall is threatened; and a few years may see the last of the picturesque old houses that gave Oxford's streets their charm and quiet beauty.
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.reason: Combines the source's explanation of danger with relevant Oxford examples, while preserving its qualification that more protests do not indicate backsliding in public opinion.

3154893ef5c27b41.txt.question: Why does the Society need more members and money?
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.answer: The Society's income falls far short of what is requisite for doing its work satisfactorily. Personal inspection by competent persons of buildings threatened with restoration or destruction is almost always positively necessary before the Committee can address any protest or give advice to their guardians; to carry this out promptly and unfailingly is beyond the Society's means. Nor is it rich enough to spend a proper sum in printing, so as to spread duly the principles of the Society by literature. The only steady addition to its income must come from the increase of subscribers, and it is much to be wished that members would let its necessities be known to those who really wish to further its principles. The list of Corresponding Members is also incomplete, and the Society loses many opportunities through this deficiency; additional help for the heavy work of the small Executive Committee would be most welcome.
3154893ef5c27b41.txt.reason: Faithfully explains the Society's financial and staffing needs using the report's language, and addresses both parts of the question without irrelevant material.

3154893ef5c27b41.txt.question: Why did you want the Society to work beyond England?
