It also says the labour war “may soon be over,” whereas the excerpt states that the war will soon be over when workers become conscious of its end. The authentic concluding explanation is useful, but this appended synthesis needs correction before training.

988418c1e5612d7f.txt.question: What does a workers’ organization need to do to be useful?
988418c1e5612d7f.txt.answer: The working-men who profess to be organized must ask and have answered questions about their circumstances and the nature of their industry if their organization is to be of any use. They must not fight against capitalism blindly, as they mostly do now, but be conscious of the nature of the fight, and especially must have a definite aim to end it. They must ask how much it is possible to save out of a precarious income of 12s. 6d. a week, and whether the getting of coal can be carried on gainfully in Lanarkshire; if it cannot, why is it carried on? And if there is a due gain in it, why are the getters starved?
988418c1e5612d7f.txt.reason: The central advice about asking and answering questions, avoiding blind opposition, and having a definite aim is faithful. However, “about their circumstances and the nature of their industry” is an unsupported replacement for the excerpt’s general “these are the kind of questions”; the examples that follow are questions Morris poses to the newspaper, not explicitly instructions that workers must ask those exact questions.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: Why do you think the public needs to care more about art?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: In order to have a living school of Art, the public in general must be interested in Art; it must be a part of their lives; something which they can no more do without than water or lighting. We must not be able to plead poverty or necessity as an excuse for ugliness or dirt. If we raise a building, whether it be palace, factory, or cottage, it must be a thing well understood that it must be sightly; if a railway has to be run from one place to another, it must be taken for granted that the minimum of destruction of natural beauty must be incurred, even if that should increase the expense of the line largely; disfiguring waste of coal-pits or manufactories must be got rid of, whatever the cost may be. All this need of real public convenience, which is the only possible foundation for Art in modern times, is quite possible to be done; and it will be done, so soon as people care about it. As things go now we are, as a community, contented to be publicly poor so long as some of us are privately rich; therefore, though the income of the country is enormous in figures, no man of us can go a few yards from his own door without seeing the tokens of quite desperate public poverty. The capacity for Art, and the desire for it, are not yet extinct among us; yet they are mostly dormant. We must awaken in people that “divine discontent” which is the mother of improvement in mankind. The essential thing is that people generally should be capable of receiving impressions through the eyes, and this process should be a joy to them, just as their receiving impressions from their palates, or their ears. The pleasure taken in art is primarily sensuous; an obvious fact, yet not so obvious but that it is generally forgotten now-a-days.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: The answer closely follows Morris’s argument and wording about public interest, public poverty, and the sensuous pleasure of art. Combining the related passages gives a coherent, direct response.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: How can you persuade people to learn to see?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: We who have not lost the use of our eyes should go on pestering the rest of the public until we have more or less convinced them that it would be a good thing for them to recover the capacity of seeing, just as it would be a good thing to recover the use of their legs if they were lame. Those who want to see, and do not really lack eyes, but only the habit of using them, can get to see, sooner or later, that is, can acquire the habit of seeing; and we who have not lost the habit are there to help them. In the art of propaganda, having enunciated your first thesis, you must not wait till you have converted all people to that before you put out your second and your third, and proceed to act as if the said first was already accepted. So let us assume that we all agree (though we do not) that it is a good thing to have the full use of our eyes, and are prepared to endure the pain, as well as to enjoy the pleasure, which that use will give us; that we are, in short, prepared to accept the responsibility of being human beings in the full possession of healthy senses. But helping those who desire to gain the use of their eyes is a far more difficult question than some may think. It cannot be answered unless people are seriously longing to be blind no longer, and are ready to pay the full price, both in money, and in trouble, and disturbance of a quiet life.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: The response preserves Morris’s distinctive eye-and-leg analogy and his remarks on propaganda and the price of learning to see. The corrected apparent typographical errors do not alter the substance.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: What should people who can see do to help others appreciate art?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: There are two things to be done by the seers for the non-seers: the first is to show them what is to be seen on the earth; and the next to give them opportunities for producing matters, the sight of which will please themselves and their neighbours, and the people that come after them. To train them, in short, in the observation and creation of beauty and incident. What is worth seeing on the earth? In one word, everything: this to love and foster, and that to hate and destroy. The results of the greed, tyranny and injustice of man, of his folly, these must be looked at in the face, as well as the results of his aspirations and his love. The disgust and grief with which we must regard these disgraces will, when we know the causes of them, give us assured hope of the reward of fresh pleasure of the eyes that will accompany every casting off of the follies which still beset us. But the things which the eyes bid us love include especially the beauties of Nature, and the beauties of Art.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: The excerpt directly supports the answer’s account of showing people what is worth seeing and giving them opportunities to create beauty. The selected material is coherent and retains Morris’s language.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: Why do you want people to appreciate ordinary English landscapes?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: Our fault in respect of regarding the beauties of Nature is that for the most part we refuse to pay attention to anything in Nature which is not tremendous and exciting; it must be an Alpine pass, or a rocky sea shore, or the richness and luxury of an Italian landscape, or at the least a piece of mountain in Scotland or Wales: less than that will scarcely draw our eyes to beholding. Yet if you can get no pleasure out of the sight of a Warwickshire meadow, or the hedgerows and little waving hills of my native Essex, or the flat fields and limestone banks of my adopted Oxfordshire-Berkshire land, I doubt your capacity for really seeing the huge Swiss mountain and valley scenery, or the flank of the Apennine, or the fairy-land of the Garda Lake, or the terror of the Thrasymene. What our modern landscape visitors usually fail to see, is a certain something which we call “character,” which does not depend on either bigness, or roughness, or richness; a something which means the expression of a human interest, the telling of a tale of life and incident, one may say, the touching the imagination through the eye. If we can give people this faculty of seeing character in landscape, almost every “flat and uninteresting country” is all changed, and becomes a fairyland full of beauty and interest; and the lead of our ordinary English landscape becomes pure gold. I will promise to any one who goes with open eyes some month or two hence into any unspoiled country-side, that they will find almost every field’s end a paradise that will cry out to them in a voice not to be resisted: “Love the earth which you dwell upon, and the soil which nourishes you.” And, surely, when we have gained by the use of our eyes such ineffable pleasure as this, we shall no longer plead poverty for failing to keep this inheritance of our fathers free from spoiling and degradation; we shall not allow the passing convenience of the minute to deprive us all of what at least should be public property, to wit, the beauty of the face of the land.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: The answer retains Morris’s examples, first-person references to Essex and Oxfordshire-Berkshire, and his explanation of landscape character. Its conclusion clearly connects seeing ordinary beauty to protecting the land.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: What do you value about the old villages and buildings in the English countryside?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: In landscapes which include building, Nature and Art, when they are happily harmonized, produce the greatest pleasure that the eye can have, and appeal most directly to the imagination. In such landscapes we have before us history in its most delightful, and even, I will say, its most instructive, shape. The circumstances of life in the Middle Ages in England, and the genius of our forefathers led them specially to what I should call the embroidery of the general face of the country. If we lacked the romance of the great walled towns of the continent, we had as a compensation abundance of ancient villages with their small but beautiful churches, full of individuality and character, and their generously-built manor houses and homesteads, which, between them all, once made an English country-side a special treasure not to be seen anywhere else. Grievous as has been the injury to this treasure-store, much as we have been robbed of it by our own folly and blindness, there is still enough of it left to teach us and delight us. I am speaking of the familiar houses and little country churches scattered all over the land. If you do not feel the beauty of the little grey cottage, which has stood so many storms and evil days, and is still sound and trim; or of the little village church, brimful of the history of six centuries, you cannot feel that of the stately cathedral. These, above all things, we want to get people to see with their eyes, and to value according to the amount of pleasure which they will get from them when their eyes are open. Keep your village houses weathertight, trim, and useful; and where you must, build others beside them. But why, when you build these, should you make them specimens of the worst buildings in the worst suburbs of a modern town? If you build them solidly and unpretentiously, using good materials natural to their own country-side, and if you do not stint the tenant of due elbow-room and garden, it is little likely that you will have done any offence to the beauty of the country-side or the older houses in it.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: The answer accurately presents Morris’s appreciation of village buildings as historical, beautiful, and instructive, while preserving his practical advice on maintenance and new construction. The omitted caveats do not reverse his position.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: Why are you so opposed to restoring old buildings?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: I appeal to you to help to put an end to this folly of restoration. If the guardians of old buildings are careful of the stability of these buildings, and will take care, and great and constant care, to preserve what they have got, they may safely leave the question of restoring them to what they have never been to a period when we have at last conquered a genuine style of architecture of our own. The restorers did not see that when they had “restored” old work, it did not look right: though their mouldings were identical of section with those of the thirteenth century, and though their carved foliage and figures were “accurately” copied from casts of that period, they did not look in the least like thirteenth-century work. If they had had the due use of their eyes, they would have seen this at once, and then fallen to reason as to why it was so; they would surely soon have found out that there were abundant reasons against the possibility of imitating the ancient work: the principal one being that since that time the whole structure of society has altered, and the position of the workman changed; that the long chain of tradition which was unbroken till the end of the Middle Ages had been snapped. They should have held their hands, remembering the fatal risk they ran, if perchance they were wrong, of destroying that which they could never have again, the living expression of the very heart and soul of their ancestors. Unhappily they never brought their quasi-knowledge to the test of their eyesight, and the result has been that they have most seriously injured all the great cathedrals of England, and almost destroyed some. The buildings of the Middle Ages are far too sturdy and rational to be injured by fair wear and tear. If an old building is well looked after, danger can be met by the engineering skill of the day, and the building made absolutely sound without any tampering with its surface; a defective stone may be replaced by a new one where it is structurally necessary. The surface in such buildings is so far from being damaged by the action of wind and weather, that, on the contrary, it adds a beauty to it: adds a beauty to its original beauties, mind. Time will most often make a good building very much more beautiful, assimilating it to the surrounding nature, until it seems scarcely to have been made, but rather to have grown up from the very soil, an unartificial, inevitable growth. To guard our ancient buildings jealously, therefore, against brutal destruction and egotistical falsification, seems to me to be one of the prime duties of those who are trying to make people use their eyes.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: Although most wording is authentic, the answer says “I appeal to you” before explaining why, then ends with a general duty to guard buildings; it largely omits the direct reasons restoration is folly. More importantly, it removes Morris’s crucial distinction between preserving stability and destructive restoration, leaving an overly sweeping portrayal of opposition to restoration.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: How should you decide whether to pursue art as a profession?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: If you are quite sure that you have got in you the irrepressible desire, you need no test of capacity to begin with; you will yourself know that you have in you some power of creation; in that case do not hesitate, but throw yourself into it for better or worse, and take what will come. But if you do not feel that you have the capacity or desire, then, by all means, if you can, study Art as a recreation or a piece of education, but do not pledge yourself to live by it; for, if you do, you will be a burden to Art, and will, if you have the insight which a serious person ought to have, feel yourself to be in a false and ignominious position. Most men who have any character or strength of will, can, by concentration and diligence, learn the practice of a profession for which they are not really fit; and this very commonly happens in the arts, and produces men who, as far as the arts are concerned, are mere mechanical pretenders, though not necessarily so wilfully. So make yourselves sure that you have in you the essentials of an artist before you study Art as a handicraft by which to earn your bread. But, if you are able to do this, and become a genuine handicraftsman, I congratulate you on your position, whatever else may happen to you, for you then belong to the only group of people in civilization which is really happy: persons whose necessary daily work is inseparable from their greatest pleasure.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: This is a direct, substantial response using Morris’s original counsel, including both the warning against treating art merely as a livelihood and his praise of work joined to pleasure.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: What standards do you expect artists to hold themselves to?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: You must be absolutely faithful to your Art, and, though I do not ask you to judge other artists severely, you must be hard with yourselves; and, though you may never be able to do your best, yet you must aim at doing so, and take yourselves, your better selves, for your judges, and not people who know nothing about Art, and whom you may easily hoodwink. Your position as modern artists makes this all the more imperative on you. To the medieval craftsman generally, ornament was only incidental. If his ornament was not good (which by the way it almost always was), at least he was making a shoe, or a knife, or a cup, or what not, as well as ornament. But you who make nothing but ornament, please to remember that a piece of white paper, or an oak panel, is a pretty thing, and don't spoil it.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: The answer faithfully preserves Morris’s standards of self-criticism, artistic integrity, and care not to spoil a surface with ornament. The omitted preamble is not needed to answer the question.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: How should you guard against becoming mannered in your art?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: Attend to that warning, though it may in some people’s mouths mean nothing except that they have no eyes for the ornamental side of Art. The corrective to overmuch manner is, first, diligent study of Nature, and, secondly, intelligent study of the work of the ages of Art. The third corrective is infallible if you have it; but you cannot all have it: it is imagination. But, at least, if you have not got it, do not pretend to it; or you had better give up Art altogether.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: The advice and its wording match the excerpt closely. “That warning” refers to a warning omitted from the answer, but the following specific correctives make the response understandable.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: What advice would you give about using colour in ornamental art?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: Be rather restrained than over-luxurious in colour, or you weary the eye. Do not attempt over-refinements in colour, but be frank and simple. If you look at the pieces of colouring that most delight you in ornamental work, as, for example, a Persian carpet, or an illuminated book of the Middle Ages, and analyse its elements, you will be surprised at the simplicity of it, the few tints used, the modesty of the tints, and therewithal the clearness and precision of all boundary lines. In all fine flat colouring, there are regular systems of dividing colour from colour. Above all, don't attempt iridescent blendings of colour which look like decomposition. They are about as much as possible the reverse of useful. One can only give warnings against possible faults; it is clearly impossible to teach colour by words, even ever so little of it, though it can be taught in a workshop, at least partially.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: The answer preserves Morris’s concrete guidance on restraint, simple tints, clear boundaries, and avoiding iridescent blends. The moved closing qualification is supported by the excerpt and gives useful context.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: What should students designing figures pay particular attention to?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: Do not spare yourselves in drawing from the living model, draped as well as undraped; in fact, draw drapery continually, for the beauty of your design must largely depend on the design of the drapery. You should aim at getting so familiar with all this that you can at last make your design with ease, and something like certainty, without drawing from models in the first draught, though you should make studies from nature afterwards.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: The advice directly answers the question and closely preserves the excerpt, including its emphasis on drawing drapery and later making studies from nature.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: What makes medieval designs more interesting as ornament than many modern designs?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: In good medieval designs, there is a peculiar kind of interest and ornamental quality, which is quite lacking in most of those of the Renaissance and of modern times. This seems to be caused by the planes of the figures being very near each other in the medieval designs, and their being separated from each other by long perspectives in the later periods; which latter method produces an emptiness and lack of interest which destroys all ornamental effect. The great hall and the solar or drawing-room at Hampton Court are a good example. The tapestries in the hall are of the Renaissance period, and fully illustrate this fault of emptiness; those in the solar show beautifully-draped figures. The hall tapestries look dull and vulgar, the solar tapestries full of interest and incident, and are the best possible ornament for the walls. The contrast is well worth noting, as both sets are fine of their kind.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: The response accurately presents Morris’s contrast between closely arranged figures and long perspective, and retains his Hampton Court example. The supplied clarification resolves a fragment without changing its meaning.

99eb41bf564e683b.txt.question: What do you hope students will take from their work?
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.answer: I have been much encouraged with what I have seen of the enthusiasm, and aspirations toward the right road, of the Birmingham School of Art during the last few years, and I beg you to go on encouraging us of the last generation, so that the next after you may need no encouragement save what they will get from their own work, the pleasure of creating beautiful things, which is the greatest pleasure in the world.
99eb41bf564e683b.txt.reason: The excerpt says students should encourage Morris’s generation, so that the next generation may gain encouragement from the pleasure of creating beautiful things. The answer retains that point but shifts the question’s focus: it does not directly explain what the students themselves should take from their work.

9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.question: Why do you think poor people need protection when they are brought before magistrates?
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.answer: No poor man has any chance of obtaining justice in a magistrate’s court; and no better instance of the necessity of some corporate protection for the victims of the law could be given than what happened when nine prisoners were able to appeal against the unjust and malignant sentences pronounced against them. I believe none of these poor men would have been able to appeal but for the responsible bail provided for them chiefly through the efforts of Mrs Besant. No one can appeal from a magistrate’s decision unless he can find two sureties who will bind themselves to pay the costs of the appeal if rejected: where can a poor man find such sureties who may have to pay £50 in case of failure?
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.reason: The answer closely preserves Morris’s wording and reasoning, but presents Headlam’s claim that no poor man could obtain justice as Morris’s own direct statement. Morris explicitly endorses Headlam’s words in the excerpt, so the attribution is not wholly misleading, but the shift should be clarified before training.

9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.question: What makes it so difficult for a poor man to appeal a magistrate’s decision?
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.answer: No one can appeal from a magistrate’s decision unless he can find two sureties who will bind themselves to pay the costs of the appeal if rejected; where can a poor man find such sureties who may have to pay £50 in case of failure? I believe none of the nine poor men would have been able to appeal but for the responsible bail provided for them chiefly through the efforts of Mrs Besant.
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.reason: It directly explains the requirement for two sureties and the potential £50 liability, then connects that obstacle to the prisoners’ bail through Mrs Besant. “The nine poor men” is a clear, supported clarification of “these poor men.”

9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.question: What do you hope the protective League will do?
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.answer: The protective League should help all persons without distinction of opinion who ‘get into trouble’ in their endeavours to defend freedom of speech. If it performs its functions duly, it will take up one side of the attack, and will assuredly do good service. Well-to-do people especially should join this League, and help it both with their money, for a good deal of that will be necessary, and also by sending in their names as persons to be relied on for the prisoners taken in the war for bail and sureties of Freedom of Speech.
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.reason: The response faithfully combines Morris’s description of the League’s promise and purpose with his specific call for financial and personal support. It answers the question directly and retains his characteristic language.

9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.question: Do you think the fight for freedom of speech will be over soon?
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.answer: The struggle for mere freedom of speech (whatever it may lead to) will certainly be a long and arduous one. Even the present idiotic Tory Government will not be easy to get rid of; and though it is possible that a Liberal Government would treat us better, at least for a while, yet such a trifle as a mere change of ministry will not cure the gangrene of the law-courts, nor will it have much influence on the reaction which is obviously setting in and which is the necessary accompaniment to the obvious progress of revolutionary ideas. The struggle will be a long one, and must be carried on by us in a manner which will mean steadily and pertinaciously harassing the apparently all-powerful executive on all sides.
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.reason: It answers the question immediately and preserves Morris’s assessment that the struggle will be long, along with his political qualifications and proposed course of action. The omitted explanatory clause does not materially change the meaning.

9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.question: What should people do to support those prosecuted for defending freedom of speech?
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.answer: The protective League should help all persons without distinction of opinion who ‘get into trouble’ in their endeavours to defend freedom of speech. Well-to-do people especially should join this League, and help it both with their money, for a good deal of that will be necessary, and also by sending in their names as persons to be relied on for the prisoners taken in the war for bail and sureties of Freedom of Speech. The struggle must be carried on by us steadily and pertinaciously, harassing the apparently all-powerful executive on all sides.
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.reason: It gives relevant practical advice about joining the League, contributing money, and providing names for bail and sureties, then adds Morris’s broader view of the struggle. The combined passages remain coherent and authentic.

9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.question: What did you think of Mrs Besant’s part in helping the prisoners?
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.answer: I believe none of these poor men would have been able to appeal but for the responsible bail provided for them chiefly through the efforts of Mrs Besant. Her untiring energy and devotion throughout the whole affair will surely win her a place in the hearts of all working men; and all Socialists will be glad to see her name on the committee as an earnest of due fulfilment of the League’s promises.
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.reason: The answer accurately preserves Morris’s praise of Mrs Besant’s efforts and connects them to the prisoners’ appeals and the League committee. Clarifying “its promises” as “the League’s promises” is harmless.

9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.question: Do you think changing the government would solve the injustice in the courts?
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.answer: Such a trifle as a mere change of ministry will not cure the gangrene of the law-courts; nor will it have much influence on the reaction which is obviously setting in and which is the necessary accompaniment to the obvious progress of revolutionary ideas. It is possible that a Liberal Government would treat us better, at least for a while, because the Liberals may be forced to take the matter up and come in on it; but even the present idiotic Tory Government will not be easy to get rid of.
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.reason: It directly answers that changing ministry would not cure the courts, while retaining Morris’s qualification that a Liberal Government might treat them better temporarily. Reordering the passage preserves its meaning and distinctive phrasing.

9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.question: Why do you believe a League for legal protection is needed?
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.answer: There is a necessity for some corporate protection for the victims of the law. No poor man has any chance of obtaining justice in a magistrate’s court, and no one can appeal from a magistrate’s decision unless he can find two sureties who will bind themselves to pay the costs of the appeal if rejected. Where can a poor man find such sureties who may have to pay £50 in case of failure? The nine prisoners were able to appeal against the unjust and malignant sentences pronounced against them, and I believe none of these poor men would have been able to appeal but for the responsible bail provided for them chiefly through the efforts of Mrs Besant.
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.reason: Most of the response closely follows the excerpt and the question, but the statement that no poor man had a chance of justice originates as Stewart Headlam’s words, which Morris endorses rather than states as his own. The answer should preserve that attribution or make the distinction clear.

9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.question: How do you regard the Pall Mall Gazette’s involvement in this agitation?
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.answer: It would be unfair and ungenerous not to acknowledge the great services which the Pall Mall Gazette has done to the popular cause throughout this agitation. The League which it has set on foot will, if it performs its functions duly, take up one side of the attack, and will assuredly do good service.
9e44e5db8edc0527.txt.reason: The answer accurately conveys Morris’s acknowledgment of the Gazette’s services and his conditional confidence in the League it established. Its reordering makes the response direct without distorting his wording or meaning.

9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.question: What do you think the labour movement is really trying to achieve?
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.answer: The question is, what is it that you really want? Higher wages; more regular employment? Shorter working hours, better education for your children; old age pensions, libraries, parks and more? These things and things like them you want, of course; but what else do you want? If this is all you want, you will get such measure of those things as your employers and their Committee, the House of Commons, can give without ruining themselves, as they phrase it. But I cannot think that the workmen mean nothing but improvement in the condition of the working-classes. Imperfect, erring, unorganised, chaotic as that movement is, there is a spirit of antagonism to our present foolish wasteful system in it, and a sense of the unity of labour as against the exploiters of labour, which is the one necessary idea for those who are ever so little conscious of working toward Socialism. What makes life worth living is something more than constant work and a ‘fair days wage for a fair days work’: self-respect, happy and fit work, leisure, beautiful surroundings—in a word, the earth our own and the fullness thereof. This good life cannot be attained to till we are essentially and practically socialised.
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.reason: The answer retains Morris's distinctive wording and faithfully presents the excerpt's contrast between limited reforms and the movement's socialist aspirations, directly addressing the question.

9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.question: Do you think workers can get lasting improvements while the present system remains?
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.answer: No serious improvement in the material condition of the working classes is to be expected while the present system lasts; that can only come from Socialism. Measures for improving their material condition without altering their position mean more or less feeding the dog with pieces of his own tail: you better the condition of one group of workers at the expense of the others, and thereby make partial content out of general discontent, hoodwink the people, and prevent their action. The unemployed cannot be provided for in the mass while the present system lasts, because periodically there are people out of work who can work, a necessity of the competition for employment; and if places were provided for those who fail in the competition, there would be a tendency for wages to fall amongst those generally employed. From neither party can you expect any measure really socialistic; by pressure you may get from the Liberals improvements in the present creaky and clumsy electoral machinery, of some use when you want to get M.P.s to do your dirty work in Parliament. While the battle for Socialism is going on, you can only have the hope of realizing Socialism.
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.reason: The answer combines passages from the excerpt without changing their argument: reforms under the system are limited, unemployment is structurally tied to competition, and lasting improvement requires Socialism. Its language remains substantially Morris's.

9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.question: Why do you expect the struggle for socialism to bring disturbance and suffering?
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.answer: I cannot for the life of me see how the great change which we long for can come otherwise than by disturbance and suffering of some kind. The rise in condition of life, if not in position, of the working-classes must disturb the smooth going ways of the market, reduce the profit of their employers, and therefore reduce their employing power and their spending power, and injure many forms of the production of useless articles on which the working men largely live. That would be a gain if we were living in a socialist condition; but as we are now, it would mean the throwing out of work of numbers of industrious men, the greater part of whom it would be difficult to find employment for. The upward movement of labour, the consciousness amongst working men that they should be citizens and not machines, will have to be paid for like other good things, and the price will be no light one. Yet we shall not be called upon to gain our point by battle in the field: war has been commercialized, and human valour must give way to the longest purse. Can the combat between Commercialism, or the system of reckless waste, and Communism, or the system of neighbourly common sense, be fought out without loss and suffering? Plainly speaking, I know that it cannot.
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.reason: The response accurately draws on the excerpt's explanation of market disruption, unemployment, and the cost of labour's upward movement. Its original phrasing is largely preserved and the reordered material remains coherent.

9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.question: What do you think workers should aim for beyond better wages and steady work?
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.answer: Those who have a wild fancy to be free men, to have their affairs under their own control; those who wish to work happily and unwastefully, to restore that part of the earth's surface which is spoilt and keep that which is unspoilt, to enjoy rest and thought and labour without fear or remorse—in a word, those who wish to live like men—let them say: good wages or bad, good times or bad, good masters or bad, let us use them now as we may, yet not so much for the present profit we may get out of them as for hastening the realization of the new society, the time when at last we shall be free because we are equal. What makes life worth living is self-respect, happy and fit work, leisure, beautiful surroundings; in a word, the earth our own and the fullness thereof. Constant work and a ‘fair days wage for a fair days work’ are but a low form of workman's prosperity; this good life cannot be attained to till we are essentially and practically socialised.
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.reason: The answer directly addresses the question by joining Morris's appeal for freedom, self-direction, fulfilling work, and equality with his account of the good life. The phrasing and argument are supported by the excerpt.

9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.question: Why do you favour forming a genuine socialist party?
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.answer: We have settled that we want to go into Parliament, and for that a party is definitely necessary. Declaring ourselves Socialists, we shall formulate our immediate tactics toward that end; such a party, once formed, would not break up any existing bodies but include them, and would have a claim on all genuine Socialists. Until it is formed, though we may do good propagandist work, we shall do nothing worth speaking of in the political way. There are two or three socialist forces in this country, partly propagandist and partly with electoral views, probably of no great strength as to count of noses; there is at least some rivalry between them and sometimes dissension. Besides these bodies are many pronounced Socialists unattached to either, and many who tend towards Socialism and would be certain to be absorbed by it when it takes more definite action. My hope is that we shall do so much propagandist work, and convert so many people to Socialism, that they will insist on having a genuine Socialist party which shall do the due work, and will not allow the personal fads and vanities of leaders to stand in the way of real business.
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.reason: The response gives Morris's stated rationale for a party and preserves his characteristic language, including the distinction between propagandist work and effective political action. The omitted material does not undermine the answer.

9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.question: What should socialists do while they are not yet strong enough to act as a party?
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.answer: Until we can do our party-work effectively, I think we had better leave off the pretence of doing it at all; we had better confine ourselves to the old teaching and preaching of Socialism pure and simple, which is more or less neglected amidst the futile attempt to act as a party when we have no party. Above all, we have to point out to working-men who feel socialist sympathies that many measures which may be for the temporary good of their class are but temporary and experimental, adapted only for the present state of things, and are not for genuine Socialists to press forward. Let our Liberal and radical, and, if they will, our Tory friends make these experiments, and take all the responsibility for their failure, for in the long term fail they will. The present system will admit of no permanent change in this direction: unlimited competition, the laissez-faire of the old Manchester school, the privileges of the possessing class, modified by gifts of the improved work-house kind—in a word, the machine-life of the useful classes made as little burdensome to them as can be—is all that can be got out of it.
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.reason: The answer faithfully preserves Morris's recommendations to return to teaching and preaching Socialism and to leave temporary reforms to other political parties. Its concise edits retain the original argument and voice.

9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.question: How do you think socialism will eventually be achieved?
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.answer: Socialists hope so far to conquer public opinion that at last a majority of the Parliament shall be sent to sit in the House as avowed Socialists and the delegates of Socialists, and on that should follow what legislation might be necessary. The time for this may be very far ahead, yet most people would now think that the hope of doing it is by no means unreasonable. Before that can be done, the thinking part of the population will have gone Socialist, so that nothing but the last act of the play will remain to be played. That is the end, a long way off doubtless but in nowise an impossible end, a dream without form.
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.reason: The response accurately describes Morris's expectation that Socialists would win public opinion and parliamentary representation, while preserving his qualification that the prospect was distant but not unreasonable. The final phrase is also present in the excerpt.

9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.question: What did you think had changed in the socialist movement?
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.answer: Within the last five years or so the movement which represents the change from the society of so-called free-contract to that of communal organization has undergone a great change. In the early days of our movement we had nothing to think of seriously except preaching Socialism to those who knew nothing of it but the name, if indeed they knew that. We hoped that amongst those we addressed our words might touch a few who were sympathetic with the movement, and capable of learning what we had to teach—or indeed a good deal more—and in that hope we were not disappointed. The idea of successful insurrection within a measurable distance of time is now only in the heads of the anarchists; almost everyone has ceased to believe in the change coming by catastrophe. Instead, Socialists hope to conquer public opinion, so that at last a majority of Parliament shall be avowed Socialists and delegates of Socialists. The working-classes are no longer hostile to Socialism: they even vaguely approve of it generally, and from time to time take action through strikes and other agitation, amounting to a claim to be recognized as citizens, and not looked upon as merely part of the machinery for profit-bearing production. The number who can vaguely be classed as Socialists has increased enormously, and there has been a very considerable increase in those who definitely profess Socialism.
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.reason: The answer accurately assembles the excerpt's account of changes in strategy, parliamentary hopes, and working-class attitudes. Though selective, it remains coherent, relevant, and strongly grounded in Morris's own language.

9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.question: Why do you think workers' demands may bring hardship even when they are justified?
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.answer: The upward movement of labour, the consciousness amongst working men that they should be citizens and not machines, will have to be paid for like other good things, and the price will be no light one. The rise in condition of life, if not in position, of the working-classes must disturb the smooth going ways of the market, reduce the profit of their employers, and therefore reduce their employing power and their spending power, and injure many forms of the production of useless articles on which working men largely live. As we are now, it would mean the throwing out of work of numbers of industrious men, the greater part of whom it would be difficult to find employment for. I had a long letter from a lady whom I knew something of, once very rich, and the wife of a very rich manufacturer in Manchester: she complained of competition, and how they who once made a large profit on their works were now carrying on at a loss; she also expostulated with me for stirring up the men to cry out for higher wages and the like, which injured the power of employment of the masters. At first when I read the letter I was angry; then I laughed. But at last I said to myself: after all she is right from her point of view; yes, and perhaps from her men's point of view also. I cannot see how the great change which we long for can come otherwise than by disturbance and suffering of some kind.
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.reason: The answer accurately combines Morris's explanation of market disruption with his anecdote about the Manchester manufacturer and his recognition of her perspective. The passage is relevant and preserves his wording and reasoning.

9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.question: What worries you about political concessions to workers?
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.answer: Measures for improving the material condition of the working classes without altering their position mean more or less feeding the dog with pieces of his own tail: you better the condition of one group of workers at the expense of the others, and thereby make partial content out of general discontent, hoodwink the people, and prevent their action. The Tory instinct is to make a showy benevolent present, which in the long run will be of no use, rather than yield a right however small. From neither party can you expect any measure really socialistic; the present system will admit of no permanent change in this direction. Concessions of the improved work-house kind leave the machine-life of the useful classes made as little burdensome to them as can be; that is all that can be got out of the present system.
9f02d7aa55c03127.txt.reason: The answer accurately conveys Morris's concerns about partial reforms, Tory concessions, and the limits of the existing system. It is focused on the question and retains his characteristic phrasing.

9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.question: How do you see the relationship between Chartism and the new Socialist movement?
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.answer: The agitation towards Socialism, which is now once more afoot in England, cannot be dissociated from the expression of discontent which flickered over England so long, and, in the opinion of many, nay most, of the contented classes, died out at Kennington Common in 1848. This expression of most righteous discontent was indeed smothered for a while by the wave of material middle-class prosperity which rolled over England after 1854; but such a prosperity, founded on class domination and the rule of the sweaters or capitalists, cannot be long-lived, as we are now on all sides beginning to find out. The discontent of the mass of the people oppressed under communal slavery—this discontent which seemed to most to have died with Chartism in 1848, has risen from the dead in the more formidable shape of Scientific Socialism.
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.reason: The answer closely preserves Morris’s wording and directly explains Chartism’s relationship to Scientific Socialism as a renewed expression of popular discontent. The omitted material does not alter that central point.

9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.question: What makes John Sketchley’s political journey important to you?
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.answer: One of the few living men who form the visible links between the past hope and the present hopes of the workers of this country, is Mr. John Sketchley, the author of this book. From his boyhood he was attracted to the cause of the people, worked steadily and faithfully through the years during which Chartism was alive and dreaded, and when to be a Chartist was no light matter, and was a weight not to be borne by a coward or a shuffler. When Chartism was dead, he yet associated himself with the forward movement, and was a pronounced Republican; finally, he went forward with the progress of events, and instead of folding his hands and looking back complacently on his old work as on a pleasant story, as many have done, has grasped the principles of Scientific Socialism which were developed on the Continent. Since the days of Chartism he has been associated with the movement abroad, and sees clearly that no social agitation which is not international has any real chance of success. His career is important and instructive for us because he represents a sleeping cause—not a dead one—awakened again.
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.reason: This is Morris’s third-person account of Sketchley, not a claim that the experiences belong to Morris. It retains the excerpt’s distinctive phrasing and explains why the career is instructive, though it is a long response to a personal-sounding question.

9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.question: Do you think getting the vote is enough to bring about real change?
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.answer: The suffrage will be but little—nay, no use in the hands of those who look upon a vote as an end and not as a means: the slaves of capital must needs elect masters and not delegates. It is but little use our having got rid of feudalism if the greed of commercialism is to rule over us.
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.reason: The wording is authentic, but the excerpt explicitly frames this as what Sketchley says to political waverers (“he can speak convincingly and with authority, showing them”). Removing that attribution and presenting the argument directly as Morris’s own leaves a significant attribution problem.

9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.question: What do you think will happen to workers who have gained a better position through trade unions?
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.answer: The time is coming, and speedily too, when those who have won a kind of position as an aristocracy of labour by means of the trades unions, will find that position slipping away from them, and will be driven to feel their solidarity with those hitherto more unfortunate workers who have been oppressed by the present system of capital and labour without licence or limit.
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.reason: The answer closely reproduces the excerpt and responds directly, but the source introduces this prediction as part of what Sketchley tells political waverers. Removing that framing makes a third-party argument appear to be Morris’s unqualified personal statement.

9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.question: Why do you believe the Socialist movement needs to be international?
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.answer: No social agitation which is not international has any real chance of success. Mr. Sketchley sees this clearly: since the days of Chartism he has been associated with the movement abroad, and has grasped the principles of Scientific Socialism which were developed on the Continent.
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.reason: The excerpt attributes the view that international agitation is necessary to Sketchley (“sees clearly”), not explicitly to Morris. The answer also gives no reason for the claim beyond restating it, despite the question asking why.

9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.question: What would you say to people who are still opposed to socialism?
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.answer: I commend this book both to our comrades and our enemies, with some sort of a hope that the latter may feel their false position while it is yet time for them to become our comrades also, and with a certain and assured hope that no resistance on their part will in the long run avail them, or prevent them from losing their position of masters of slaves.
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.reason: The answer closely follows Morris’s introductory appeal to the book’s opponents, preserving both the invitation to join the cause and his confidence that resistance will fail. It is a relevant, historically voiced response.

9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.question: How do you describe the purpose of the book you are introducing?
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.answer: The following pages form a book giving information concerning that Social Revolution which may be said rather to be in progress than to be at hand; information to those who stand outside it, either as curious spectators, or as declared enemies, but encouragement to those who are within it, and are doing their best in their generation to hasten its progress, or to light the way for its footsteps in the earliest hours of the new day.
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.reason: The answer reproduces the excerpt’s description of the book’s dual purpose—information for outsiders and encouragement for participants—and retains Morris’s characteristic language and imagery.

9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.question: Why do you think this book matters to the Socialist movement?
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.answer: The literature of Scientific Socialism in the English tongue is yet but scanty, and a book planned as this, and carried out with so much care as to figures—to speak of nothing else—will doubtless be heartily welcomed by all our comrades in the cause. Besides its intrinsic worth, the book has another and special claim on our attention in being the work of an old Chartist. Mr. Sketchley has many special qualifications for writing it, and the mere fact of his doing so with the care and completeness he has exercised ought to be an encouragement to us, since he represents a sleeping cause—not a dead one—awakened again.
9f1f48e7ae26c561.txt.reason: The answer combines two relevant passages without changing their meaning: the book fills a scarcity in English-language Socialist literature, and its careful work by an old Chartist encourages the movement. It retains Morris’s wording and voice.

9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.question: What did you think of Professor Stuart's election speeches?
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.answer: Nothing could have been more commonplace and unsatisfactory than Professor Stuart's election speeches; he is obviously taking his place in the House of Commons as an advocate of laissez-faire. If Professor Stuart has very advanced opinions he at least did not venture to put them forward even before such a very Radical constituency as Hackney. The Liberal press has been engaged in singing the praises of the new member as a useful politician and much advanced thinker; this may be, but if a man is to be judged by his utterances, all this jubilant praise is a little overdone.
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.reason: The excerpt directly describes the speeches as commonplace and unsatisfactory, identifies Stuart as an advocate of laissez-faire, and calls the praise overdone. The answer preserves Morris's wording and directly addresses the question.

9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.question: Why did you call the free-trade and fair-trade dispute a battle of the Kites and Crows?
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.answer: For the workers this is just a battle of the Kites and Crows. Whether the landlords tax their victuals in order to gain higher rents by means of protection, or the capitalists lower their wages, and land them in such terribly bad times as the present by means of free trade, they will be fleeced all the same until they make up their minds to take matters into their own hands.
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.reason: The answer reproduces the excerpt’s explanation that workers are fleeced under either protection or free trade, retaining Morris’s characteristic imagery and phrasing.

9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.question: What should workers do if they want to stop being fleeced?
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.answer: They will be fleeced all the same until they make up their minds to take matters into their own hands. Whether the landlords tax their victuals in order to gain higher rents by means of protection, or the capitalists lower their wages, and land them in such terribly bad times as the present by means of free trade, the workers are fleeced all the same.
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.reason: The first sentence gives Morris’s answer, but the reordered second sentence repeats the claim and weakens the original construction, which explains that workers will be fleeced under either system until they take matters into their own hands.

9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.question: Why were you disappointed with the Hackney Radicals?
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.answer: It is disappointing indeed that the Hackney Radicals could see no other course open to them than voting for a man who does not hold their views. They had lately issued so Democratic a programme, yet were so blinded by the excitement of an electoral contest as not to see that, for the workers, the contest between so-called fair-trade and free-trade was just a battle of the Kites and Crows. They were terrified at the idea of being represented by such an extinct monster as a protectionist Tory, and a little doubtful as to whither their Radicalism would lead them in the long run. But even supposing the said queer monster had been returned, it would not have damaged Radicalism so much as the watering down of the present very feeble Radical party in the House by such a man as Professor Stuart. If they had no candidate whom they could vote for with a clear conscience, why should they have voted at all? Abstention from the poll, accompanied by a protest so distinct as to make it obvious that the abstention was organised, and was the result, not of political languor, but of political insight, would have read a sharp lesson to those politicians, so-called Radicals, who are hanging about waiting to see how the cat will jump.
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.reason: Most of the answer closely follows Morris’s argument, but it combines passages and paraphrases the link between the trade dispute and the Radicals’ decision, including the added phrasing “the contest between so-called fair-trade and free-trade.” A more source-faithful answer should avoid that connective reframing.

9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.question: What do you think Radicalism ought to mean?
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.answer: If Radical is to mean anything else than Whig “writ large,” it must mean some one who claims full political power for the people, in order that it may be used by them for dealing with the social questions which really concern them. The workers will be fleeced all the same under protection or free trade until they make up their minds to take matters into their own hands.
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.reason: The definition is directly from the excerpt and answers the question clearly. The added observation about workers being fleeced is also supported by the adjacent passage and remains relevant.

9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.question: Would you have advised the Hackney Radicals to abstain from voting?
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.answer: If they had no candidate whom they could vote for with a clear conscience, why should they have voted at all? Abstention from the poll, accompanied by a protest so distinct as to make it obvious that the abstention was organised, and was the result, not of political languor, but of political insight, would have read a sharp lesson to those politicians, so-called Radicals, who are hanging about waiting to see how the cat will jump. Even supposing the protectionist Tory had been returned, it would not have damaged Radicalism so much as the watering down of the present very feeble Radical party in the House by such a man as Professor Stuart.
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.reason: The excerpt explicitly argues that abstention with an organised, politically insightful protest would teach the so-called Radicals a lesson, and compares its consequences with Stuart’s election. The answer preserves the original language and responds directly.

9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.question: What kind of protest would have made abstention meaningful?
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.answer: Abstention from the poll accompanied by a protest so distinct as to make it obvious that the abstention was organised, and was the result, not of political languor, but of political insight, would have read a sharp lesson to those politicians, so-called Radicals, who are hanging about waiting to see how the cat will jump.
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.reason: This is a faithful extract explaining that abstention should be visibly organised and result from political insight rather than languor. It directly answers the question and retains Morris’s distinctive wording.

9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.question: Do you think the old political parties will survive?
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.answer: Society will presently wake up and find the Whigs extinct, the Liberals extinct, the true Radicals rapidly becoming Socialists and facing a party which will have been forced to drop its mask; which may be called Tory or what you will, but which proclaims at last without hypocrisy its real maxim, “Keep them Down.”
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.reason: The answer reproduces Morris’s prediction that the Whigs and Liberals will become extinct, while true Radicals become Socialists and face a party openly committed to keeping them down. It is authentic, though its answer is more a prediction than a direct yes-or-no response.

9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.question: What did you see happening to the true Radicals?
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.answer: The true Radicals were rapidly becoming Socialists and facing a party which would have been forced to drop its mask; which might be called Tory or what you will, but which would proclaim at last without hypocrisy its real maxim, “Keep them Down.” Morris also points to Henry George's statement, quoted with approval by the Pall Mall Gazette, that the late election in America had destroyed the two old parties there, and that a new party was springing up in their place whose business it would be to solve the social questions of the day.
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.reason: The answer changes Morris’s future-facing prediction (“will presently wake up and find” and “which will have been forced”) into past and conditional constructions, altering its temporal stance. The added Henry George context is supported but does not directly answer the question, and the third-person “Morris also points” is not suited to the persona.

9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.question: What did you believe the people needed political power for?
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.answer: Full political power for the people, in order that it may be used by them for dealing with the social questions which really concern them. The workers, whether under protection or free trade, will be fleeced all the same until they make up their minds to take matters into their own hands.
9f6cdf606ab13abb.txt.reason: The central answer is Morris’s wording: political power is for dealing with social questions that concern the people. The added workers’ observation is grounded in the excerpt and thematically relevant, though the fragment opening is slightly less conversational.

a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.question: Why do you think people need to learn about socialism to understand the society they live in?
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.answer: It is only by learning something of Socialism that we can understand what the present society is, what it aims at doing, and what are the means whereby it carries out its aims. Most people, I fancy, never put to themselves the question: why am I in the position in which I am? Why is the workman, the beggar, the pauper, the criminal in his position; and why is the great capitalist, the land owner, in his position? Few have doubted the necessity for the existence of the classes into which society is divided, or suspected that the arrangement might not go on for ever. We Socialists, on the contrary, believe that we know why these classes exist and how they have grown into what they are, a growth inevitable indeed, but so far from being eternal that it will itself destroy itself and give place to something else, a society in which there will be no rich and no poor. Therefore, before we look specially into what Socialism is, let us consider how our present society is composed; by the light of that contrast we shall see things clearly that might otherwise be obscure.
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.reason: The response closely retains the excerpt's wording and reasoning, with the minor “Most people” adjustment making its address more conversational. It directly explains why understanding socialism illuminates existing class society.

a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.question: What do you see as the basic injustice in the way society divides work and wealth?
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.answer: For ages both the work and the wealth won by it from nature have been unequally divided: there has always, since the dawn of history in communities called civilized, been a class which has had much work and little wealth living beside another class which has had much wealth and little work. Today it is still a rule of our society, amidst all our refinement, all our shrinking from violence and rudeness, that those who work most shall fare the hardest, and that the reward of idleness shall be abundant wealth. Either the precepts of morality which inculcate justice and fair dealing are mere foolish dreams and bid us to do what we recognize now to be impossible; or else those class by-laws which bid us evade them with a clear conscience are ruinously misleading, the foundation of continuous unhappiness and of future degradation and the downfall of civilization. That, to my mind, is the alternative.
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.reason: The answer faithfully combines the excerpt's account of unequal division with its explicit moral alternative. Its retained phrasing, including “those who work most shall fare the hardest,” is distinctive and directly answers the question.

a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.question: Why do you reject the idea that individual kindness can fix the misery of class society?
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.answer: To fight feebly against the results of the very machine that we have made to uphold, conscious all the time of certain defeat: thus do we the well to do and prosperous dull the sting of conscience, and yield ourselves to the stream of class violence. Our best hope, on that view, is that joy may oppose itself to grief, health to disease, right to wrong, life to death for a little while, but that the sum of all is and must be irresistible evil. With this modern pessimism, which has taken the place of the stern hope of mediaeval pietism, and with the pessimism of the well to do of a luxurious age, we Socialists have nothing to do. We say those precepts of morality were not and are not mere “Counsels of perfection,” the birth of dreamy fanaticism, but rather the principles of reasonable action, rules of mutual defence against the tyranny of nature; and the society which acts on them will be far wealthier and infinitely happier than our present one.
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.reason: The language is largely Morris's, but the answer omits his explicit description of the proposed individual kindliness as a “hapless and futile compromise” and begins mid-argument. It also shifts the original's “our best hope being” into “Our best hope, on that view,” making the referent less clear. Restore enough of the omitted framing for a self-contained answer.

a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.question: How do you describe the two classes in modern society?
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.answer: Since the full development of the Commercial period, the elaborate groups of the feudal period have been resolved into two great classes: those who possess all the means of the production of wealth save one, and those who possess nothing except that one, the power of labour. The first class, the rich, can compel the latter, or the poor, to sell that power of labour to them on terms which ensure the continuance of the rich class, and therefore properly speaking own the poor class and indeed are called their masters. The class which lacks wealth is the class which produces it; the wealth owners only consume it. If by any chance the whole of the wage earners or “lower classes” were to perish or leave the community, production of wealth would come to a standstill unless the masters were to descend to the level of their former slaves and learn to work for their livelihood; if, on the contrary, the masters were to disappear, production of wealth would go on pretty much as before, though we might reasonably hope that its method of distribution would be altered.
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.reason: The answer accurately joins Morris's description of the two classes with his distinction between producers and consumers of wealth. It corrects the excerpt's apparent duplicated wording and remains coherent and directly relevant.

a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.question: Why do you say workers are compelled to accept such poor terms?
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.answer: Unless they rebel the workers must accept these terms, since they must live from day to day. They possess nothing but the power of labour inherent in their own bodies, while the other class possesses everything necessary to make that labour fruitful; so the labourers cannot work until they have obtained leave from their masters. The masters grant it only on the condition that the workers yield up to them all the produce over and above their livelihood, which is mostly only just enough to live on and seldom or ever rises much above that. Moreover, owing to the ever-increasing productivity of labour, helped by the wonderful machines of our epoch and organized for production with so much skill, and owing also to the long hours of labour and the employment in most trades of women and children, there are, taking one year with another, more workers than there is work for them to do. They compete with each other for employment, or in other words sell their labour-power in the market at Dutch Auction to their masters, so that the latter are able now-a-days to dispense with the exercise of visible force in compelling them to work.
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.reason: The reordered opening directly answers the question, and the rest preserves the excerpt's explanation of ownership, subsistence, competition for work, and the absence of visible force. The omitted qualification is not needed to maintain the argument.

a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.question: What do you mean when you say the rich live on the unpaid labour of others?
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.answer: The privilege of the possessing class consists in their power of living on the unpaid labour of others. If the capital of the rich man consists of land, he forces his tenant to improve his land for him, exacts tribute from him in the form of rent, and still has his land improved generally when the transaction has come to an end, so that he can begin the game over again, and carry it on for ever, he and his heirs. If he has houses on his land, he has rent for them, also often receiving the value of the buildings many times over, and at the end house and land once more. Or the earth beneath the surface is found out to be rich in minerals, and he is paid enormous sums for leave and license to labour them into marketable wares. If his capital consists in cash, he directly or indirectly buys the labour-power of men, women, and children and uses it for the production of wares which shall bring him a profit, keeping down their livelihood to as low a point as they will bear in order that the profit may be greater. Nor does he do anything to earn this profit, nothing useful in any case, and he need do absolutely nothing; he can buy the brain power of managers and foremen on terms a little higher than he buys the hand-power of the ordinary workmen.
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.reason: The answer uses Morris's own examples and wording to explain the claim across land, buildings, minerals, and cash capital. The omitted digressions are not necessary for the question, and the response remains coherent.

a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.question: Why do you call the conflict between employers and workers a class struggle?
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.answer: The interests of the two classes are opposed to each other: it is the object of the employing class to get as much as it can out of its privilege, the possession of the means of production, and all it makes can only be made at the expense of the workers; any increase in the fertility of the possessions of the rich must come from the labour of the poor. On the other hand, if the workers succeed in raising their standard of life they can only do so at the expense of the rich; what one gains the other loses. There is therefore constant war between them, and yet it is a war in which the capitalist must always win until the workers resolve to be an inferior class no longer.
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.reason: The answer directly gives Morris's reasons for calling it a class struggle: opposed interests, gains at one class's expense, and constant conflict. It closely preserves the excerpt's language and meaning.

a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.question: What do you think is wrong with the idea that employers are necessary to provide work?
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.answer: The occupation of fighting for the share of the surplus-value wrung from the workers is useless and wasteful. The workers must no longer depend on people to employ them who will very naturally make them pay for the fulfillment of that function. Trade is said to be suffering a depression caused by over-production: over-production of what, of wealth? That should mean that every person in the country has more than he needs to eat, more than he needs to wear, more and better house-room than he wants; well, that would be a curse we might soon modify into a blessing. But it does not mean that. At Manchester, I was told that it was the personal opinion sustained by one of the economical lights there that the one thing needed to amend the Depression of Trade was a great European war and that some of the surplus wealth might be destroyed. One's brain whirls at the enormity of the confession of helplessness or stupidity in the present system which this involves. In short, what this depression of trade really means, this overproduction, is that for the time at least the middle-class who live on our labour and fight among themselves for their share of what it produces are finding that their warfare does not even pay them. If they, the plunderers, must teach us this, surely we, the plundered, should not be slow to learn the lesson, which is simply that they are not needed.
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.reason: The response retains Morris's argument that the employing class's role is wasteful and unnecessary, supported by his critique of over-production and the reported Manchester proposal. The omitted rhetorical passage is not essential to the answer.

a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.question: What kind of society do you hope socialism will create?
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.answer: The aim of Socialism is to make the best by man's effort of the chances of happiness which the life of man upon the earth offers us, using the word happiness in its widest and deepest sense, and to assure to every one born into the world his full share of that chance. Society must offer a chance of happiness to every one, that is to say an opportunity for the full development of each human life; it denies the title of society to any system which degrades one class to exalt another. If we injure any one member for the benefit of all the rest, we have poisoned and corrupted our society: an injury to one will be an injury to all, and will so be felt in the long run. Combination for livelihood and the assurance of equal chance for everyone are what we Socialists want to bring about. Instead of a system which exacts a tribute from one class in order that another may be freed from the necessity of labour, each should pay his tribute of labour to nature, and each in turn receive his share of the wealth which each has done his best to create. So only shall we avoid the waste of the few and the want of the many, and rise above that perpetual condition of war.
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.reason: This combines authentic statements from the excerpt into a clear account of socialism's aims: shared livelihood, equal opportunity, and an end to class degradation and want. The direct framing is a minor, accurate adjustment.

a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.question: What do you mean by saying that socialism would make wealth ours rather than mine or thine?
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.answer: We want to make people leave off saying “this is mine and that is thine,” and to say “this is ours.” A socialist community would hold wealth only to use it, and it could only use it as a community by satisfying with it the needs of all its members, since a community consists of each and all the individuals composing it: there is none left out, or it has no right to call itself a community, a Commonwealth. Property at present means the power of preventing other people from using wealth; as, for instance, a man may and often does refuse to cultivate a tract of land himself or to allow others to do so. But as we understand property it means the possession of wealth which we can use ourselves. Everyone's reasonable needs must be satisfied, first for food and shelter, and next for pleasure bodily and mental, which would include the full development of any individual according to his capacity, an aim which Socialism would foster as sedulously as the present system depresses it.
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.reason: The response answers the question by preserving Morris's distinction between property as exclusion and property as usable possession, alongside his explanation of communal wealth meeting everyone's needs. It is coherent and faithful to the excerpt.

a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.question: Would a socialist society expect everyone to do the same work or receive the same things?
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.answer: No arbitrary conditions would be imposed on the members of a true Commonwealth for the satisfaction of their reasonable needs: but there is one Condition which is not arbitrary and which all must accept: they must all work for the Commonwealth or there will be in the long term no wealth. Their needs need not be estimated conventionally by the supposed value or dignity of the work which they do, because that would at once give rise to a fresh system of classes, of privileged people tormenting the unprivileged. All kinds of labour are necessary to the Commonweal; nor is the difficulty and labour of exercising a specially excellent capacity at all proportioned to its excellence. The man who can do the higher work does it as easily as he who does the lower; and neither again is the expensiveness of the workman's needs necessarily proportioned to the excellence of his work. The man who does the rougher work may need the more expensive livelihood, and if he does he ought to have it. In short the maxim which true Socialism would carry out is: “From each what he can do; to each what he needs.” The sick, the weak, the old, the infants are not stinted of food or shelter or such pleasures as they can enjoy simply because they add little or nothing to the wealth that the family subsists on: they do what they can and have what they need.
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.reason: It directly distinguishes the common obligation to work from the principle of meeting needs without ranking people by their work. Morris's family example and maxim are preserved accurately and make the answer informative.

a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.question: Why do you believe a society based on equal fellowship could be happier and more prosperous?
a05680ebb45d5d83.txt.answer: Those precepts of morality are not mere “Counsels of perfection,” the birth of dreamy fanaticism, but rather the principles of reasonable action, rules of mutual defence against the tyranny of nature; and the society which acts on them will be far wealthier and infinitely happier than our present one. The sum of its wealth will be so great that even the rich men of the present day would find in it ample compensation for the loss of riches which they cannot use for their own happiness but which, whether they will it or not, must be used for the unhappiness of their fellows. Socialism asserts that each should pay his tribute of labour to nature, and each in turn receive his share of the wealth which each has done his best to create: so only shall we avoid the waste of the few and the want of the many.
