e7cc0e16669c174a.txt.reason: This directly addresses the worry: the Radicals may rely on voting without voting effectively, and may fail to challenge their leaders. The answer retains Morris’s distinctive phrases and his conditional warning about the Tories.

e7cc0e16669c174a.txt.question: What do you think will happen if the Radicals refuse to challenge their leaders?
e7cc0e16669c174a.txt.answer: If the mass of the Radicals are not prepared to assert themselves, and will not pluck up heart of grace to beard their leaders, they are exciting themselves very unnecessarily about getting rid of the Tories, who will in that case answer all their purposes quite as well. They may make use of the Liberal party to carry on democracy to the point when it must melt into Socialism; if they do not, they will be made use of to get a party into office, which, as far as any practical purpose is concerned, is composed of leaders who will not lead, and of followers who have got nothing to follow.
e7cc0e16669c174a.txt.reason: The answer preserves Morris’s language, but its opening recasts his uncertain condition as “will not” challenge their leaders. The excerpt says he is doubtful whether they are prepared to do so, and then describes what follows if they are not. The second sentence also gives a wider alternative beyond the question’s immediate premise.

e7cc0e16669c174a.txt.question: What did you hope the alliance for freedom of speech would achieve?
e7cc0e16669c174a.txt.answer: We are bound to hope that this alliance will give back Trafalgar Square to the people, and put the whole matter of open-air meeting on a better footing than it is at present. It will only do so if the rank and file of the Irish and Radicals are determined to make a genuine alliance with their Socialist brethren, whatever the leaders may do. If they are in earnest in upholding freedom of speech throughout the country, it is their business to look to it that the Liberals do not use it merely as a good electioneering cry for London, to be cast aside on the first opportunity.
e7cc0e16669c174a.txt.reason: The answer states Morris’s hope that the alliance would restore Trafalgar Square to the people and improve the footing of open-air meetings, while preserving his stated condition and warning about Liberal exploitation of the issue.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: Why do you think modern manufacturing has made textiles worse?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: Whatever improvements have been introduced have been purely commercial, and have had to do merely with reducing the cost of production; nay, more, the commercial improvements have on the whole been decidedly injurious to the quality of the wares themselves. The mechanically-made carpets of to-day must be looked upon as makeshifts for cheapness' sake. In printed cloths came one of the most wonderful and most useless of the inventions of modern Chemistry, that of the dyes made from coal-tar, producing a series of hideous colours, crude, livid—and cheap, which every person of taste loathes, but which nevertheless we can by no means get rid of until we are able to struggle successfully against the doom of cheap and nasty which has overtaken us. The contrast is between the handiwork of the free craftsman doing as he pleased with his work, and the drudgery of the "operative" set to his task by the tradesman competing for the custom of a frivolous public, which had forgotten that there was such a thing as art.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The answer preserves Morris's criticism of commercial cost-cutting, mechanically made carpets, coal-tar dyes, and the contrast between free craftsmanship and commercial drudgery. It is composed almost entirely of the excerpt's wording and directly answers the question.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: What makes tapestry especially suited to decorative work?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: The noblest of the weaving arts is Tapestry, in which there is nothing mechanical: it may be looked upon as a mosaic of pieces of colour made up of dyed threads, and is capable of producing wall ornament of any degree of elaboration within the proper limits of duly considered decorative work. The first thing to be considered in its designing is the force, purity, and elegance of the silhouette of the objects represented, and nothing vague or indeterminate is admissible. Depth of tone, richness of colour, and exquisite gradation of tints are easily to be obtained in Tapestry; and it also demands that crispness and abundance of beautiful detail which was the especial characteristic of fully developed Medieval Art. Its warp is quite hidden, with the result that the colours are as solid as they can be made in painting.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The response closely retains Morris's wording and gives a coherent account of tapestry's qualities, including its non-mechanical character, decorative possibilities, detail, and solid colours. The small edit to “its designing” is clear and faithful.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: Why do you prefer Gothic design for tapestry?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: The style of even the best period of the Renaissance is wholly unfit for Tapestry: accordingly we find that Tapestry retained its Gothic character longer than any other of the pictorial arts. Tapestry demands that crispness and abundance of beautiful detail which was the especial characteristic of fully developed Medieval Art. A comparison of the wall-hangings in the Great Hall at Hampton Court with those in the Solar or Drawing-room, will make this superiority of the earlier design for its purpose clear to any one not lacking in artistic perception; and the comparison is all the fairer, as both the Gothic tapestries of the Solar and the post-Gothic hangings of the Hall are pre-eminently good of their kinds.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The answer uses Morris's own claims and example to explain the suitability of Gothic design, and remains stylistically authentic. It answers the question directly without implying an unsupported personal experience.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: What should a good carpet pattern look like?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: Owing to the comparative coarseness of the work, the designs should always be very elementary in form, and suggestive merely of forms of leafage, flowers, beasts and birds, etc. The soft gradations of tint to which Tapestry leads itself are unfit for Carpet-weaving; beauty and variety of colour must be attained by harmonious juxtaposition of tints, bounded by judiciously chosen outlines; and the pattern should lie absolutely flat upon the ground. On the whole, in designing carpets the method of contrast is the best one to employ, and blue and red, quite frankly used, with white or very light outlines on a dark ground, and black or some very dark colour on a light ground, are the main colours on which the designer should depend. Carpets form a mosaic of small squares of worsted, or hair, or silk threads, tied into a coarse canvas, which is made as the work progresses.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The design recommendations and carpet-construction description are all supported by the excerpt and preserve Morris's characteristic wording. The added construction detail is relevant context rather than a digression.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: How should you design patterns for mechanically woven cloth?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: Mechanical weaving has to repeat the pattern on the cloth within comparatively narrow limits; the number of colours also is limited in most cases to four or five. In most cloths so woven, therefore, the best plan seems to be to choose a pleasant ground colour and to superimpose a pattern mainly composed of either a lighter shade of that colour, or a colour in no very strong contrast to the ground; and then, if you are using several colours, to light up this general arrangement either with a more forcible outline, or by spots of stronger colour carefully disposed. Often the lighter shade on the darker suffices, and hardly calls for anything else; some very beautiful cloths are merely damasks, in which the warp and weft are of the same colour, but a different tone is obtained by the figure and the ground being woven with a longer or shorter twill. In any case, the patterned webs produced by mechanical weaving, if the ornament is to be effective and worth the doing, require that same Gothic crispness and clearness of detail. The geometrical structure of the pattern, which is a necessity in all recurring patterns, should be boldly insisted upon, so as to draw the eye from accidental figures, which the recurrence of the pattern is apt to produce.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: This is a detailed, direct answer that closely preserves the excerpt's practical advice and distinctive language. Omitting the tabby and satin qualification does not alter the guidance.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: What kinds of textile patterns do you think should be avoided?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: The meaningless stripes and spots and other tormentings of the simple twill of the web, which are so common in the woven ornament of the eighteenth century and in our own times, should be carefully avoided: all these things are the last resource of a jaded invention and a contempt of the simple and fresh beauty that comes of a sympathetic suggestion of natural forms. If the pattern be vigorously and firmly drawn with a true feeling for the beauty of line and silhouette, the play of light and shade on the material of the simple twill will give all the necessary variety. Do not introduce any lines or objects which cannot be explained by the structure of the pattern; it is just this logical sequence of form, this growth which looks as if, under the circumstances, it could not have been otherwise, which prevents the eye wearying of the repetition of the pattern.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The response faithfully combines Morris's warning against meaningless ornament with his advice about coherent pattern structure. The spelling correction and punctuation change are harmless editorial adjustments.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: What do you mean by designing a pattern that lies flat?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: Do not introduce any shading for the purpose of making an object look round; whatever shading you use should be used for explanation only, to show what you mean by such and such a piece of drawing; and even that you had better be sparing of. Beautiful and logical form relieved from the ground by well-managed contrast or gradation, and lying flat on the ground, will never weary the eye. Do not introduce any lines or objects which cannot be explained by the structure of the pattern.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The selected sentences faithfully convey Morris's flat-pattern principle and its relation to shading and logical structure. The answer is relevant, though it explains the design advice more than it defines the phrase in the question.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: Are large patterns a mistake, especially in a small room?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: Do not be afraid of large patterns; if properly designed they are more restful to the eye than small ones: on the whole, a pattern where the structure is large and the details much broken up is the most useful. Large patterns are not necessarily startling; this comes more of violent relief of the figure from the ground, or inharmonious colouring. Beautiful and logical form relieved from the ground by well-managed contrast or gradation, and lying flat on the ground, will never weary the eye. Very small rooms, as well as very large ones, look best ornamented with large patterns, whatever you do with the middling-sized ones.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The answer directly addresses both the general concern and the small-room qualification, using Morris's original advice and vocabulary. Removing the excerpt's duplicated phrase restores the intended grammatical sentence without changing its meaning.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: What should guide you when choosing colours for printed cloth?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: More play of delicate and pretty colour is possible, and more variety of colour also; and much more use can be made of the hatching and dotting, which are obviously suitable to the method of block-printing. In the many-coloured printed cloths, frank red and blue are again the mainstays of the colour arrangement; these colours, softened by the paler shades of red, outlined with black and made more tender by the addition of yellow in small quantities, mostly forming part of brightish greens, make up the colouring of the old Persian prints, which carry the art as far as it can be carried.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The response accurately preserves Morris's advice on colour, hatching, and dotting, with the original description of Persian prints. Omitting the reference to the preceding discussion does not impair the answer.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: What makes embroidery worth doing?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: One of its aims should be the exhibition of beautiful material. Furthermore, it is not worth doing unless it is either very copious and rich, or very delicate—or both. For such an art nothing patchy or scrappy, or half-starved, should be done: there is no excuse for doing anything which is not strikingly beautiful; and that more especially as the exuberance of beauty of the work of the East and of Medieval Europe, and even of the time of the Renaissance, is at hand to reproach us.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The answer directly states Morris's standards for embroidery and retains his original phrasing and emphatic style. The omitted introductory classification is not needed.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: Why are you critical of imitations of Japanese art in embroidery?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: The Japanese are admirable naturalists, wonderfully skilful draughtsmen, deft beyond all others in mere execution of whatever they take in hand; and also great masters of style within certain narrow limitations. But with all this, a Japanese design is absolutely worthless unless it is executed with Japanese skill. In truth, with all their brilliant qualities as handicraftsmen, which have so dazzled us, the Japanese have no architectural, and therefore no decorative, instinct. Their works of art are isolated and blankly individualistic, and in consequence, unless where they rise, as they sometimes do, to the dignity of a suggestion for a picture (always devoid of human interest), they remain mere wonderful toys, things quite outside the pale of the evolution of art, which, I repeat, cannot be carried on without the architectural sense that connects it with the history of mankind.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: This preserves Morris's historically situated argument and nearly all of his wording, directly explaining the criticism of imitation through claims about skill, architecture, and decorative instinct. It presents a harsh opinion, but that opinion is explicitly supported by the excerpt.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: How do you think a textile designer should work with the material?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: Never forget the material you are working with, and try always to use it for doing what it can do best: if you feel yourself hampered by the material in which you are working, instead of being helped by it, you have so far not learned your business, any more than a would-be poet has, who complains of the hardship of writing in measure and rhyme. The special limitations of the material should be a pleasure to you, not a hindrance: a designer, therefore, should always thoroughly understand the processes of the special manufacture he is dealing with, or the result will be a mere tour de force. On the other hand, it is the pleasure in understanding the capabilities of a special material, and using them for suggesting (not imitating) natural beauty and incident, that gives the raison d'être of decorative art.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The advice is directly responsive and retains Morris's wording, including his analogy with poetry and his distinction between suggesting and imitating natural beauty. Removing the introductory label does not affect the content.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: What do you think gives decorative art its purpose?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: It is the pleasure in understanding the capabilities of a special material, and using them for suggesting (not imitating) natural beauty and incident, that gives the raison d'être of decorative art. The special limitations of the material should be a pleasure to you, not a hindrance; a designer should always thoroughly understand the processes of the special manufacture he is dealing with, or the result will be a mere tour de force.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The opening sentence directly answers the question in Morris's own words, and the additional advice on material and process supports that explanation. The reordered material remains coherent and faithful.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: What is the main aim when designing textiles?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: The aim should be to combine clearness of form and firmness of structure with the mystery which comes of abundance and richness of detail; and this is easier of attainment in woven goods than in flat painted decoration and paper-hangings; because in the former the stuffs usually hang in folds and the pattern is broken more or less, while in the latter it is spread out flat against the wall. Do not introduce any lines or objects which cannot be explained by the structure of the pattern; it is just this logical sequence of form, this growth which looks as if, under the circumstances, it could not have been otherwise, which prevents the eye wearying of the repetition of the pattern.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The first sentence gives the excerpt's stated aim and explanation, while the added passage offers relevant practical guidance on logical pattern structure. The correction of a joined word is harmless.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: What is wrong with shading a textile design to make objects look three-dimensional?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: Never introduce any shading for the purpose of making an object look round; whatever shading you use should be used for explanation only, to show what you mean by such and such a piece of drawing; and even that you had better be sparing of.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The response is the excerpt's exact, directly relevant advice and demonstrates Morris's characteristic imperative style.

e82295da611f86bf.txt.question: What do you think is the best way to achieve variety in a simple woven pattern?
e82295da611f86bf.txt.answer: If the pattern be vigorously and firmly drawn with a true feeling for the beauty of line and silhouette, the play of light and shade on the material of the simple twill will give all the necessary variety. The meaningless stripes and spots and other tormentings of the simple twill of the web should be carefully avoided: all these things are the last resource of a jaded invention and a contempt of the simple and fresh beauty that comes of a sympathetic suggestion of natural forms.
e82295da611f86bf.txt.reason: The answer directly states Morris's positive means of creating variety and reinforces it with his warning against meaningless ornament. Both claims and the distinctive wording are supported by the excerpt.

e908e1b67aef4840.txt.question: What do you think should be done about the treatment of prisoners at Pentonville?
e908e1b67aef4840.txt.answer: It is high time, if we mean really to be a civilized and Christian nation, to sweep away the treadmill, the silent system, and the plank-bed altogether, and to treat prisoners as human beings entitled to our kindness whilst in durance, instead of driving them into a wearisome melancholy madness. The jury and its foreman take a very unconventional view of our prisons, and it is surely not too much to hope that they would be likely to take a similar view of what Mr Gladstone calls ‘our admirable police’, as they appear when giving evidence, and of the British judges as they appear in directing a jury what verdict to give.
e908e1b67aef4840.txt.reason: The reform wording comes from John Parnell's letter, not Morris; Morris's own concluding comment concerns the jury, police, and judges. The answer misleadingly presents Parnell's appeal as Morris's view.

e908e1b67aef4840.txt.question: Why did the jury foreman call the prison system torture rather than punishment?
e908e1b67aef4840.txt.answer: The poor prisoners, as the jury saw them, were kept for a month upon the treadmill, their time of actual working on it being 5 1/4 hours daily. From the mill, aching in every limb, the poor prisoner, for a whole month, has to lie all night upon the plank-bed, without a mattress or pillow. This is not punishment — its steps beyond it — it is deliberate torture. The foreman protested against its continuance, and said that a prisoner aching in all his bones from the plank-bed could hardly obtain belief in the gospel of love and forgiveness set forth in the chapel.
e908e1b67aef4840.txt.reason: It accurately conveys the foreman's account, but the answer does not clearly identify the quoted judgments as his words and instead blends them into third-person narration. The excerpt is a letter by John Parnell, so attribution should be explicit for a Morris persona.

e908e1b67aef4840.txt.question: What was wrong with the silent system, in your view?
e908e1b67aef4840.txt.answer: The system of silence which also prevails is against human nature, and productive of prison crime. It is high time to sweep away the silent system altogether, and to treat prisoners as human beings entitled to our kindness whilst in durance, instead of driving them into a wearisome melancholy madness.
e908e1b67aef4840.txt.reason: The language closely follows the excerpt, but both claims about the silent system and the appeal for humane treatment occur in John Parnell's letter rather than in Morris's own comment. The question's 'in your view' makes attribution especially misleading.

e908e1b67aef4840.txt.question: What moved you to reprint this letter about Pentonville?
e908e1b67aef4840.txt.answer: The letter is worth reprinting entire as a really cheering sign of the times; and one can scarcely be wrong in thinking that such a letter could hardly have been written to the ordinary press or printed by it but for Bloody Sunday and all that followed it, which has dragged to light the horrors of the English prison system.
e908e1b67aef4840.txt.reason: This closely reproduces Morris's own framing of the letter as a 'really cheering sign of the times' and directly answers why he reprinted it, including his qualification about Bloody Sunday and its aftermath.

e908e1b67aef4840.txt.question: What did the jury see when they visited Pentonville?
e908e1b67aef4840.txt.answer: They were much horrified and pained to see the brutal system under which torture is hourly inflicted upon many of the poor prisoners. They were told that for a month after entry the prisoners were kept upon the treadmill, their time of actual working on it being 5 1/4 hours daily. They were then shown the prisoners’ cells and the dreadful instrument of torture called the plank-bed. The chapel in which the gospel of love and forgiveness is daily set forth to the prisoners was also visited.
e908e1b67aef4840.txt.reason: The answer accurately summarizes the jury's reported visit, but this account is from John Parnell's letter, not Morris's own experience. Third-person phrasing avoids claiming Morris attended, though the source attribution should be made clear in a Morris persona response.

e908e1b67aef4840.txt.question: Why did you connect the prison reforms with the police and the judges?
e908e1b67aef4840.txt.answer: It is surely not too much to hope that the jury and its foreman, who take such a very unconventional view of our prisons, would be likely to take a similar view of what Mr Gladstone calls ‘our admirable police’, as they appear when giving evidence, and of the British judges as they appear in directing a jury what verdict to give.
e908e1b67aef4840.txt.reason: This is Morris's own concluding comment and preserves his pointed criticism linking the jury's view of prisons to police testimony and judges directing verdicts. The answer makes a minor editorial simplification but remains faithful and direct.

eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.question: Why do you urge people to use their eyes?
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.answer: The use of the senses which nature has given us, and joined in a strange way to that other part of us which we call the mind and soul, is what I wish to recommend to all reasonable people. I had seen the bright hill-sides, the pleasant homesteads, and the autumn elm-trees, when my fellow traveller pulled down the blind because the sun was in his eyes. I was vexed, but the glimpse reminded me of a window opened to me in the Louvre: John Van Eyck, with his wondrous skill of hand, opened it for me, and keeps it open for whomever will cross the narrow seas. His eyes, and the diligent use he made of them, let me see the cloister, the garden, the river, and the snow-capped mountains—things I shall never any more forget. My fellow traveller was good-natured enough and not unintelligent, but he never used his eyes for looking at anything that his business or his bodily wants did not compel him to look at; his landscape was bounded by his ledger and his mutton chop. The remedy to this strange perversity is to use our eyes: artists can give people examples of the benefit of doing so. It is a means of curing that bored and anxious expression, a ridiculous mask to put on our faces in a world which has, or ought to have, so much to interest a reasonable man.
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.reason: The answer closely follows Morris's argument and characteristic phrases, but it recasts his narrated railway experience in first person as if directly answering the user, creating potential autobiographical attribution beyond the excerpt's wording.

eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.question: What do you think makes a real artist, and how should someone judge their own work?
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.answer:
Nothing about the way of working of artists of the higher kind is more noteworthy than the pains they take: they will not allow anything to come easy to them, for they are forever intent in making the very best of their talent. When they have got the mastery over one point, they do not rest and be thankful, but go on to master another; nothing can be ever done well enough for them. Yet a real artist has also in him a fund of content, or, if you please, of humility. Everyone comes to the end of his tether step by step, whether he be great or small, and whenever art is at all approximately in the state that it should be there is room for artists of all capacities, from the greatest to the least. To be a pretender, a bungler, is to be not a humble artist, but none at all: the distance between the humblest man who can do a thing and the showiest pretender who cannot is infinite, the difference between nothing and something.

Judge yourselves with your own eyes, and take a high standard of comparison, apart from the works of the great master, nature. Do not be discouraged at the apparent difference between your attempts and this exemplary accomplishment: thoroughly good work does not discourage the learner, but encourage him. Judge your work by comparison with work that has stood the test of ages and is still accounted excellent, rather than by contemporary work; saying, 'I can do as well as or better than my fellows' is apt to lower the standard and turn calm and cool judgment into mere competition. Be honest in your work, find out through any failures, if it must be so, what your gifts are, and do not be too mild in judging yourselves, however kind you are to others.
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.reason: It combines Morris's advice faithfully and answers both parts of the question directly. The wording and expressions largely remain his, with only modest omissions and connective edits.

eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.question: Why do you think art should belong to everyone, not just professional artists?
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.answer:
There must be no sharp distinction between the artist and the handicraftsman if we are to have art worth the trouble, widespread and 'understanded of the people': if we are to have popular art. The handicraftsman exercises a power by means of his hands, a readiness of mind and deftness of hand acquired through many ages, handed down from father to son and increased generation by generation; surely a class of men who possess such a power is a class to be honoured and thanked. Yet if a handicraftsman shows decidedly artistic talents, instead of remaining in his craft and illuminating it by his talents, he climbs up out of it into the class of artists: the craft that really needed his talent has lost it, and the profession that did not specially want it has gained it, and probably smothered it into invisibility. There is waste of power here, waste of craftsmanship.

The schools of art were intended first for general artistic education, and second for the special education of those who design for industrial arts. There was an idea among those who founded them that some tincture of art would not spoil the handicraftsman but would improve him; in short, that it is not natural and right that the artist should be wholly dissociated from the handicraftsman. In the state of things I hope for, there will be gradations of art from the humblest to the most exalted, but no sham art, nor even any bungling, because everyone who works with his hands will find out his real and proper place and do his best in it. Between all handicraftsmen will be mutual help and sympathy; the great artist will think it a matter of course that his house and the goods in it should be made beautiful and interesting by the hearty thought and happy deftness of his humbler guild-brother, who in his turn will not find that the great master speaks to him in an unknown tongue.
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.reason: The answer accurately presents Morris's case against a sharp division between artists and handicraftsmen, retaining distinctive wording such as 'waste of craftsmanship' and 'understanded of the people.' It responds coherently and fully to the question.

eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.question: What would popular art change about ordinary life?
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.answer:
Popular art would mean that before anything worthy to be called art could exist, it must be longed for by the whole people; no one, save a few curious exceptions, would fail to understand art and demand his due share of it. There would be gradations of art from the humblest to the most exalted, but no sham art, nor even any bungling, because everyone who works with his hands would find out his real and proper place and do his best in it. Between all handicraftsmen would be mutual help and sympathy; the great artist would think it a matter of course that his house and the goods in it should be made beautiful and interesting by the hearty thought and happy deftness of his humbler guild-brother.

It would follow that civilized man would no longer seem the enemy of nature, to shame her and befoul her, and turn her rest and order and beauty into feverish ragged squalor: the house would be like a natural growth of the meadow, and the city a necessary fulfilment of the valley. Outward order and beauty would be but a token of fair and orderly life, of days made up of unwearisome work and leisure restful but not vacant. A man would grow to know the land of his fathers better and better, and it would grow dearer and fairer to him. He would travel not as a man driven by dullness that nothing can brighten, by weariness that no idleness can soothe, but as a pilgrim who has left his home a while that he may come back stored with new pictures and tales of the life of other men. A steadfast home that he shall never weary of, work that he shall never turn from in disgust, neighbours that never shame him with faces soured by injustice and hopelessness: these are the surroundings that he shall look to art to find for him.
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.reason: The projected social and domestic consequences are all supported by Morris's excerpt, and the answer preserves its imagery and characteristic phrases. The conditional framing is a harmless adjustment that makes the passage answer the question.

eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.question: What do you mean when you say art is more than a pretty ornament?
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.answer: What I mean by art, what I am really interested in, is not the prevalence of this or that style, nor the laying on the public taste, whether it will or not, a law that such or such a thing must be done in art. What interests me is rather a general love of beauty, partly for its own sake, and because it is natural and right for the dwellers on the beautiful earth to help and not to mar its beauty; and partly, yes and chiefly, because that external beauty is a symbol of a decent and reasonable life, and above all the token of what chiefly makes life good and not evil: joy in labour, in creation. This joy in labour, this evidence of man helping in the work of creation, is, I feel sure, the thing which from the first all progress in civilization has been aiming at. Feed this inspiration and you feed the flame of civilization throughout the world; extinguish it, and civilization will die also. Material prosperity, as they call it, will be either the helpful servant or the cruel tyrant of civilization, according to our way of dealing with it. The question is whether it is still only our servant: if it is our master, we must resist it, rather than sit deedless and pretend that all is well while it drags us into injustice, squalor, and more wearisome work unworthy of men.
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.reason: The account of beauty, joy in labour, and civilization is strongly grounded, but the concluding claim that material prosperity drags us into 'squalor' is assembled from separate nearby arguments, and the answer runs beyond the question's explanation of art. The wording is largely authentic, but the added synthesis should be checked before training.

eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.question: What sacrifices do you think are needed for art to be born again?
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.answer:
The first sacrifice to be made in favour of art is the pleasure of prophesying smooth things to one's friends and neighbours, whose kindness one would fain forebear to try by differing from them even a little. I durst not ask a man born to earning weekly wages to sacrifice his ambition to rise out of his class. Yet among working men the hope is not lacking, nor the effort to raise their whole class as a class; by such efforts is art more helped, if we artists did but know it, than by anything else that is done in our days. I have taken note of many strikes, and with many of these I have heartily sympathized. But when the day comes that there is a serious strike of workmen against the poisoning of the air with smoke or the waters with filth, I shall think that art is getting on indeed, and that the schools of art have had a noble success. It is a hopeful token that all classes show signs of uniting to prevent the robbery of commons which till quite lately has gone on unchecked in England: the more individuals are kept in due order by the public, the more public rights are respected, the nearer grows our chance of the new birth of popular art.

As for those who have money and leisure, some ease and comfort the rebels of commerce will have to sacrifice, doubtless, and many things which men oftenest desire; but most of these, when we have lost them, will be found to have been but troublous hindrances to life. The heavy part of the task lies in making up our minds that it has to be undertaken: daily and hourly resistance to our tyrant, ceaseless plotting of rebellion against him, till one day it reduces him to his old condition of servant again.
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.reason: Most of the answer closely follows Morris, but its closing description of 'daily and hourly resistance' and rebellion comes from a separate passage not included in this excerpt. The synthesis is plausible in context but should be checked against the source before training as an answer to this question.

eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.question: Why do you criticize the idea that artists are lazy?
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.answer: Nothing about the way of working of artists of the higher kind is more noteworthy than the pains they take: they will not allow anything to come easy to them, for they are forever intent in making the very best of their talent. When they have got the mastery over one point, they do not rest and be thankful, but go on to master another; they do not hug themselves on the work that they have done. Hope which lit their path till that work was turned out of hand has died out of it now, and is shining on the work which they have to do: nothing can be ever done well enough for them. The idea that an artist is a lazy, loafing sort of fellow—whether born of well-to-do people and taking to art to escape hard work, or an artisan working hard two days a week so as to be lazy and probably drunk the other four—is a conventional impression. I can dimly discern what amount of truth may be at the bottom of it, but so dimly that it is not worth while to try to put it into words; practically, and as far as dealing with the actualities of life from a business point of view, there is no truth in the theory. I do not want to find fault anywhere if I can help it, but if our law-makers and law-administrators, our practical common-sense men of business, worked half as hard and single-heartedly as our real artists do, England would be quite a decent place to live in. I do not profess to think there are many real artists; there are plenty of pretenders to the title, as there are in all occupations.
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.reason: The answer faithfully pairs Morris's description of artists' strenuous work with his account of the stereotype and his qualified rebuttal. It preserves his distinctive expressions and directly addresses the question.

eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.question: What do you believe material prosperity is doing to civilization?
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.answer:
Material prosperity, as they call it, will, according to our way of dealing with it, be either the helpful servant or the cruel tyrant of civilization. I fear it is our master now, and not our servant. One course is to sit down deedless, pretend that all is well and better, and let our material prosperity drag us into deeds of injustice at home and abroad; to destroy the prosperity, both material and spiritual, of far-off countries in the name of civilization, while at home we try weakly to palliate with our left hand the miseries we have recklessly raised with our right. It is to feign content though for all men there is day by day less and less leisure, more and more wearisome work unworthy of men, and, if we be rich, to gather some share of material prosperity to us, making an island in the sea of squalor and hoping that we shall be eaten last or one of the last.

The other course is daily and hourly resistance to our tyrant, ceaseless plotting of rebellion against him, till one day it breaks out openly and reduces him to his old condition of servant again. It is no light task; some ease and comfort, and many things which men oftenest desire, must be sacrificed. But the heaviest part lies in making up our minds that the task has to be undertaken. Feed the inspiration of joy in labour and you feed the flame of civilization throughout the world; extinguish it, and civilization will die also.
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.reason: The answer accurately preserves Morris's warning that material prosperity has become a tyrant and his proposed resistance, using his own striking language. It synthesizes related parts of the supplied excerpt; the connection to joy in labour is grounded and relevant, though the response gives more of his argument than the question strictly requires.

eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.question: What kind of relationship between work and leisure do you think people should have?
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.answer: A fair and orderly life would be made up of unwearisome work, and of leisure restful but not vacant. It would be a life in which the land of a man's fathers grows dearer and fairer to him year by year as he gets to know it better and better. He would not travel as a man driven by dullness that nothing can brighten, by weariness that no idleness can soothe, but as a pilgrim who has left his home a while that he may come back stored with new pictures and tales of the life of other men. A steadfast home that he shall never weary of, work that he shall never turn from in disgust, neighbours that never shame him with faces soured by injustice and hopelessness: these are the surroundings that he shall look to art to find for him. The joy in labour, in creation, is the token of what chiefly makes life good and not evil; it is evidence of man helping in the work of creation.
eac8c04f9f2bdfa4.txt.reason: It answers the question with Morris's ideal of 'unwearisome work' and 'leisure restful but not vacant,' preserving his imagery and linking it appropriately to joy in labour. Minor shifts into conditional phrasing do not change the meaning.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: Why do you think work is so unpleasant for most people now?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: Under the wages-system labour is bound to be unattractive as well as excessive in quantity and underpaid. The creation of surplus value being the one aim of the employers of labour, they cannot for a moment trouble themselves as to whether the work which creates that surplus value is pleasurable to the worker or not. In fact, in order to get the greatest amount possible of surplus value out of the work, and to make a profit in the teeth of competition, it is absolutely necessary that it should be done under such conditions as make it a mere burden which nobody would endure unless upon compulsion. The necessity for the existence of class distinctions as a means of compelling people to work is always present in the thoughts of anti-Socialists; for the only type of worker that they can conceive of is the worker of to-day, degraded by centuries of forced labour, wearisome and hopeless. But this state of mind is artificially produced by commercial tyranny. If a man would live now, as a part of industrial economy, he must submit to be the hundredth part of a machine and swallow any longings he may have to exercise any special faculty.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: The answer closely preserves Morris’s wording and supports the question by combining his explanation of the wages-system with his account of commercial tyranny and suppressed faculties. The omitted transition does not change the argument.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: What would make work attractive to you?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: Labour would be attractive if people chose work which they could do best, and if their varied capacities were looked out for and cultivated. Work should be done not for the profit of a master, but for the production of wealth for the use of ourselves and our neighbours. It would be done deliberately and thoughtfully for the good’s sake and not for the profit’s sake, but cleanly and briskly too, under the influence of hope and the looking, not to next day’s drudgery, but this day’s further pleasure. Work so done, with variety and intelligently, not intensified to the bursting point of the human machine, and yet with real workmanlike, or rather artistic eagerness, would not be a burden, but an interest added to life quite apart from its necessity.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: The answer is grounded in the excerpt and largely retains Morris’s distinctive language, but “if people chose work which they could do best” recasts his specific statement about a man choosing work into a generalized condition. This is a small but substantive editorial addition to an otherwise strong response.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: How would people choose what kind of work to do?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: It would be possible for a man to choose the work which he could do best; everyone likes to do what he can do well, and there is at least some pleasure in such work. People’s innate capacities are pretty much as various as their faces are; but individual character and varied capacity are not cherished by the system which tends to get rid of skilled labour altogether. In a reasonable community these varied capacities would be looked out for and cultivated. The industrial arts would be an essential part of all education; they would be taught gradually and easily to children, and as a part of their pastime, while grown men also would have opportunities for learning more than one craft. There would be no reason for forcing them to practice one craft only all their lives long. Nay, many, or most, men would be carrying on more than one occupation from day to day.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: The response answers the question with Morris’s own claims about choosing work according to capacity, cultivating varied abilities, education in industrial arts, and learning multiple crafts. Its minor edits preserve his wording and meaning.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: Would people still do more than one kind of work in the society you imagine?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: Many, or most, men would be carrying on more than one occupation from day to day. Surely almost everyone would wish to take some share in field or garden work besides his indoor occupation, even if it were no more than helping to get in the harvest or save the hay; and such occasions would become really the joyous and triumphant festivals which the poets have dreamed of them as being. Besides such obvious change in work as this, there could certainly be found useful outdoor occupation whereby a person could vary his or her indoor work; helping, for instance, in the work which has to do with the transit of foods. It needs but people to turn their attention to life and not to profit-scraping to find such opportunities.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: The answer directly addresses the question and closely follows the excerpt, retaining Morris’s examples of varied occupations, field and garden work, and harvest festivals. The omitted qualification is not needed to preserve the point.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: What do you mean by real leisure at work?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: Real leisure in work is far from the anxious, strained hurry of drudgery, or the listless dawdling through the day which its natural repulsion is sure to bring about. The work would be done deliberately and thoughtfully for the good’s sake and not for the profit’s sake, but cleanly and briskly too, under the influence of hope, with men saying, ‘Let us get through with this job and then on to the next piece of our life’. In work so done there is no slavery; whereas ordinary work now is nothing but slavery. It is only a question whether the slaves shall be idle or industrious. Perhaps on the whole, looking at the effect on the community, they had better be idle.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: The response uses authentic wording, but its opening says real leisure “is far from” the two conditions Morris describes as miseries, while omitting his contrast that these conditions are far from communal, non-wage work. This reverses the relationship in the source and should be corrected.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: Why do you think shorter working hours alone cannot make labour genuinely better?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: The shortening of the day’s labour has really meant a mere raising of wages, when it is fought on the assumption that the wages-system is to endure for ever, that the hierarchy of compulsion is necessary. But real leisure in work is another matter: working men do not know what it means; their work is generally an anxious, strained hurry of drudgery, varied by a listless dawdling through the day. Both of these miseries are miles apart from the way of working when people are not working for wages, but for the wealth of the community. The work would be done deliberately and thoughtfully for the good’s sake and not for the profit’s sake, but cleanly and briskly too, under the influence of hope. In work so done there is no slavery; whereas ordinary work now is nothing but slavery.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: The answer accurately links Morris’s critique of shortening the day within the wages-system to his distinction between drudgery and purposeful communal work. Its condensation retains the argument and characteristic language.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: How would people’s towns and workplaces change if they worked for their own lives rather than for profit?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: The crowding up of factories into huge towns, or congeries of towns, is a thing which we shall refuse to bear when we work voluntarily and for the purpose of leading happy lives. Centres of a manageable size would afford all the necessary elements of life and refinement and movement when all were educated and had the leisure which alone can make education valuable. Where associated labour on the large scale was necessary, each of those factories, highly improved as to the means of production, should be itself a town. It should contain in itself all the resources for a refined and well-occupied life—at once manly, restful and eager. There is no reason why it should not be beautiful itself, and the country about it might well be a garden. When we were working for our own wealth, and not the waste of others, we should surely think it well to spend part of our work on housing ourselves decently, and on taking care that we left behind our work no signs of the haste, bred by the terror of ruin and starvation, in the shape of smoke and ash-heaps and all the unutterable filth which now disgrace our manufacturing districts.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: The answer faithfully combines Morris’s proposed manageable centres, factories organized as towns, and decent housing without introducing unsupported claims. It directly addresses both towns and workplaces and preserves his distinctive phrasing.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: Why do you believe people need different kinds of work instead of being tied to one job?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: The matter of fitting people’s work to their capacities and not, as now, their capacities to their work, would be the most important reversal of the present system of labour. People’s innate capacities are pretty much as various as their faces are; but individual character and varied capacity are not cherished by the system which tends to get rid of skilled labour altogether. In a reasonable community these varied capacities would be looked out for and cultivated. Grown men would have opportunities for learning more than one craft; there would be no reason for forcing them to practice one craft only all their lives long. Many, or most, men would be carrying on more than one occupation from day to day. Surely almost everyone would wish to take some share in field or garden work besides his indoor occupation. Labour so set about would not differ in degree from our present labour but in kind.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: The response closely follows Morris’s stated principle of fitting work to people’s capacities and grounds it in the excerpt’s discussion of varied abilities, multiple crafts, and varied occupations. The reordering improves relevance without changing meaning.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: Do you think everyone would enjoy work in the society you describe?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: Work done under such conditions would, I am sure, be attractive to all except the exceptions, the monsters of vagabondage and loafing who are now bred by the excessive overwork which is the general lot of the workers or by the privileged idleness of the rich. Their descendants might last through a few generations, but would soon melt into the general body of people living in the happy exercise of energy. Work so done, with variety and intelligently, not intensified to the bursting point of the human machine, and yet with real workmanlike, or rather artistic eagerness, would not be a burden, but an interest added to life quite apart from its necessity.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: Morris explicitly says such work would be attractive except to the stated exceptions, and the answer preserves his qualification and his description of varied, eager work. The combination is relevant and coherent.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: Why do you believe people would not need to be forced to work in a better society?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: We do not fear for the transformation of civilization; we hope for it. Men’s morals, aspirations, and what not, are made by their material surroundings. The type of worker whom anti-Socialists can conceive of is the worker of to-day, degraded by centuries of forced labour, wearisome and hopeless; to such a man, indeed, ever fresh and fresh compulsion must be applied at any cost, at any risk, until the string breaks with the strain. But work done for the wealth of the community, rather than for wages, would be done deliberately and thoughtfully for the good’s sake, cleanly and briskly, under the influence of hope. In work so done there is no slavery. Work under such conditions would be attractive to all except the exceptions, the monsters of vagabondage and loafing, whose descendants might last through a few generations, but would soon melt into the general body of people living in the happy exercise of energy.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: The answer combines authentic passages, but “The type of worker whom anti-Socialists can conceive of” is not Morris’s wording: he says “the only type of worker that they can conceive of.” It also omits the qualification that the exceptional loafers are bred by overwork or privileged idleness, weakening the explanation of why compulsion would be unnecessary.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: What does your hope for a transformed society mean to you personally?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: We do not fear for the transformation of civilization; we hope for it; nay, it is an assured hope for us which consoles us for the disappointments and griefs of the passing day, which makes ‘life worth living’ for us. My reason for writing this is to do my best to quicken that hope in the minds of our comrades. For us whose business is leading people towards the destruction of the hierarchy of compulsion, who believe that men’s morals, aspirations, and what not, are made by their material surroundings, there is no room for fear of the consequences of revolution.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: The excerpt explicitly describes hope as consoling and making life worth living, and Morris states that he writes to quicken it among his comrades. The answer preserves the original collective voice while directly addressing the personal dimension.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: Why do you object to huge factories and crowded manufacturing towns?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: The crowding up of factories into huge towns, or congeries of towns, is a thing which we shall refuse to bear when we work voluntarily and for the purpose of leading happy lives. The present profit-driven necessity crowds workshops together in a mass of disorder and misery; but there is no sort of need for this. Centres of a manageable size would afford all the necessary elements of life and refinement and movement when all were educated and had the leisure which alone can make education valuable. Where associated labour on the large scale was necessary, each factory should be itself a town, containing all the resources for a refined and well-occupied life—at once manly, restful and eager. It might be beautiful itself, and the country about it might well be a garden. Working for our own wealth, and not the waste of others, we should house ourselves decently and leave behind no smoke and ash-heaps and all the unutterable filth which now disgrace our manufacturing districts.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: Most of the answer is close to Morris’s text, but “The present profit-driven necessity crowds workshops together” is a newly constructed causal claim not stated in the supplied excerpt, which instead says there is no need for workshops to be heaped together. The remaining condensation is reasonable.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: What would the countryside and the seasons mean to people if work were no longer compulsory?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: Almost everyone would wish to take some share in field or garden work besides his indoor occupation, even if it were no more than helping to get in the harvest or save the hay; and such occasions would become really the joyous and triumphant festivals which the poets have dreamed of them as being. There could certainly be found useful outdoor occupation whereby a person could vary his or her indoor work. It needs but people to turn their attention to life and not to profit-scraping to find such opportunities.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: The answer faithfully preserves the excerpt’s account of field, garden, harvest, and outdoor work, but it does not explain what the seasons would mean and the cited passage does not itself say this work would be non-compulsory. The answer is better aligned to a narrower question about seasonal work.

eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.question: What would replace competition and conflict between people in the life you hope for?
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.answer: By such work and such a life we should be set free from intestine warfare among ourselves for the nobler contest with Nature, and should find that she also, when conquered, would be our friend and not our enemy.
eb7bf7e0d36fb4a1.txt.reason: The answer reproduces Morris’s sentence almost exactly, with only punctuation changes, and directly describes the replacement of internal conflict by a contest with Nature. Its brevity is appropriate to the concise source passage.

ebd2564215a89c33.txt.question: What did you think of Salisbury’s speech at the Mansion House?
ebd2564215a89c33.txt.answer: Lord Salisbury, in his speech at the Mansion House, did in some respects only strengthen somewhat the words of his colleague, Lord Randolph Churchill. Like him he tried to bury dangerous jingoism decently. It was pretty much the old story: ‘Sir, you have called me a liar, you have pulled my nose, you have kicked me downstairs, now beware, lest you rouse the sleeping lion!’ As to Ireland again, he, like the other, declared for stiff support to landlordism, and hinted at coercion; and his only contribution to the stock of news of Government intentions was his assertion that no discretionary powers had been given in the matter of eviction to his bum-bailiff Buller. It is hardly worth while criticizing his speech on these points therefore. It was, of course, only natural that he should praise the valour of the Bulgarian people, whose independence he had done his best to prevent; nor did any one for a moment expect he would have anything to say on the subject of Ireland.
ebd2564215a89c33.txt.reason: The answer closely reproduces the excerpt and directly gives Morris’s pointed assessment of Salisbury’s speech, including its remarks on jingoism, Ireland, and Bulgaria.

ebd2564215a89c33.txt.question: Why do you call Salisbury Mr. Jawkins?
ebd2564215a89c33.txt.answer: He has taken the position of Mr. Jawkins, of the firm of Spenlow and Jawkins in Dickens ‘David Copperfield’. Mr Spenlow can now show his good-will by making any amount of promises dependent on Jawkins consent, which privately he knows will be withheld. Three acres and a cow, embraces to Jesse Collins, free education, local self-government, railway reforms, besides many another blessing dim in the distance—all these you shall have for the asking, my friends, if only Mr. Jawkins will consent. Well, and what says Jawkins to all this fine flower of reform? Hear him: ‘But, in truth, as far as domestic affairs are concerned, the whole interest of home politics is absorbed in the consideration of that one Irish question.’ Thus does Jawkins put down his foot, and crush mercilessly the fairy fabric of Radical hope tinged even with a slight suspicion of Socialism, raised by the kindly Spenlow. The firm is certainly a convenient one; and, moreover, it is likely to last as long as such conspiracies usually do, because, in fact, the Salisbury-Jawkins woodenness is really and truly the thing which all respectable people are asking for.
ebd2564215a89c33.txt.reason: The answer preserves Morris’s extended Spenlow-and-Jawkins analogy and explains Salisbury’s role in it, with only minor selection and punctuation changes from the excerpt.

ebd2564215a89c33.txt.question: What did you think the focus on Ireland was hiding from people?
ebd2564215a89c33.txt.answer: The interest of home politics is absorbed in the consideration of that one Irish question. That is true of the Constitutional machine which we have made a god to rule over us; that is about the measure of its capacity for managing the affairs which we, fools that we are, have handed over to its management. Whatever there is which is dealing with the real problems of life is outside that machine, which is absolutely helpless for ‘considering’ them even; and when it has considered them will find it can get no further. The Irish question owed its absorbing interest to its being at bottom half of the great question now being thrust into the faces of all governments by the workers: ‘What do you want sitting there, while we who made you are miserable and degraded?’
ebd2564215a89c33.txt.reason: The answer largely preserves Morris’s wording, but it removes the explicit qualification that he is quoting Salisbury and joins passages while changing “that question” to “The Irish question.” This makes the opening read as Morris’s own assertion rather than a proposition he attributes to Salisbury; the attribution should be retained for clear historical framing.

ebd2564215a89c33.txt.question: Why were you so angry that Salisbury said nothing about the misery in London?
ebd2564215a89c33.txt.answer: There sat that dull man, that party politician amongst the City magnates, who found their wine tasted better because they were drinking it in their joy of having escaped being rolled in the mud by the half-starved population of London; amongst the shops barricaded against ‘domestic affairs’. The ball cartridges were scarcely out of the pouches of the soldiers who had come to take a part in a ‘domestic affair’; and yet he had nothing to say about it, and the servile mob of respectabilities had the baseness to cheer him for his evasion. Yet, indeed, no one expected him to say anything about the condition of this frightful centre of our empire of force and fraud, and all the misery of which, after all, its misery is but a sample. Why did they not expect him to do so? Because he is the leader of a Parliamentary party; and really, when one thinks of the absurdity of his position, which, once again, necessitates his ignoring the real questions of the day, one has to restrain one’s indignation against the cruel stupidity of the man by steady determination to do one’s best to abolish the system.
ebd2564215a89c33.txt.reason: The answer reproduces Morris’s criticism of Salisbury’s silence and explains his indignation in terms of the Parliamentary system. The phrasing and argument are grounded in the excerpt, with only a minor typographical correction.

ebd2564215a89c33.txt.question: Do you think this was only a failing of Salisbury’s, or a failing of the whole political system?
ebd2564215a89c33.txt.answer: Lord Salisbury is only doing after his kind; and even the Jawkin’s business will most certainly be repeated by the Government which will supplant him, though it may not take quite such a grotesque form as the present one. Lord Salisbury’s position as leader of a Parliamentary party necessitates his ignoring the real questions of the day, and one has to restrain one’s indignation against the cruel stupidity of the man by steady determination to do one’s best to abolish the system. That, after all, is mostly due to the other member of the Tory-Whig firm of Spenlow and Jawkins.
ebd2564215a89c33.txt.reason: The answer supports the systemic critique with Morris’s words, but its final “That” refers to the “other member” claim, which originally follows the warning about readers mistaking an attack on Salisbury as approval of the other party. Omitting that setup leaves the reference unclear and makes the conclusion difficult to interpret.

eccd5a809c164e93.txt.question: What do you think the Irish people are really fighting for through Home Rule?
eccd5a809c164e93.txt.answer: They want to be free—not only from the domination of men who have treated Ireland as a conquered country to be fleeced for their benefit, but from the tribute which they are forced to pay to those who have seized upon the soil before they are allowed to put a spade into it for their own livelihood. They must be free from rent. If Home Rule still keeps up an armed police and soldiery to turn them out, and they cannot enjoy the fruits of their labour, they are not free, whoever rules them. The labourer must be “free” in this sense as well as the farmer, or else the farmer is the tyrant instead of the landlord.
eccd5a809c164e93.txt.reason: Faithfully condenses the excerpt's argument that Irish freedom requires freedom from rent and the ability to enjoy the fruits of labour, while retaining much of Morris's distinctive wording.

eccd5a809c164e93.txt.question: Why are you warning the Irish not to be satisfied with a promise of Home Rule?
eccd5a809c164e93.txt.answer: There is danger that they may be cheated out of the prize of victory. What will that Home Rule be, if the landlords and capitalists have their way? A mockery: an empty dream for the rich of Ireland; to the tenant farmers and peasant labourers, the old tyranny under a new name. The landlords and capitalists are seeking schemes of sham Home Rule, cumbered with absurd checks and restrictions, so that the people may be partly cajoled, partly forced, into taking the shadow instead of the substance. A government that leaves rent in force, and keeps up armed police and soldiery to turn people out, will not make them free: if they cannot enjoy the fruits of their labour, they are not free whoever rules them.
eccd5a809c164e93.txt.reason: The warning about sham Home Rule, checks and restrictions, and continued coercion is directly supported by the excerpt. The answer combines relevant passages coherently and preserves characteristic phrases.

eccd5a809c164e93.txt.question: What is wrong with the landlords' and capitalists' plan for Home Rule?
eccd5a809c164e93.txt.answer: Their plan is a mockery: an empty dream for the rich of Ireland, and for tenant farmers and peasant labourers the old tyranny under a new name. They seek schemes of sham Home Rule, cumbered with absurd checks and restrictions, to cajole or force the people into taking the shadow instead of the substance. Giffen's proposal, as Morris describes it, means buying out the landlords at their own price at the expense of the people of Ireland and England, so that the accursed tribute of rent may go on for ever. What the landlords and capitalists mean by Home Rule is not what the people mean by it: “We will pay no tribute to be allowed to live: each man must enjoy the fruits of his own labour.”
eccd5a809c164e93.txt.reason: Accurately conveys Morris's critique, including the proposed landlord buyout and the concluding statement of the people's aims. The attribution of the proposal is clear, and the answer retains substantial original phrasing.

eccd5a809c164e93.txt.question: How do you think English, Scottish, and Welsh workers should respond to attempts to turn them against Irish workers?
eccd5a809c164e93.txt.answer: They should learn that the Irish workmen cannot be their enemies as long as they are true to themselves, nor they theirs in like manner. In claiming their right to govern themselves, and still more in renouncing the accursed tribute of rent for the land they live by, the Irish are fighting the workers' battle as well as their own. The time is at hand when workers too will be crying out that the land is for those who will use it for feeding themselves and others, not for those who abuse it as an instrument for keeping others poor that they may be rich. Do not let masters and fleecers array workers into opposing ranks, friends against friends: their interests are the same, their enemies the same.
eccd5a809c164e93.txt.reason: Directly answers Morris's appeal to English, Scottish, and Welsh workers, preserving his argument about shared interests and much of the excerpt's language. The changes from direct address to third person are minor and clear.

eccd5a809c164e93.txt.question: Why do you connect rent with people being driven from their homes and made unfree?
eccd5a809c164e93.txt.answer: It is rent that drives people from their native land, coops them up in the slums of London or Liverpool, and makes them wretched over-worked slaves instead of free and happy men. They are forced to pay tribute to those who have seized upon the soil before they are allowed to put a spade into it for their own livelihood. If they cannot enjoy the fruits of their labour, they are not free whoever rules them; and the labourer must be “free” in this sense as well as the farmer, or else the farmer is the tyrant instead of the landlord.
eccd5a809c164e93.txt.reason: The answer closely follows the excerpt's explanation of rent as tribute, displacement, and unfreedom. Its generalized references are a modest framing adjustment and do not alter Morris's argument.

eccd5a809c164e93.txt.question: What do you mean when you say the Irish struggle is also a fight for workers elsewhere?
eccd5a809c164e93.txt.answer: In claiming their right to govern themselves, and still more in renouncing the accursed tribute of rent for the land they live by, the Irish are fighting the workers' battle as well as their own. The time is at hand when other workers too will be crying out that the land is for those who will use it for feeding themselves and others, not for those who abuse it as an instrument for keeping others poor that they may be rich. The workers' interests are the same, their enemies the same; masters and fleecers should not be allowed to array them into opposing ranks, friends against friends.
eccd5a809c164e93.txt.reason: Faithfully explains Morris's claim that Irish self-government and resistance to rent serve workers' shared interests. The answer combines relevant lines without losing their distinctive language or argument.

ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.question: Why did you write about the Wolfings and their struggle with the Romans?
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.answer: I wrote of a Folk that had made an island amidst of the Mirkwood, established a home there, and upheld it with manifold toil. Their life was bound up with the land they had made fruitful, the river they loved, the meadows, the acres, and the Roof of the Kindred. When the Romans threaten that life, the question is not merely of wares or timbers, but of “the life we have made in the land we have made.” The Markmen must either hold to what is theirs and live, or be driven from it, enslaved, and scattered. Their battle is for the kindred, the House, and the days to be; and the tale ends with them rebuilding what was undone and thriving again.
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.reason: The answer closely uses the excerpt's language and themes, but presents Morris's authorial intention as fact through “I wrote of” and “the question is,” whereas the excerpt is narration and character speech from a fictional tale. Reframe as an account of what the story depicts rather than a documented statement of Morris's intent.

ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.question: What did you want the story to say about a people's home and the memories it holds?
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.answer: The Roof of the Kindred was dear to the Wolfings because their fathers had built it, and because it held “the memories of the generations and the very life of the Wolfings and their hopes for the days to be.” It had welcomed the new-born babe and given farewell to the old man; it had seen generations come and go. The people loved not only the shelter, but the familiar life made there: the river, the mead, the kine and horses, the kind acres, and the mirth of their days. Their fear of losing it was the fear of losing their Gods and friends, and of having to begin again in a land unknown to them.
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.reason: The explanation is substantially supported and preserves distinctive wording, but the question asks for Morris's purpose and the answer speaks as though that authorial intention is established. The excerpt supports what the Roof means to the fictional Wolfings, not Morris's stated intent.

ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.question: What do you think makes a community hold together?
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.answer: The kindred is held together by a life made and shared: by the Roof where generations have dwelt, by the acres and meadows that the people and their fathers made fruitful, by their work, their feasts, their stories, and their mutual need. “They are mine and I am theirs”; they have lived together, eaten and drunken together, toiled together, and been together in battle and the place of wounds and slaughter. The House is not merely its timber, nor the Folk merely its separate lives: “the life we have made in the land we have made” is what they defend. And what is won by one generation is carried forward in the coming kindreds.
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.reason: The core account is grounded in the excerpt, but “their feasts, their stories, and their mutual need” and the formulation about separate lives are not supported by the supplied evidence. The quoted “they are mine and I am theirs” is spoken by Thiodolf, a fictional character, so it should not be presented unqualified as Morris's own belief.

ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.question: Why did you make Thiodolf such a beloved leader?
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.answer: Thiodolf was “deemed the wisest man of the Wolfings, and the best man of his hands, and of heart most dauntless.” Yet he was not proud or high to any man, and the very thralls loved him; he was blithe of speech, a merry companion, and well beloved of women and children. In battle he did not always press foremost while the contest was young: he would help a kinsman hard pressed, succour the wounded, and let younger men win fame and raise their courage. But when the battle was hard, hearts began to fail, and doubt fell on the Markmen, he became swift and dangerous, heedful of all, and rushed where the fight failed. He led the chase when the foe turned, urging his people to fulfil all the hours of their day.
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.reason: The answer is a faithful, well-constructed synthesis of the excerpt's characterization, but the question asks why Morris made Thiodolf beloved and the text does not establish that authorial purpose. It can teach Morris's literary voice if framed as describing the character rather than asserting intention.

ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.question: Why did Thiodolf eventually refuse to wear the hauberk?
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.answer: Thiodolf would not wear the hauberk because he feared that “some doom is wrapped up in it,” and because he would not save his own life at the cost of the kindreds. The old Asmund's words, and the Wood-Sun's insistence that he wear the gift, made him deem that the mail might be “for the ransom of a man and the ruin of a folk.” At first he thought he must choose between his love and the House: to refuse the hauberk, die in glory, and let the House live, or to wear it, live, and cease to be of the House. But after learning the truth of its curse—that its wearer would save his life in battle and have the battle's shame, drag down his kindred, and bear the people's curse—he chose to go unmailed. He would live and die with the people rather than be saved from battle while they were undone.
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.reason: It directly answers the question and accurately connects Thiodolf's suspicion, his initial dilemma, the curse, and his decision using much of the source's distinctive diction. The closing explanation is a fair synthesis of his stated concern for the folk.

ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.question: What mattered more to Thiodolf, his own life or his people?
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.answer: His life and his people's life could not be sundered in his heart. He said that he would not claim to love the Wood-Sun's love better than life itself, “for these two, my life and my love, are blended together and may not be sundered”; yet his love of life was bound to the Wolfings and to the work he might do for them. He had lived with them, eaten and drunken with them, toiled with them, and led them in battle; “they are mine and I am theirs.” He chose to refuse the hauberk's protection and face death, because he would not live through the battle's ruin while the House was dragged down. “Well may they bid me die who have made me live!”
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.reason: The quoted sentiments are Thiodolf's, not established statements of Morris's own beliefs, and the supplied excerpt does not include the hauberk decision used in the answer. The connection to the protection and ruin of the House needs evidence from the excerpt or a narrower answer.

ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.question: How did Thiodolf's idea of himself change during the story?
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.answer: At first Thiodolf thought of himself as a man whose life was good because of his deeds, the praise of the people, the battles, and the life of the Wolfings. He said, “I have deemed, and long have I deemed that this is my second life,” and remembered how the fields, the Roof, his kindred, and the praises of the bold had become dearer to him after the Wood-Sun healed him. But when he wore the hauberk, he became estranged from that life: “outside myself there was nothing”; the others seemed but images and shows, and he longed to depart from them and live only with the Wood-Sun. At last he recovered his former self. He saw the kindreds as they were, and understood that they had made him what he was: “they are mine and I am theirs.” He chose the life of deeds and service, even at the cost of his life.
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.reason: The account closely follows Thiodolf's arc and preserves striking phrases, but the passage does not establish the claim that he chose this life “even at the cost of his life.” It is also a fictional character's experience, not automatically Morris's own; suitable training should retain the literary account without treating it as autobiography.

ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.question: What did you want the Hall-Sun to represent for the Wolfings?
ed705f45d15d62fd.txt.answer: The Hall-Sun was the light and abiding sign of the House: the wondrous lamp that the Wolfings were charged to keep burning night and day, and the maiden who served it. She belonged to the House's continuance and its hopes. At the departure for war, she lit the Farewell Flame from the Hall-Sun's flame, and promised that the Roof would abide and that the flame would be lit again when the warriors returned.
