That they have been resisted as widely as they have been should give us good hope of even the average material of the ‘masses’ on whom we depend for the body of assent which must be the first step towards the new Society.
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.reason: The answer retains Morris’s specific explanation of pressures on workmen voters and his conclusion that their resistance offered hope for the new Society. Its edits make the passage direct without changing its meaning.

fadaee3bf845af14.txt.question: Why did you want the Irish question settled, even though you thought it was not the main socialist issue?
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.answer: Peace with Ireland would have been a great advantage to the Socialist propaganda, because it would have cleared the ground of a question which very naturally excites political passions deeply, and at the same time has only an indirect bearing on our great object, the destruction of monopoly and exploitation. It would not only have forced the consideration of their own economical condition on the Irish themselves, but would have left nothing for us to consider in England, Scotland, and Wales, except our economical condition—unless some scare of a Russian war could have been set on foot by our ‘rulers’.
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.reason: The response answers why peace with Ireland would benefit socialist propaganda while preserving Morris’s qualification that the Irish question bore only indirectly on the destruction of monopoly and exploitation. The wording is substantially from the excerpt.

fadaee3bf845af14.txt.question: What did you think the election figures really showed about popular opinion?
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.answer: The elections as they are now conducted cannot be looked on as a test of opinion. According to Mr Dell’s figures in the Daily News of July 13th, 512,415 Home Rule votes produced 50 members, while 512,415 Tory and Jingo votes made 97 members. Every one really knows that this is but a specimen of the juggling of our Representation. It would be idle to take the apparent desertion of democratic opinion by the working-classes at face value: the electoral arrangements are a humbug, and the figures themselves dispose of the pretence that the elections, as now conducted, test opinion.
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.reason: The evidence and conclusion are grounded in the excerpt, but “It would be idle to take the apparent desertion ... at face value” and the restatement of the conclusion are newly composed rather than Morris’s wording. This is a correctable, somewhat repetitive departure from the language-authenticity objective.

fadaee3bf845af14.txt.question: How did you expect the new government to be put together?
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.answer: A Whig-Tory Government it will be, then, from the first, and, as to the Irish business, it will plainly be inexpugnable. The Whig-Tory party has triumphed; though probably the name of coalition will be avoided in forming the new government, it will really be a coalition. But this will be a coalition not depending on temporary circumstances, but on the open admission of the fact that Whig and Tory no longer indicate real party differences, much less any ghost of a difference as to principles. It will be strong in other matters also, because the fear of playing into the hands of the Separationists will always be present to the minds of the jingo-Liberals whenever they may be inclined to assert their liberty. They have begun by letting themselves be made the tools of the Whig-Tory party, and they must play out their part to the end—unless any of them should repent and swallow Home Rule after all, which is by no means impossible.
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.reason: This combines Morris’s account of the coalition and expected government without materially altering its argument or distinctive phrasing. It directly addresses the question and preserves the qualification about Jingo-Liberals possibly accepting Home Rule.

fadaee3bf845af14.txt.question: What did you think Gladstone should do after losing the election?
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.answer: The plain truth is that no mechanical contrivances will hold together even the semblance of a Liberal party. The suggestions that Mr Gladstone might gather up all the different opinions on Home Rule and frame a measure to satisfy everybody, or hold office for the rest of the year and bring in a Home Rule Bill in the spring session, offered no sound way forward. A bill would be defeated; and, from Mr Labouchere’s point of view, it is hard to see what could be gained by merely putting off the evil day, except the satisfaction of appetite for loaves and fishes for a short time. The Whig-Tory party has triumphed; although the name of coalition will probably be avoided, it will really be a coalition, founded on the open admission that Whig and Tory no longer indicate real party differences, much less any ghost of a difference as to principles.
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.reason: The answer accurately reports the proposals and Morris’s broader conclusion, but “offered no sound way forward” is an added summary, and it converts the reported expectation that the bill would be defeated into an unattributed assertion. The excerpt specifically presents that view in its account of Labouchere’s reasoning. It also digresses into the coalition, which does not directly answer what Gladstone should do.

fadaee3bf845af14.txt.question: What course did you think the Irish party might take if Westminster refused Home Rule?
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.answer: It is possible that when they see that the Westminster Parliament is determined not to yield to their just demand, they should leave it to do as it will, and return to Ireland and there sit to give help and counsel, if nothing else, to the Irish people. The Irish party’s ordinary parliamentary tactics are hard to discern. As long as they are in close alliance with the Gladstonian party their old game of parliamentary obstruction must be in abeyance; nor, indeed, was it ever anything more than a protest against the shelving of the Irish question. The position of tail to the Gladstonian party, or even head of it under Gladstone, would not be a very exciting one for them; but they will have to accept it unless they take this other course. Morris acknowledges that this might precipitate “mere violent coercion” on the English part, but asks: “Are not the English preparing for veiled coercion at least? Will they not be driven to use that? And might it not be well to strip the veil from the ugly thing and show it for what it is?”
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.reason: The proposal and discussion of coercion accurately follow the excerpt. However, “Morris acknowledges” is an editorial framing that breaks the first-person response style, and “ordinary parliamentary tactics are hard to discern” modernizes and softens the original wording (“it is difficult to see what amongst ordinary parliamentary tactics they can take to”).

fadaee3bf845af14.txt.question: What did you think the Irish party should say to England if it returned home?
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.answer: They might say: “Since you must govern us, and against our consent; since you can no longer pretend not to know what we want—govern us, then! And take on yourselves the responsibility for the government! We have besought you, argued with you, taught you, warned you—in vain. We will do so no longer; we have no more to do with you. Take your own course, and find out for yourselves that Ireland is not England.” Such a voice as this would ring throughout all history, if only it could be uttered. But it is not likely to be. The cause of Irish Independence will most probably have to be dragged through all kinds of pettiness and intrigue before its true aim, the happiness of the Irish people, becomes visible.
fadaee3bf845af14.txt.reason: The passage is explicitly framed in the excerpt as a hypothetical declaration, not an actual event. The answer retains Morris’s original speech and reflective conclusion, while “They might say” appropriately clarifies the imagined nature of the words.

fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.question: What did you think was the most important result of the Lord Mayor’s Show?
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.answer: The most important fact was that the crowd everywhere were in sympathy with the Socialists; and this is a very important fact, and shows that the propaganda of the past year has produced its effect. The net gain of this strange Lord Mayor’s Show is that, as far as it goes, it has struck a blow at bourgeois authority, and that it has emphasized the class distinctions which rob us all of our due life. That at least is something.
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.reason: The answer closely preserves Morris’s wording and directly combines his claims about socialist sympathy and the Show’s effect on bourgeois authority and class distinctions.

fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.question: Why did you see the crowd’s sympathy for the Socialists as significant?
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.answer: The crowd everywhere were in sympathy with the Socialists; they were there supporting the Socialists in general, who they believed were trying to raise them from the terrible condition in which they are. They were at least in a fair way of understanding that they are poor because the masters of the police and soldiers are rich. This shows that the propaganda of the past year has produced its effect.
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.reason: The answer draws directly on Morris’s account of the crowd’s support and developing class understanding, and explains why he considered their sympathy significant. The wording remains substantially authentic.

fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.question: What did you think the demonstration could do about the coming hardship in the East End?
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.answer: The action of the Government which the whole agitation is meant to force on would certainly do something towards ‘preventing the winter sorrow’. But the very little that the Government could be forced to do for poor people, even the whole of the resolutions, do not mean Socialism or anything like it, though they do mean an attempt to palliate present poverty. An attempt which, even as a palliative, is bound to fail, because it is a palliative that looks towards Socialism. No bourgeois government could carry out the measures claimed by these resolutions, even if they would; and certainly none will try to do so, or can be forced to try, so long as they are a constitutional government and not a revolutionary body.
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.reason: The source supports the argument about government action, palliative relief, and constitutional limits, but the answer drops the original qualification “let alone” and produces a confusing clause: “the very little ... even the whole of the resolutions, do not mean.” This needs correction before training.

fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.question: Why did you say that the resolutions were not Socialism?
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.answer: Even the whole of the resolutions do not mean Socialism or anything like it, though they do mean an attempt to palliate present poverty. The action of the Government which the whole agitation is meant to force on would certainly do something towards ‘preventing the winter sorrow’; but it is the very little that the Government could be forced to do for poor people. And the attempt, even as a palliative, is bound to fail, because it is a palliative that looks towards Socialism. No bourgeois government could carry out the measures claimed by these resolutions, even if they would; and certainly none will try to do so, or can be forced to try, so long as they are a constitutional government and not a revolutionary body.
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.reason: The response retains Morris’s distinction between relief measures and Socialism, but “but it is the very little that the Government could be forced to do” is an awkward, incomplete construction not present in the source. The answer should preserve the original qualification more coherently.

fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.question: What did you mean when you said the crowd was beginning to understand why they were poor?
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.answer: They were at least in a fair way of understanding that they are poor because the masters of the police and soldiers are rich. When the poor begin to know that they are poor not by irremediable accident, but because they are robbed by a useless class who can be got rid of, the beginning of the end is at hand.
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.reason: Both sentences are drawn directly from Morris’s explanation, and together they clearly answer the question while retaining his characteristic phrasing and political argument.

fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.question: What did you think had to happen before real change for the better was possible?
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.answer: Until people find out either by learning to see it, or by instinctive feeling, that there is a class war going on, great change for the better is impossible. When the poor begin to know that they are poor not by irremediable accident, but because they are robbed by a useless class who can be got rid of, the beginning of the end is at hand.
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.reason: The excerpt says, “Until people find out ... that there is a class war going on, and great change for the better is impossible.” Removing “and” silently changes the source’s sentence structure and leaves the relationship between recognizing class war and impossibility less certain than the answer asserts.

fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.question: Why were you so critical of the newspapers’ reaction to the demonstration?
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.answer: The press has shown its disappointment clearly enough, though some part of it has tried to hide its uneasiness at the affair. The Standard probably expresses the general feeling on the matter, and the tone of its article is regret that the police did not stop the meeting at any cost, because authority has received a blow from what took place — as indeed it has. The Pall Mall admits the collapse of authority. The Daily News loses its respectable head from sheer peevishness, even to the extent of allowing itself to publish this remarkable sentence: ‘The spirit in which they [the Socialists] conduct their agitation is a good deal more important than their principles.’ Really, Mr Bourgeois, ‘even for your own purposes’, you should try not to be so empty as that. Socialist principles, whether they are right or wrong, profess to deal with a subject no less than the whole of human life; and however rude and offensive we, the present agitators, may be in our agitation, those principles will be discussed, whether they are acted upon or not, long after the world has got rid of such passing matters as us and our rudeness.
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.reason: The answer closely reproduces Morris’s critique, makes clear that the quoted claim belongs to the Daily News, and explains his objection by contrasting agitators’ conduct with the scope and lasting importance of Socialist principles.

fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.question: Why did you think Socialist principles mattered more than how agitators behaved?
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.answer: Socialist principles, whether they are right or wrong, profess to deal with a subject no less than the whole of human life; and however rude and offensive the present agitators may be in their agitation, those principles will be discussed, whether they are acted upon or not, long after the world has got rid of such passing matters as the agitators and their rudeness.
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.reason: The argument is authentic, but the answer rewrites Morris’s first-person “we, the present agitators” and “us and our rudeness” into third-person language. This weakens a distinctive persona signal and makes Morris’s self-identification as an agitator less direct.

fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.question: Did you think the police had really won on Lord Mayor’s Day?
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.answer: The procession was far from being a triumphant one, and was escorted by hoots and groans all along. The success of the police in preventing a demonstration was only partial, since a huge meeting was held and harangued in Trafalgar Square, in spite of Sir Charles Warren’s proclamation, besides the large meeting in Hyde Park held together by members of the League in spite of the pouring rain. All this is not very like a police triumph. The allies counted on by the police, judging by Colonel Fraser’s letter, entirely failed then. The net gain of this strange Lord Mayor’s Show is that, as far as it goes, it has struck a blow at bourgeois authority.
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.reason: The answer directly responds that the police did not achieve a full triumph and supports that judgment with Morris’s account of the meetings, the failed allies, and the blow to bourgeois authority. The source typo is harmlessly corrected.

fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.question: How did you describe the purpose and limits of the Trafalgar Square resolutions?
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.answer: The resolutions meant an attempt to palliate present poverty, not Socialism or anything like it. The action of the Government which the whole agitation is meant to force on would certainly do something towards ‘preventing the winter sorrow’; but the very little that the Government could be forced to do for poor people would not resolve the poverty. An attempt, even as a palliative, is bound to fail, because it is a palliative that looks towards Socialism. No bourgeois government could carry out the measures claimed by these resolutions, even if they would; and certainly none will try to do so, or can be forced to try, so long as they are a constitutional government and not a revolutionary body.
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.reason: Most of the answer closely follows the excerpt, but “would not resolve the poverty” is an added interpretation, not Morris’s wording. The source calls the measures a palliative and says the attempt is bound to fail, so this extra claim should be removed or kept closer to that phrasing.

fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.question: What did you believe the press and respectable people had expected to happen?
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.answer: The all middle-class — the respectables — certainly expected it to be all the other way. The procession was far from being a triumphant one, and was escorted by hoots and groans all along; the crowd everywhere were in sympathy with the Socialists. The press has shown its disappointment clearly enough, though some part of it has tried to hide its uneasiness at the affair.
fbc2df70fb3257c5.txt.reason: The expectations and press reaction are directly supported, but the answer inserts the crowd’s sympathy between them without explaining the connection. The excerpt supports that detail elsewhere, yet the insertion makes the explanation less coherent and is unnecessary to the question.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: What did you mean by calling some art modern?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: By modern art I do not mean the art of the Victorian era. The nearest possible period to our own days must stand for modern art; and to my mind that is the period between the days of the Emperor Justinian and the Emperor Charles the Fifth. The present century has no school of art but such as each man of talent or genius makes for himself to serve his craving for the expression of his thought while he is alive, and to perish with his death. The two preceding centuries had styles, which dominated the practice of art, but those styles were not alive and progressive. The art I call modern had its very first roots spreading when the Roman Empire was tending towards disruption; its last heavily fruited branches were aloft in air when feudal Europe first felt shaken by the coming storm of revolution in Church and State. Between that time and this, art has been shut up in prison; all I can say of it in that condition is that I hope it has not died there.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: The answer preserves substantial Morris wording and his stated period, but the excerpt does not support the added chronology about art's roots, its “last heavily fruited branches,” or revolution in Church and State. Its opening explanation of Victorian art also omits Morris's qualifications about contemporary art.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: What do you think pattern-designing is for?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: The use of this subordinate, but by no means unimportant art is to enliven with beauty and incident what would otherwise be a blank space, wheresoever or whatsoever it may be. The absolute necessities of the art are beauty of colour and restfulness of form. Its colour may be brought about by the simplest combinations; its form may be merely that of abstract lines or spaces, and need not of necessity have any distinct meaning, or tell any story expressible in words. On the other hand, it is necessary to the purity of the art that its form and colour, when these bear any relation to the facts of nature (as for the more part they do), should be suggestive of such facts, and not descriptive of them.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: The answer directly explains the purpose and essential qualities of pattern-designing using Morris's wording almost verbatim. Removing the introductory hedge makes it more directly conversational without changing the meaning.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: Why do you think pattern-designing mattered, if it was a subordinate art?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: This subordinate, but by no means unimportant art enlivened with beauty and incident what would otherwise be a blank space. Even these lesser arts, being produced by man's intelligence, cannot really be separated from the greater, the more purely intellectual ones, or from the life which creates both. Pattern-designing fully shared in the exaltation of the master art; now at last it began to be really delightful in itself, since now at last the mind of a man happy in his work did more or less guide all hands that wrought it. No beauty in the art has ever surpassed the beauty of those its first days of joy and freedom.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: The answer combines directly relevant statements from the excerpt and explains both the art's value and its connection to makers' work. The slight grammatical adjustment at the opening is harmless, and the rest retains Morris's characteristic language.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: What makes a pattern beautiful in your view?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: The absolute necessities of the art are beauty of colour and restfulness of form. Its form and colour, when they bear any relation to the facts of nature, should be suggestive of such facts, and not descriptive of them. The most necessary qualities of pattern-work are richness and mystery; without them, indeed, it must be kept in the strictly subordinate place which the scientific good taste of Greece allotted to it. In the first days of its joy and freedom, the great rolling curves of the Roman acanthus had life, growth, variety, and refinement infused into them; the clean-cut accuracy and justness of line of one side of Greek ornament had gained a crisp sparkling richness, and a freedom and suggestion of nature; and the straying wreath-like naturalism of the other side had gained a knitting-up of its lines into strength, and an interest in every curve, which made it like the choice parts of the very growths of nature.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: The general criteria closely follow Morris, but the closing historical description changes his tense and framing: the excerpt says the Roman acanthus “have not been forgotten” and that Greek ornament “has gained” qualities, not that these transformations occurred “in the first days of its joy and freedom.” This conflates separate passages and adds a misleading chronology.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: Why do you admire St Sophia so much?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: St Sophia is most vigorously alive. It has gathered to itself all those elements of change which, having been kept apart for so long, were at last mingled and seething, and bringing about so many changes, so much of death and life. It is not bound by the past, but it has garnered all that there was in it which was fit to live and produce fresh life; it is the living child and the fruitful mother of art, past and future. That, even more than the loveliness which it drew forth from its own present, is what makes it the crown of all the great buildings of the world.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: The response answers the question with Morris's own explanation and preserves the passage's distinctive imagery and wording. Omitting the preceding reference to St Sophia as the “second building” does not impair comprehension.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: What do you think was wrong with the art of ancient Greece?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: The freedom of these free people was a narrow freedom. Their society was founded on slavery; slavery, mental as well as bodily, of the greater part of mankind, the iron exclusiveness which first bound their society, after no long while unsettled it, and at last destroyed it. In their art, the constant demand for perfection on every side was not an unmixed gain, for it made renunciation of many delightful things a necessity, and not unseldom drove it into being hard and unsympathetic. Greek art preferred blankness to the richness that might be given by the work of an unrefined or imperfectly taught hand; its demand for perfection in quality of workmanship deprived effort of all hope of reward in this lower region of art, and crushed all experiment, all invention and imagination. Its pattern-designs were generally well fitted for the purpose of decoration, graceful and temperate, but they had not, and did not pretend to have, any share of the richness, the mastery, or the individuality of nature.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: The answer accurately presents Morris's criticisms of Greek society and artistic standards, using language directly from the excerpt. It gives a coherent and sufficiently detailed response to the question.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: Why do you think the later, or Gothic, art came to life?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: When the Roman tyranny grew sick, when that recurring curse of the world, a dominant race, began for a time to be shaken from its hold, men began to long for the freedom of art. Amidst the confusion and rudeness of a time when one civilization was breaking up that another might be born of it, the mighty impulse which this longing gave to the expression of thought created speedily a glorious art, full of growth and hope, in the only form which in such a time art could take, architecture to wit; which, of all the forms of art, is that which springs direct from popular impulse, from the partnership of all men, great and little, in worthy and exalting aspirations. The chief element of life that Byzantine art gave expression to was freedom, the freedom of the many, in the realm of art at least. The workman was rising under the load of contempt that crushed him, and could do something that people would stop to look at. It was an architecture pure in its principles, reasonable in its practice, and beautiful to the eyes of all men, even the simplest: which can never exist in any state of society under which men are divided into intellectual castes.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: The explanation of the impulse behind the new art and the passage's account of freedom are grounded in the excerpt. However, the answer calls it “Gothic” in the question and then attributes the workman's rise specifically to Byzantine art; the excerpt discusses the workman in one passage and the origin of “modern art” in another, so the combined attribution risks conflating distinct discussions.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: What do you value most about the old buildings in England?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: The poor remains of our ancient buildings in themselves, as memorials of history and works of art, are worth more than any temporary use they can be put to. In this turbulent island, the home of rough and homely men, simple folk laboured for those that should come after them. Here, in the land we yet love, they built their homes and temples; if not so majestically as many peoples have done, yet in such sweet accord with the familiar nature amidst which they dwelt, that when by some happy chance we come across the work they wrought, untouched by any but natural change, it fills us with a satisfying untroubled happiness that few things else could bring us. These buildings are touching memories of our stout forefathers and their troublous days, that won our present peace and liberties; their beauty and the education they give are goods of the people of England, now and in time to come. We who are now alive are but life-renters of them. In destroying or injuring one of these buildings, we are destroying the pleasure, the culture, in a word, the humanity of unborn generations.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: The answer faithfully combines Morris's statements about the buildings' historical, artistic, and intergenerational value. It directly addresses what he values and retains his distinctive language and argument.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: Why are you so strongly against restoring old buildings?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: It is in the interest of living art and living history that I oppose so-called restoration. I love art, and I love history; but it is living art and living history that I love. What history can there be in a building bedaubed with ornament, which cannot at the best be anything but a hopeless and lifeless imitation of the hope and vigour of the earlier world? It is a strange folly for us who live among these bricken masses of hideousness to waste the energies of our short lives in feebly trying to add new beauty to what is already beautiful. Let us leave the dead alone, and, ourselves the living, build for the living and those that shall live. Since it is disputed whether restoration be good or not, and since we are confessedly living in a time when architecture has come on the one hand to jerry-building, and on the other to experimental designing, let us take breath and wait; let us sedulously repair our ancient buildings, and watch every stone of them as if they were built of jewels. If the buildings are not worth anything they are not worth restoring; if they are worth anything, they are at least worth treating with common sense and prudence.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: The answer accurately states Morris's objection to restoration and his alternative of careful repair and waiting. It preserves the source's forceful wording and is directly responsive.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: What should people do instead of restoring ancient buildings?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: Let us sedulously repair our ancient buildings, and watch every stone of them as if they were built of jewels; but otherwise let the dispute rest till we have once more learned architecture, till we once more have among us a reasonable, noble, and universally used style. Since it is disputed whether restoration be good or not, and since we are living in a time when architecture has come on the one hand to jerry-building, and on the other to experimental designing, let us take breath and wait. If the buildings are not worth anything they are not worth restoring; if they are worth anything, they are at least worth treating with common sense and prudence.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: This is a direct and coherent summary of Morris's recommendations: repair carefully, defer restoration, and act with prudence. Its reordered presentation preserves the source's meaning and characteristic phrasing.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: What did you think of the way Oxford's historic beauty was treated?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: The one most beautiful city of England, the city of Oxford, has been ravaged for many years past, not only by ignorant and interested tradesmen, but by the University and College authorities. Those whose special business it is to direct the culture of the nation have treated the beauty of Oxford as if it were a matter of no moment, as if their commercial interests might thrust it aside without any consideration. To my mind in so doing they have disgraced themselves. There are many places in England where a young man may get as good book-learning as in Oxford; not one where he can receive the education which the loveliness of the grey city used to give us.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: The response reproduces Morris's criticism of the treatment of Oxford and his view of the city's distinctive educational value. It answers the question directly and retains the original voice.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: What did you hope your society would do for old buildings?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: Our Society has had much to do in cases of what I should call the commercial destruction of buildings; we have carefully examined these cases to see if we had any ground to stand on for resisting the destruction; we have argued the matter threadbare on all sides; and above all we have always tried to suggest some possible use that the buildings could be put to. The Society has also taken great pains to try to get guardians of ancient buildings to repair their buildings. For we know well, by doleful experience, how quickly a building gets infirm if it be neglected. There are plenty of cases where a parish or a parson will spend two or three thousand pounds on ecclesiastical finery for a church, and let the rain sap the roof all the while; such things are apt to make the most polite people rude.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: The answer describes the Society's efforts to resist commercial destruction, find uses for buildings, and encourage repairs, all supported by the excerpt. It retains Morris's vivid criticism and answers the question thoroughly.

fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.question: Do you think the history of pattern-designing can be covered in a single lecture?
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.answer: To give anything like a history of the art of pattern-designing would be impossible within the limits of one lecture, for it would be doing no less than attempting to tell the whole story of architectural or popular art, a vast and most important subject. All I can pretend to do at present is to call your attention to certain things I have noticed in studying the development of the art of pattern-designing from ancient times to modern, and to hint at certain principles that have seemed to me to lie at the bottom of the practice of that art, and certain tendencies which its long course has had. Even in doing this I know I shall have to touch on difficult matters and take some facts for granted that may be, and have been, much disputed; and I must, therefore, even treating the subject thus, claim your indulgence for a necessary curtness and incompleteness.
fbcd3c36f53a0131.txt.reason: The answer is an exact, relevant passage that clearly answers the question and conveys Morris's scope and qualifications. It is coherent, informative, and highly useful for learning his voice.

fbf374d04560da82.txt.question: Why did you see the Paris Commune as so important in the overthrow of the monarchy?
fbf374d04560da82.txt.answer: The insurrection of the 10th August, which culminated in the final downfall of the monarchy and the imprisonment of the King and royal family in the Temple, was headed and organised by a new body definitely revolutionary, intended to be the expression of the power of the proletariat: the Commune of Paris, the moving spirit of which was Marat. The Convention declared as its foundation the sovereignty of the people and the abolition of royalty; but it also decreed that landed and other property was sacred for ever. So far, therefore, we have got no further than the complete triumph of bourgeois republicanism. The possibility of its retaining its position depended on the support of the proletariat, which was only given on the terms that the material condition of the workers should be altered for the better by the new regime. Those terms, in the long run, bourgeois republicanism could not keep, and therefore it fell.
fbf374d04560da82.txt.reason: The excerpt supports the Commune’s role in the August insurrection, but the answer attaches the Convention’s later declaration to the Commune passage in a way that blurs chronology and does not directly explain why the Commune mattered in overthrowing the monarchy.

fbf374d04560da82.txt.question: Why did you think the Girondins were out of sympathy with ordinary people?
fbf374d04560da82.txt.answer: The Girondins leaned on the support of the provinces, where respectability was stronger than in Paris, and tried to levy a bodyguard for the defence of the Convention against the Paris populace; though they got the decree for it passed, they could not carry it out. In their character of political economists, also, they resisted the imposing of a maximum price on grain, a measure which the scarcity caused by the general disturbance made imperative, if the proletariat were to have any share in the advantages of the Revolution. In short, the Girondins were obviously out of sympathy with the mass of the people.
fbf374d04560da82.txt.reason: The answer closely preserves the excerpt’s wording and reasoning: the Girondins’ provincial support, proposed bodyguard, and opposition to a grain price maximum support the conclusion that they were out of sympathy with the people.

fbf374d04560da82.txt.question: What do you think the French Revolution failed to understand about the working class?
fbf374d04560da82.txt.answer: The revolutionists had not the key to the great secret; they were still bourgeois, and still supposed that there must necessarily be a propertiless proletariat led by bourgeois, or at least served by them; they had not conceived the idea of the extinction of classes, and the organisation of the people itself for its own ends. The proletarians were disunited, ignorant of principles, and used to trust to leaders; they could make no head against the Society, which they had shaken indeed, owing to its internal dissensions, but which they were not yet able to destroy.
fbf374d04560da82.txt.reason: It directly answers the question using Morris’s distinctive phrasing about bourgeois assumptions, the extinction of classes, and the proletariat’s disunity and dependence on leaders.

fbf374d04560da82.txt.question: How do you explain the September Massacres?
fbf374d04560da82.txt.answer: They took place amid immediate danger to Paris and the French people: an armed coalition of the absolutist countries was gathering, one of its armies, commanded by the Duke of Brunswick, was already within a few days’ march of the city, and nothing was between Paris and destruction but undisciplined levies and the rags of the neglected army formed under the old regime. Verdun fell on the 2nd September, and Brunswick boasted that he would presently dine in Paris; on the same night the irregular trials and slaughter of the prisoners in Paris, known as the September Massacres, took place. The next day a circular was issued by the Committee of Public Safety, approving of the massacre. The Girondins kept quiet for the time, though they afterwards used the event against the Jacobins.
fbf374d04560da82.txt.reason: The excerpt explicitly connects the massacres with the imminent military threat and gives their timing and subsequent political response. The answer is a faithful condensation, with only minor connective wording added.

fbf374d04560da82.txt.question: What changed for workers during the Terror?
fbf374d04560da82.txt.answer: The law of maximum was passed, however, and a cumulative income tax, so that, as Carlyle remarks, the workman was at least better off under the Terror than he had ever been before.
fbf374d04560da82.txt.reason: The answer reproduces the excerpt almost verbatim and directly states the cited improvement in workers’ conditions under the Terror.

fbf374d04560da82.txt.question: Why did Robespierre lose power?
fbf374d04560da82.txt.answer: Robespierre seems to have worn out the patience of the people by his continued executions. Had he proclaimed an amnesty after his Feast of the Supreme Being, he would probably have had a longer lease of power; as it was, he and his tail died on the 28th July. His law Prairial had enabled him to condemn any one to the guillotine at pleasure, and at this ominous grumblings began to be heard. When he met unexpected opposition in the Convention, he lacked the military instinct to use the respite: Henriot failed in his attempt to crush the Convention, and the armed sections of Paris, on being appealed to by the Convention, wavered and gave way.
fbf374d04560da82.txt.reason: The account is largely drawn from the excerpt, but the added phrase “His law Prairial” is misleading: the passage says Robespierre got the law passed, not that it was his law. The answer also awkwardly places the law after the reference to his fall.

fbf374d04560da82.txt.question: What did Napoleon’s rise mean for the Revolution?
fbf374d04560da82.txt.answer: Napoleon did not so much crush the Revolution as put on it the final seal of law and order. The Revolution was set on foot by the middle classes in their own interests; the sentence that Napoleon accepted as the expression of his aims, “la carriére ouverte aux talens”—“the career thrown open to talent”—is the motto of middle-class supremacy. It implies the overthrow of aristocratic privilege and the setting up in its place of a money aristocracy, founded on the privilege of exploitation, amidst a world of so-called “free competition.” The middle-class, after a long and violent struggle, has conquered and is supreme from henceforth.
fbf374d04560da82.txt.reason: The direct-answer recasting preserves the excerpt’s argument and characteristic language, explaining Napoleon’s role as consolidating middle-class supremacy rather than simply crushing the Revolution.

fbf374d04560da82.txt.question: Why did you regard the first Socialist propaganda as a failure?
fbf374d04560da82.txt.answer: The attempt of Baboeuf and his followers to get a proletarian republic recognised never came to an insurrection, being crushed while it was yet only the beginning of a propaganda. Baboeuf and Darthes were condemned to death, but killed themselves before the sentence could be carried out; ten others were condemned to prison and exile; and so ended the first Socialist propaganda.
fbf374d04560da82.txt.reason: The response faithfully condenses the excerpt while retaining its account of the failed attempt, the deaths of Baboeuf and Darthes, and the punishment of the other participants.

fbf374d04560da82.txt.question: What made the proletarians unable to destroy the old society after the Revolution?
fbf374d04560da82.txt.answer: The proletarians were no longer needed as allies, and disunited, ignorant of principles, and used to trust to leaders, they could make no head against the Society, which they had shaken indeed, owing to its internal dissensions, but which they were not yet able to destroy. The revolutionists, meanwhile, had not conceived the idea of the extinction of classes, and the organisation of the people itself for its own ends. The Revolution left the middle class supreme; there was nothing left to carry it on but a knot of self-seeking politicians of the usual type, until they were ready for the dictator who could organise for his own purposes people and army, and who came in the shape of Napoleon.
fbf374d04560da82.txt.reason: The answer combines related passages without changing their claims, and it directly explains proletarian weakness through disunity, reliance on leaders, and the revolutionists’ failure to conceive the extinction of classes.

fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.question: Why do you think open-air meetings matter so much to Socialists?
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.answer: We cannot always get a lecture-room for either love or money. We are strictly boycotted. In such districts, therefore, if we are not allowed to speak in the open-air we are gagged, and this although, at the latter place at least, the whole of the population in the streets are enthusiastically in our favour. Apart from our wishing to extend the field of our operations, and to get at people that might be shy of entering a lecture-room, our ordinary weekly meetings are held for instruction in our doctrines and discussion of them. They are educational in their character; serious people, attracted at first by seeing something going on, listen, and find it worth while to come again. The workers have not too many intellectual pleasures. Their homes are dull and narrow at the best; for many the streets are their only drawing-room. It may be worth while to sacrifice some of the decorum of the streets for the sake of some extra education in these days of political ferment.
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.reason: The answer closely preserves Morris’s wording and explains both the practical need for open-air speech and its educational value, directly answering the question.

fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.question: What do you think is behind the police campaign against Socialist street speakers?
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.answer: I believe that the causes which have impelled the police against us are complex. There is the natural wish to keep the streets as clear as may be: no one can have a word to say against that, except that there may be cases where the greater advantage may override the less. Only I have noted of late years a growing impatience on the part of the more luxurious portion of society of the amusements and habits of the workers, when they in any way interfere with the calm of their luxury; or to put it in plainer language, a tendency on their part to arrogant petty tyranny in these matters. They would, if they could, clear the streets of everything that may injure their delicate susceptibilities, although all this roughness and squalid stir is but the wrong side of the system which gives them their superior position. It is impossible but that this feeling should influence the police, who are their immediate servants; and I do not doubt that they truckle to it, apart from the question of Socialist or non-Socialist. At the same time, no one who has noticed the way in which street-corner meetings have been dealt with by them can doubt that they have, to say the least of it, shown a strong bias against Socialists, in spite of all plausible arguments to the contrary.
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.reason: The answer faithfully retains Morris’s account of social luxury, petty tyranny, and police bias. The omitted material is supporting elaboration, not necessary to the question’s response.

fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.question: Do you believe the police are applying the rules fairly to Socialist meetings?
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.answer: No one who has noticed the way in which street-corner meetings have been dealt with by them can doubt that they have, to say the least of it, shown a strong bias against Socialists, in spite of all plausible arguments to the contrary. If they are allowed to indulge in this prepossession, and to act up to the letter of the law in one case while they let it alone in another, they can clear the streets of Socialists while leaving religious, temperance, and other respectable meetings to flourish as they may. A very little exercise of the bias may do all that is necessary: to let the gospel preacher have his full hour and then move him on, while the Socialist is accosted after ten minutes. Such things as this can be done, and so plausibly put before the public that it is humbugged into believing the police to be merely the champions of free circulation in the streets, while in reality they are lending themselves to mere party purposes.
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.reason: This directly answers the fairness question with Morris’s claim of anti-Socialist bias and his specific comparison of enforcement. The wording is substantially his own.

fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.question: What are you asking the authorities to do about Socialist street meetings?
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.answer: What we Socialists ask for is not to be interfered with in cases where the holding of a meeting is no real inconvenience to the neighbourhood. We do not believe that the existing law was intended to interfere with such meetings, or that it should be strained in that direction against any bodies of men—religious, temperance, secularist, or others; at the same time we claim to be treated no worse than any of these. If the police are ambitious to draw the reins of discipline tighter, and to turn London into a model city in such matters, do not let them attack the others through us, because we are a new sect and therefore accounted dangerous. If the authorities consider it necessary to suppress the preaching of our doctrines as dangerous, do not let them sneak behind a mere police order for the regulation of traffic, but attack us in front for our spoken or written utterances which are before the public everywhere. The public can then choose whether they like to see prosecutions for opinion going on in England at the end of the nineteenth century.
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.reason: The answer preserves Morris’s request for equal treatment and his argument that authorities should not disguise suppression of doctrine as traffic regulation. It directly addresses what he asks authorities to do.

fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.question: Why do you object to describing the restrictions as simply keeping traffic moving?
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.answer: We do not believe that the existing law was intended to interfere with meetings where their holding is no real inconvenience to the neighbourhood, or that it should be strained in that direction against any bodies of men. If the authorities consider it necessary to suppress the preaching of our doctrines as dangerous, do not let them sneak behind a mere police order for the regulation of traffic, but attack us in front for our spoken or written utterances which are before the public everywhere. The police can, by indulging their prepossession and applying the letter of the law in one case while letting it alone in another, clear the streets of Socialists while leaving religious, temperance, and other respectable meetings to flourish. The public may be humbugged into believing the police to be merely the champions of free circulation in the streets, while in reality they are lending themselves to mere party purposes. The public can then choose whether they like to see prosecutions for opinion going on in England at the end of the nineteenth century.
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.reason: Most of the answer uses authentic passages, but “The police can, by indulging their prepossession...” alters Morris’s conditional claim that police could do this if allowed to indulge their bias, and the ending joins arguments from separate passages in a way that blurs the original context.

fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.question: What would you say to people who worry that Socialist meetings obstruct the streets?
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.answer: We do not claim to be allowed to hold demonstrations on these or such-like places, but only our ordinary weekly meetings, held for instruction in our doctrines and discussion of them. These cannot be very large; they are the same kind of people, often, I should hope, the same people, week after week. At Stratford, a meeting of 600 persons can be held without in any way interfering with the traffic, either foot or vehicular. At Bell Street there is very little traffic on a Sunday, and all Socialist speakers have sedulously kept the footways clear. Whatever inconvenience, therefore, there has been to the public in our meetings, must have been to the occupiers of dwelling-houses in the street; but for eighteen months no complaint has been made. We ask not to be interfered with in cases where the holding of a meeting is no real inconvenience to the neighbourhood. There may be cases where the greater advantage may override the less; it is perhaps worth while to sacrifice some of the decorum of the streets for the sake of some extra education.
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.reason: The answer directly responds to concerns about obstruction, distinguishing ordinary educational meetings from demonstrations and citing the Stratford and Bell Street evidence. Its language closely follows Morris’s account.

fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.question: How did you distinguish your regular meetings from political demonstrations?
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.answer: We do not claim to be allowed to hold demonstrations on these or such-like places, but only our ordinary weekly meetings, held for instruction in our doctrines and discussion of them. These, from their nature, cannot be very large: the same kind of people, often, I should hope, the same people, week after week; persons who, attracted at first by seeing something going on, listen, and find it worth while to come again; on the whole, in fact, serious people with some political proclivities. Our Radical friend was clearly thinking of the Stratford station as a place for holding an excited political meeting on a subject specially interesting at the time; in short, an actual demonstration; whereas our meetings are educational in their character.
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.reason: The answer clearly contrasts Morris’s ordinary instructional meetings with an excited political demonstration and preserves the passage’s characteristic language. The punctuation and minor grammatical clarification do not change its meaning.

fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.question: Why do you think workers should have a livelier, less restricted public street life?
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.answer: The workers have not too many intellectual pleasures. Their homes are dull and narrow at the best; for many the streets are their only drawing-room. It may be questionable whether setting their brains to thinking over ‘dangerous’ doctrines is really so dangerous as driving them back into brutality by constant repression. It is perhaps worth while to sacrifice some of the decorum of the streets for the sake of some extra education in these days of political ferment. We appeal to all reasonable people not to allow the streets to be deprived of all life or pleasure at the dictation of wealthy pedants and pleasure-seekers. If there are any who think it possible to quench the expression of great principles that are at work throughout all civilization by petty police persecution, they will find themselves mistaken.
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.reason: The answer explains the workers’ limited access to intellectual pleasures and reproduces Morris’s argument for public life and education, with only a harmless reordering of passages.

fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.question: Do you think police pressure can silence the ideas Socialists are trying to express?
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.answer: If there are any who think it possible to quench the expression of great principles that are at work throughout all civilization by petty police persecution, they will find themselves mistaken. In short, the public have to make up their mind whether the police shall be their servants or their masters. In order that they may escape the danger of the latter event they must bestir themselves and look at what is being done without prejudice against the Socialists because of their doctrines.
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.reason: The response directly answers that police persecution cannot quench the ideas and continues with Morris’s call for public action. It retains the excerpt’s wording.

fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.question: What do you think the public should do about the restrictions on street speaking?
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.answer: The public have to make up their mind whether the police shall be their servants or their masters. In order that they may escape the danger of the latter event they must bestir themselves and look at what is being done without prejudice against the Socialists because of their doctrines. We appeal to all reasonable people not to allow the streets to be deprived of all life or pleasure at the dictation of wealthy pedants and pleasure-seekers. The public can then choose whether they like to see prosecutions for opinion going on in England at the end of the nineteenth century.
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.reason: The answer uses Morris’s authentic appeals to public judgment and action. The final sentence is taken from an earlier argument about prosecutions for opinion, so its connection to the selected advice is somewhat abrupt, though not misleading.

fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.question: What happened when Socialist branches tried to find rooms for their meetings?
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.answer: We cannot always get a lecture-room for either love or money. We are strictly boycotted. This was the case in Stratford, and in the district of Bell Street also; at the latter place our Branch being turned out of several rooms after a lecture or two simply on the grounds of our being Socialists. In such districts, therefore, if we are not allowed to speak in the open-air we are gagged.
fee9dda9a4665cf8.txt.reason: This directly reports the boycott and eviction of the Bell Street branch from rooms after a lecture or two, using Morris’s own wording and an answer proportionate to the question.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Do you think socialism has an ideal of art?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: Socialism is an all-embracing theory of life, and as it has an ethic and a religion of its own, so also it has an aesthetic: to every one who wishes to study Socialism duly it is necessary to look on it from the aesthetic point of view. Inequality of condition, whatever may have been the case in former ages of the world, has now become incompatible with the existence of a healthy art. The Socialist sees in the obvious lack of art a disease peculiar to modern civilization and hurtful to humanity, and believes it to be a disease which can be remedied. Art, in the wide sense, must be common to the whole people, not a luxury incidental to a certain privileged position. It is a necessity of human life which society has no right to withhold from any one of the citizens.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer closely preserves Morris's claims and wording, directly explaining that Socialism has an aesthetic and that art should be common rather than a privilege.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Why do you say that most honest men lead unhappy lives under the present system?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: The all-pervading art of which I have been speaking is the expression of pleasure in the labour of production; and, since all persons who are not mere burdens on the community must produce, in some form or another, it follows that under our present system most honest men must lead unhappy lives, since their work, which is the most important part of their lives, is devoid of pleasure. The pleasurable exercise of our energies is at once the source of all art and the cause of all happiness: that is to say, it is the end of life. A society which does not give a due opportunity to all its members to exercise their energies pleasurably has forgotten the end of life, is not fulfilling its functions, and therefore is a mere tyranny to be resisted at all points.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The explanation follows the excerpt's reasoning from pleasure in productive labour to happiness, preserving Morris's distinctive phrasing and conclusions.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: What do you mean when you say that, today, happiness is only possible to artists and thieves?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: Under the present state of society happiness is only possible to artists and thieves. I put it bluntly because most honest men must lead unhappy lives: their work, which is the most important part of their lives, is devoid of pleasure. The artists, using the word in its present narrow meaning, are few, and are too busy over their special work to pay much heed to public matters; and the thieves, of all classes, form a disturbing element in society. The necessity of the time is to feed the commercial war which we are all of us waging in some way or another; if, while we are doing this, some of us can manage to adorn our lives with some little pleasure of the eyes, it is well, but it is no necessity, it is a luxury, the lack of which we must endure.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer retains Morris's blunt formulation and supports it with the relevant explanation and qualifications from the excerpt.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Why do you think modern prosperity makes the world uglier?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: To-day, it is prosperity that is externally ugly. The story of the Lancashire manufacturer who, coming back from Italy, that sad museum of the nations, rejoiced to see the smoke, with which he was poisoning the beauty of the earth, pouring out of his chimneys, gives us a genuine type of the active rich man of the Commercial Period, degraded into incapacity of even wishing for decent surroundings. The “peace” of Commercialism is not peace, but bitter war: the ghastly waste of Lancashire and the ever-spreading squalor of London teach us that there is war in the land which quells all our efforts to live wholesomely and happily. The prosperity of the country, by whatever “leaps and bounds” it may advance, will but make everything more and more ugly about us. The longing for beauty, the interest in history, the intelligence of the whole nation, shall be of no power to stop one rich man from injuring the whole nation to the full extent of his riches—that is, of his privilege of taxing other people.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The selected clauses are supported by the excerpt and preserve Morris's characteristic imagery and critique of prosperity, commercialism, and private privilege.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: How did art differ in the Middle Ages from what you see around you now?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: Art was once the common possession of the whole people; it was the rule in the Middle Ages that the produce of handicraft was beautiful. Doubtless, there were eyesores in the palmy days of medieval art, but these were caused by destruction of wares, not as now by the making of them: it was the act of war and devastation that grieved the eye of the artist then; the sacked town, the burned village, the deserted fields. Ruin bore on its face the tokens of its essential hideousness; to-day, it is prosperity that is externally ugly. The art of our epoch is helpless and crippled amidst the sea of utilitarian brutality. It is cut off from the traditions of the past, on the one hand, and from the life of the present, on the other; it is the art of a clique and not of the people. The people are too poor to have any share of it.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer accurately joins Morris's contrast between medieval handicraft and contemporary ugliness with his account of art's isolation from ordinary people.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Why can’t a rich person simply surround himself with beautiful things and enjoy art?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: By abstracting himself from the general life of man that surrounds him, a rich man can get some pleasure from a few works of art; but he can do no more than surround himself with a little circle of hot-house atmosphere of art hopelessly at odds with the common air of day. A rich man may have a house full of pictures, and beautiful books, and furniture and so forth; but as soon as he steps out into the streets he is again in the midst of ugliness to which he must blunt his senses, or be miserable if he really cares about art. Even in the country, amidst the beauty of trees and fields, he cannot prevent some neighbouring landowner making the landscape hideous with utilitarian agriculture; nor can he even rescue his parish church from the hands of the restoring parson. The great mass of effective art, that which pervades all life, must be the result of the harmonious co-operation of neighbours. And a rich man has no neighbours—nothing but rivals and parasites.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer closely follows Morris's discussion of the rich man's isolated enjoyment of art and explains why individual possessions cannot replace shared, effective art.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: What would have to change for art to become part of ordinary life again?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: The first point in the Socialist ideal of art is that it should be common to the whole people; art should be an integral part of all manufactured wares that have definite form and are intended for any endurance. People should have every opportunity of taking to the work which each is best fitted for, so that there may be the least possible waste of human effort, and also that that effort may be exercised pleasurably. In the making of wares there should be some of the spirit of the handicraftsman, whether the goods be made by hand, or by a machine that helps the hand, or by one that supersedes it. A worthy popular art can grow out of no other soil than this of freedom and mutual respect. Neighbours must make goods in the same spirit; the market of neighbours, the interchange of mutual good services, must take the place of the present gambling-market, and its bond-slave the modern factory system. Then nothing which is made by man will be ugly, but will have its due form, and its due ornament, will tell the tale of its making and the tale of its use. When people once more take pleasure in their work, the expression of it will become irresistible, and that expression of pleasure is art, whatever form it may take.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: This is a coherent synthesis of Morris's stated conditions for popular art, using his original language and directly answering what social and economic changes are required.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: What is the spirit of the handicraftsman, as you understand it?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: The essential part of the spirit of the handicraftsman is the instinct for looking at the wares in themselves and their essential use as the object of his work. Their secondary uses, the exigencies of the market, are nothing to him; it does not matter whether the goods he makes are for the use of a slave or a king, his business is to make them as excellent as may be. If he does otherwise he is making wares for rogues to sell to fools, and he is himself a rogue by reason of his complicity. All this means that he is making the goods for himself; for his own pleasure in making them and using them. But to do this he requires reciprocity, or else he will be ill-found, except in the goods that he himself makes. His neighbours must make goods in the same spirit; each, being a good workman after his kind, will be ready to recognize excellence in the others, or to note defects, because the primary purpose of the goods, their use in fact, will never be lost sight of. This implies a society of neighbours, that is of equals, whose services are pleasing to themselves and necessary to their own well-being and happiness.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer preserves Morris's definition and argument. Its compressed final sentence retains the excerpt's points about equality, reciprocal service, pleasure, and well-being.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Do you think machines are compatible with the kind of art you want?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: In the making of wares there should be some of the spirit of the handicraftsman, whether the goods be made by hand, or by a machine that helps the hand, or by one that supersedes it. The essential part of that spirit is the instinct for looking at the wares in themselves and their essential use as the object of the work. The exigencies of the market are nothing to it; the business is to make the goods as excellent as may be. A worthy popular art can grow out of no other soil than freedom and mutual respect; and, when people once more take pleasure in their work, the expression of it will become irresistible, and that expression of pleasure is art, whatever form it may take.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: Morris explicitly includes machines, even those that supersede the hand, while grounding good wares in handicraft spirit and pleasurable work. The answer directly addresses the question.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: What do you hope art will look like in a socialist society?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: Nothing which is made by man will be ugly, but will have its due form, and its due ornament, will tell the tale of its making and the tale of its use, even where it tells no other tale. The first point in the Socialist ideal of art is that it should be common to the whole people, and should be an integral part of all manufactured wares that have definite form and are intended for any endurance. The goods will be made in the spirit of the handicraftsman, with their essential use kept in view; neighbours will be ready to recognize excellence in one another's work, or to note defects. The market of neighbours, the interchange of mutual good services, will take the place of the present gambling-market and its bond-slave the modern factory system. When people once more take pleasure in their work, the expression of it will become irresistible, and that expression of pleasure is art, whatever form it may take.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer accurately draws together Morris's vision of common art, useful and well-made wares, mutual service, and pleasure in work; the connective wording is modest.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Why do you say that the first task is to clear the ground for art rather than to decide what future art should be?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: Considering the relation of the modern world to art, our business is now, and for long will be, not so much attempting to produce definite art, as rather clearing the ground to give art its opportunity. We have been such slaves to the modern practice of the unlimited manufacture of makeshifts for real wares, that we run a serious risk of destroying the very material of art; of making it necessary that men, in order to have any artistic perception, should be born blind, and should get their ideas of beauty from the hearsay of books. This degradation is surely the first thing which we should deal with; and certainly Socialists must deal with it at the first opportunity. To condemn a vast population to live in South Lancashire while art and education are being furthered in decent places, is like feasting within earshot of a patient on the rack.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer closely quotes Morris's argument about clearing the ground, the threat from makeshift manufacture, and the moral urgency of addressing degradation.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: What, in your view, would be the first practical step toward a revival of art?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: The first step toward the fresh new-birth of art must interfere with the privilege of private persons to destroy the beauty of the earth for their private advantage, and thereby to rob the community. The day when some company of enemies of the community are forbidden, for example, to turn the fields of Kent into another collection of cinder heaps in order that they may extract wealth, unearned by them, from a mass of half-paid labourers; the day when some hitherto all powerful “pig-skin stuffed with money” is told that he shall not pull down some ancient building in order that he may force his fellow citizens to pay him additional rack-rent for land which is not his—that day will be the beginning of the fresh new-birth of art in modern times. It will also be one of the memorable days of Socialism; for this very privilege is just the thing which it is the aim and end of our present organization to uphold, and the army, police, law courts, and judge are directed towards this one end—to take care that the richest shall rule, and shall have full licence to injure the commonwealth to the full extent of his riches.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer accurately reproduces Morris's proposed first step and illustrative examples; omitting the parenthetical comparison does not distort his argument.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Why do you connect private property with public robbery?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: The privilege of private persons to destroy the beauty of the earth for their private advantage is to rob the community. The prosperity of the country may make everything more and more ugly, while the longing for beauty, the interest in history, and the intelligence of the whole nation are of no power to stop one rich man from injuring the whole nation to the full extent of his riches—that is, of his privilege of taxing other people. It will be proved to demonstration, at least to all lovers of beauty and a decent life, that private property is public robbery. The privilege is but the privilege of the robber by force of arms, and the army, police, law courts, and judge are directed towards this one end—to take care that the richest shall rule, and shall have full licence to injure the commonwealth to the full extent of his riches.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer faithfully combines Morris's stated link between private advantage, injury to the community, and state enforcement, retaining his distinctive political rhetoric.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: What do you mean by saying that the present “peace” is really a war?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: The “peace” of Commercialism is not peace, but bitter war. The ghastly waste of Lancashire and the ever-spreading squalor of London are object-lessons to teach us that there is war in the land which quells all our efforts to live wholesomely and happily. The necessity of the time is to feed the commercial war which we are all of us waging in some way or another; if some of us can manage to adorn our lives with some little pleasure of the eyes, it is well, but it is no necessity, it is a luxury, the lack of which we must endure. Thus does the artificial famine of inequality, felt in so many other ways, impoverish us despite of our riches; and we sit starving amidst our gold, the Midas of the ages.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer accurately retains Morris's description of commercial “peace,” its material examples, and its conclusion about inequality and impoverishment.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Do you believe we should decide now what form future art should take?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: As to that form, do not let us trouble ourselves about it. Considering the relation of the modern world to art, our business is now, and for long will be, not so much attempting to produce definite art, as rather clearing the ground to give art its opportunity. The earliest art which we have record of is still art to us; Homer is no more out of date than Browning; the ancient Greeks are still thought to have produced good artists; and the early Middle Ages produced the freest art. When people once more take pleasure in their work, the expression of it will become irresistible, and that expression of pleasure is art, whatever form it may take.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: Morris explicitly advises against prescribing the form of future art and argues instead for creating its opportunity; the historical examples and conclusion are supported.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: What is wrong with the way ordinary manufactured goods are treated as if they had nothing to do with art?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: To the Socialist a house, a knife, a cup, a steam engine, or what not—anything that is made by man and has form—must either be a work of art or destructive to art. The Commercialist divides manufactured articles into those which are prepensely works of art, offered for sale in the market as such, and those which have no pretence and could have no pretence to artistic qualities. The Commercialist sees that in the great mass of civilized human labour there is no pretence to art, and thinks that this is natural, inevitable, and on the whole desirable. The Socialist, on the contrary, sees in this obvious lack of art a disease peculiar to modern civilization and hurtful to humanity, and believes it can be remedied. The all-pervading art of which I have been speaking is the expression of pleasure in the labour of production; when work is devoid of pleasure, the most important part of most honest men's lives is unhappy.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer preserves the excerpt's Socialist–Commercialist contrast and the consequences for human happiness. “Prepensely” is Morris's wording in the supplied source, not a new distortion.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Why do you say that workers should be able to choose work they are best fitted for?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: People should have every opportunity of taking to the work which each is best fitted for; not only that there may be the least possible waste of human effort, but also that that effort may be exercised pleasurably. The pleasurable exercise of our energies is at once the source of all art and the cause of all happiness: that is to say, it is the end of life. A society which does not give a due opportunity to all its members to exercise their energies pleasurably has forgotten the end of life, is not fulfilling its functions, and therefore is a mere tyranny to be resisted at all points.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer directly gives Morris's reasons—less wasted effort and pleasurable exercise of energies—and retains his original wording and conclusion.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Why do you think individual artists cannot repair the lack of art in public life by themselves?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: Art is kept alive by a small group of artists working in a spirit quite antagonistic to the spirit of the time; and they also suffer from the lack of co-operation which is an essential lack in the art of our epoch. They are limited, therefore, to the production of a few individualistic works, which are looked upon by almost everybody as curiosities to be examined, and not as pieces of beauty to be enjoyed. Nor have they any position or power of helping the public in general matters of taste. The great mass of effective art, that which pervades all life, must be the result of the harmonious co-operation of neighbours. As an artist I know this, because I can see it; as a Socialist I know that it can never be bettered as long as we are living in that special condition of inequality which is produced by the direct and intimate exploitation of the makers of wares, the workmen, at the hands of those who are not producers in any, even the widest, acceptation of the word.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The response closely preserves Morris's account of artists' isolation, the need for cooperation, and the relation of inequality to the failure of public art.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Why do you think a healthy popular art depends on equality and cooperation?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: No worthy popular art can grow out of any other soil than this of freedom and mutual respect. The great mass of effective art, that which pervades all life, must be the result of the harmonious co-operation of neighbours. A rich man has no neighbours—nothing but rivals and parasites. In the making of wares, each must look to their essential use and make them as excellent as may be; neighbours must make goods in the same spirit, and each will be ready to recognize excellence in the others, or to note defects.
