This unforced and instinctive reciprocity of service implies a society of neighbours, that is of equals, who expect to be made use of by others only so far as the services they give are pleasing to themselves, and necessary to their own well-being and happiness.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The synthesis accurately reflects Morris's account of popular art, cooperation, and equal neighbours. The opening asks about equality and cooperation, which the answer addresses through freedom, mutual respect, and reciprocity.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Why do you object to art being treated as a luxury for the rich?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: The Socialist claims art as a necessity of human life which society has no right to withhold from any one of the citizens. Art should be common to the whole people and an integral part of all manufactured wares that have definite form and are intended for any endurance. At present art is only enjoyed, or indeed thought of, by comparatively a few persons, broadly speaking, by the rich and the parasites that minister to them directly. The poor can only afford to have what art is given to them in charity, of the inferior quality inherent in all such gifts—not worth picking up except by starving people. The people are too poor to have any share of art, though they make almost the whole mass of things that have form. To keep art as a luxury incidental to a privileged position is therefore to withhold a necessity of human life from the many.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer combines supported passages and Morris's argument that art is a necessity, not a privilege. The closing sentence restates that argument rather than introducing a new claim.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: What do you see as the harm caused by the modern factory system and the gambling-market?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: The market of neighbours, the interchange of mutual good services, should take the place of the present gambling-market, and its bond-slave the modern factory system. Under the present system, most honest men must lead unhappy lives, since their work, which is the most important part of their lives, is devoid of pleasure. The all-pervading art of which I have been speaking is the expression of pleasure in the labour of production; when work is without that pleasure, the common life is deprived of art and happiness. The modern practice of the unlimited manufacture of makeshifts for real wares also runs a serious risk of destroying the very material of art.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: Most claims are supported, but the answer adds “when work is without that pleasure, the common life is deprived of art and happiness,” a broad causal summary not stated in the excerpt. The other quoted claims do not fully explain the specific harms caused by the factory system and market.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: What does art have to do with the way things are made?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: Art is the expression of pleasure in the labour of production. Anything that is made by man and has form must either be a work of art or destructive to art. The spirit of the handicraftsman is the instinct for looking at the wares in themselves and their essential use as the object of his work; his business is to make them as excellent as may be. When people once more take pleasure in their work, the expression of it will become irresistible, and that expression of pleasure is art, whatever form it may take. The goods will have their due form, and their due ornament, and will tell the tale of their making and the tale of their use.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer gives Morris's definition of art and links it to the purpose, quality, and expressive form of wares, using language supported by the excerpt.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: What do you mean when you say that art should tell the tale of a thing’s making and use?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: Nothing which is made by man will be ugly, but will have its due form, and its due ornament, will tell the tale of its making and the tale of its use, even where it tells no other tale. The primary purpose of the goods, their use in fact, will never be lost sight of; the handicraftsman's business is to make them as excellent as may be. When people once more take pleasure in their work, the expression of it will become irresistible, and that expression of pleasure is art, whatever form it may take.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer accurately assembles Morris's claims about use, craftsmanship, form, and pleasurable labour. It explains the statement, though it mostly repeats rather than interprets the phrase.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Why do you think the poor have so little share in art?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: The poor can only afford to have what art is given to them in charity; which is of the inferior quality inherent in all such gifts—not worth picking up except by starving people. The people are too poor to have any share of art, though they make almost the whole mass of those that make anything that has form. At present art is only enjoyed, or indeed thought of, by comparatively a few persons, broadly speaking, by the rich and the parasites that minister to them directly. The art of this epoch is the art of a clique and not of the people, because the people are too poor to have any share of it.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The answer faithfully draws on Morris's statements about charity, poverty, and art's confinement to a clique. It repeats the poverty conclusion, but the response remains clear and relevant.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: What do you think the role of artists should be in public decisions about beauty?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: Artists ought to have a position or power of helping the public in general matters of taste. In laying out parks and pleasure grounds acquired for the public, they ought to have been consulted; they ought to have been laid out by a committee of artists. Even a badly chosen committee, and it might easily be well chosen, would have saved the public from most of the disasters which have resulted from handing them over to the tender mercies of the landscape gardener.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The recommendation and park example are supported by the excerpt. Recasting the impersonal criticism as a direct statement about artists' role is a minor, accurate adjustment.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: What does your Lancashire manufacturer story show about the rich and their surroundings?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: The story of the Lancashire manufacturer who, coming back from Italy, that sad museum of the nations, rejoiced to see the smoke, with which he was poisoning the beauty of the earth, pouring out of his chimneys, gives us a genuine type of the active rich man of the Commercial Period, degraded into incapacity of even wishing for decent surroundings. It shows how the pursuit of prosperity can injure the beauty of the earth, and how the longing for beauty and the intelligence of the whole nation may be of no power to stop one rich man from injuring the whole nation to the full extent of his riches.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The manufacturer's story is Morris's, and the summary is consistent with the immediately following passage. The answer's inference about prosperity is a reasonable condensation of the supported argument.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Why do you think merely having money cannot protect someone who cares about art?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: A rich man may have a house full of pictures, and beautiful books, and furniture and so forth; but as soon as he steps out into the streets he is again in the midst of ugliness to which he must blunt his senses, or be miserable if he really cares about art. Even when he is in the country, amidst the beauty of trees and fields, he cannot prevent some neighbouring landowner making the landscape hideous with utilitarian agriculture; he cannot even rescue his parish church from the hands of the restoring parson. He can go where he likes and do what he likes outside the realm of art, but there he is helpless. The great mass of effective art, that which pervades all life, must be the result of the harmonious co-operation of neighbours.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The examples and explanation closely follow the excerpt, directly showing why private wealth cannot overcome the ugliness of shared surroundings or replace collective art.

ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.question: Why do you think the present lack of art is a social problem rather than just an artistic one?
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.answer: The obvious lack of art is a disease peculiar to modern civilization and hurtful to humanity. It is no trifling matter, but a grievous deduction from the happiness of man: the all-pervading art of which I have been speaking is the expression of pleasure in the labour of production, and since all persons who are not mere burdens on the community must produce, it follows that under our present system most honest men must lead unhappy lives, since their work, which is the most important part of their lives, is devoid of pleasure. Art is also cut off from the life of the present; it cannot perform the most necessary functions, and the people are too poor to have any share of it. It is therefore a disease and injury to humanity, and a deduction from the happiness of man, not merely a matter for the few artists.
ff1e9a1cca91879a.txt.reason: The main argument is well grounded, but the final phrase “not merely a matter for the few artists” is an added inference, and the answer combines clauses in a way that blurs Morris's distinction between the lack of art and its effects on labour and happiness.
